lessons.lessonTitle: Global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes

lessonKeywords.description: the point on Earth's surface that is directly above where an earthquake happens underground
a measure of the energy released by an earthquake
the boundary where tectonic plates meet
an area in Earth's mantle where unusually hot magma rises toward the surface, creating volcanic activity

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There is a pattern in the global distribution of earthquakes.
There is a pattern in the global distribution of volcanoes.
The global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes coincides with plate margins.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While earthquakes are produced by tectonic movements at all plate margins, volcanoes are not found at conservative plate margins.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That both volcanoes and earthquakes occur at all types of plate margin.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how most earthquakes and volcanoes are located at plate margins.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson uses AQA terminology for plate margins; for Edexcel B plate boundaries are used instead of plate margins, destructive margins are convergent boundaries and constructive margins are divergent boundaries.

lessons.lessonTitle: Examples of management of volcanic hazards

lessonKeywords.description: the likelihood or chance of being affected by a natural hazard, such as an earthquake or volcanic eruption
techniques used to reduce hazard risk, including short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Management can reduce the impacts of volcanic hazards.
Management involves short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction.
Volcanic hazards may be managed differently at contrasting locations.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: People in developing countries have expert understanding of volcanic hazards and local communities are fully aware of hazards. Management problems are often due to lack of resources for effective prediction, preparation and relief.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: People in developing countries are less prepared because they lack understanding of volcanic hazards.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how volcanoes are managed differently at contrasting locations.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There are amazing drone videos of the 2024 eruptions in Iceland available on YouTube and expert information on the Icelandic Met Office website. Reminder: although Oak has resourced both, students study *either* volcanic hazards *or* earthquake hazards for this part of the Edexcel B specification.

lessonKeywords.description: techniques used to reduce hazard risk, including short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Management can reduce the impacts of earthquake hazards.
Management involves short-term relief and long-term planning, preparation and prediction.
Earthquake hazards may be managed differently at contrasting locations.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Japan had invested in a tsunami warning system, but due to how close the epicentre was, there were only 30 minutes before tsunami waves arrived, meaning that not everyone was evacuated safely. The height of the tsunami was not accurately predicted.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Japan’s tsunami evacuation failed because it had not invested in a tsunami warning system.

lessons.lessonTitle: Reducing risks from earthquakes and volcanoes

lessonKeywords.description: the likelihood or chance of being affected by a natural hazard, such as an earthquake or volcanic eruption
techniques used to reduce hazard risk, including monitoring and prediction and planning and preparation
techniques used to detect and record indicators of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: People continue to live in areas at risk from a tectonic hazard.
Monitoring and prediction can reduce the risks from a tectonic hazard.
Protection and planning can reduce the risks from a tectonic hazard.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While scientists can identify areas that are at high risk of earthquakes, exact predictions for when and where an earthquake will occur (or what magnitude it will be) are not possible.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Because we know the location of plate margins, scientists can predict when earthquakes will happen.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain why people continue to live in areas at risk from tectonic hazards and how management can reduce the effects of a tectonic hazard.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use real-world case studies to show how simple measures - like evacuation plans and building design- make a massive difference in disaster outcomes.

lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: the downhill movement of material under the influence of gravity
the process of being worn down due to long exposure to the atmosphere
erosion is the process of Earth’s surface, e.g. rock or soil, being worn away and transported from its original site

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mass movement is the downhill movement of sediment under the influence of gravity.
The main types of mass movement are rockfall, sliding, and slumping.
Slumping is common on coastlines.
Weathering and erosion lead to mass movement when combined with wet weather conditions.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Mass movement can happen anywhere there are slopes, even in places with mild weather conditions. While extreme weather can trigger events, even light rainfall can cause mass movement if the slope is steep or the material is already weathered.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Students may believe that mass movement only occurs in mountainous areas or during extreme weather events.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand mass movement and know how gravity causes sediments to move downhill.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use real-life examples, such as famous coastal cliffs or landslide events, to make the topic more relatable. Show videos to highlight the dramatic effects of mass movement, and consider using physical demonstrations (e.g., using sand and water to simulate a mudflow) te exemplify.

lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: the loose upper layer of Earth’s surface where plants grow (formed of minerals, organic matter, air and water)
the process of Earth’s surface, e.g. rock or soil, being worn away and transported from its original site
something that absorbs and holds carbon
the process by which Earth’s surface is worn down due to exposure to the atmosphere

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Soil is made up of minerals, dead plants and animals, water and living organisms.
Soil takes hundreds of years to form.
There are three main particle sizes in soil, clay, sand and silt.
Soil is important for farming; infertile soil can make growing crops very difficult.
Soil is an important carbon store and protecting it can help us reduce global warming.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Soil is a complex and vital resource made of minerals, organic matter, water, and living organisms. It is important for growing food, storing carbon, and maintaining ecosystems. Without healthy soil, agriculture and natural habitats wouldn't survive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Soil is just dirt.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain what soil is made of, how it forms, and understand its importance.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could use different types of chocolate to represent different soil: dark chocolate chunks represent rocky soil, white chocolate shavings can represent sandy soil, which is light and crumbly, milk chocolate fudge can represent clay soil, which is sticky and holds moisture well.

lessonKeywords.description: a piece of data that does not seem to fit the trend shown by all the other pieces of data
data that is able to answer or partially answer an enquiry question
data that could be replicated if the data collection were to be repeated

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Analyses of data can sometimes reveal data that does not seem to fit with the general pattern.
Geographers should try to find explanations for anomalous data.
Geographers look for evidence that their data is both valid and reliable.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Geographers will always try to find explanations for data that does not fit the general trend before they dismiss it as being caused by human error during the data collection stage.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Anomalous data can be ignored in the data analysis stage as it is due to human error in the data collection stage.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can analyse and reflect on my soil data to create meaningful conclusions and an evaluation.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Listing the geographical variables that were not measured in the data collection stage can be a good way of helping students to formulate sensible reasons for anomalies.

lessonKeywords.description: the timeline of Earth’s history
the largest division of geological time, lasting hundreds of millions to billions of years
a subdivision of an eon, lasting tens to hundreds of millions of years
a subdivision of an era, lasting millions of years
the smallest measurement of geological time, a subdivision of a period, lasting thousands to millions of years

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Geological timescales are measured in millions of years.
A period is a basic unit of geological time and they last for millions of years.
An epoch is a subdivision of a geological time period.
We are currently in the quaternary period in the holocene epoch.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Geological timescales are much greater than human history.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Geological timescales go back as far as human history.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how geological time is divided, and identify the current period and epoch we live in.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could teach students to remember the order of the older geological time divisions with the mnemonic:  Camels, Often, Sit, Down, Carefully. Perhaps, Their, Joints, Creak.

lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: the solid mineral material forming part of the surface of Earth
a process is an ordered series of actions, events or changes that make something happen
pressure is a force pushing or pressing on a given area
the process of Earth’s surface, e.g. rock or soil, being worn away
The process of being worn down due to exposure to the atmosphere.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are three types of rock; igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.
Igneous rocks are volcanic rocks and examples include basalt, obsidian and granite.
Sedimentary rocks are formed from sediments and examples include sandstone, limestone and chalk.
Metamorphic rocks are formed through heat and pressure and examples include slate, gneiss and marble.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Students will explore the three main types of rock found on Earth, and understand how rocks are recycled through the rock cycle.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: There is only one type of rock, and rocks can't change.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify the three main types of rocks, and recognise how they are formed by different processes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could use rock samples or edible models (e.g. crumbled cookies for sedimentary rocks, melted chocolate for igneous rocks, and compressed marshmallows for metamorphic rocks) to help students understand the differences between the rock types and how they change over time.

lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: a hard sedimentary rock
deep cracks on the surface of limestone pavements
exposed blocks of limestone
a form of chemical weathering where rock is slowly dissolved by acidic water
flat, exposed area of limestone

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Limestone is a sedimentary rock made of calcium carbonate.
Grykes are deep cracks on the surface on limestone formed by chemical weathering.
Clints are exposed blocks of limestone separated by grykes.
Limestone landscapes include limestone pavements, such as Malham Cove, and limestone caves, such as Gough's Cave.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Students will be taught what clints and grykes are in relation to limestone.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Some students may think that grykes and clints are type of rock, rather than being a feature of limestone landscapes.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify the key features of limestone, and describe different limestone landscapes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: A helpful way to remember what clints and grykes are, is: clints are clumps, and grykes are gaps.

lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: data that can be split up into constituent parts
a graph with three axes used to display proportional data with three constituent parts
a symbol on a map or in a graph that shows a value of data by the size at which it has been drawn

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Data made up of three parts can be shown on a triangular graph.
Proportional shapes or symbols can be used to compare the size of data values.
All forms of data presentation need to conform to particular standards and use conventions to make them readable.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A pie chart is by far the most common method that geographers use, but any shape can be split into proportional sections.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Proportional data can only be presented using a pie chart.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can present soil texture data using creative techniques.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If you have access to a visualizer, use this to structure and plot the points on a triangular graph in real time. This tricky skill is often easier to comprehend when it is modelled to students.

First of all, proportional data.
This is data that can be split up into constituent parts.
A triangular graph is a graph with three axes and it's used to display proportional data with three constituent parts.
A proportional shape is a symbol on a map or on a graph, and that shows the value of data by the size at which it has been drawn.
There are two parts in this lesson.
We're first going to be looking at how we might present proportional data, and then we're going to be a bit more creative and a bit more experimental and look at some different ways of presenting our data as well.

The one we're interested in right now is this one at the end, the soil type, because this is proportional data.
It is made up of three parts: sand, silt, and clay, and we've presented it here as percentages.
Proportional data is often shown in a pie chart.
You can see an example of one right here from our data.
It's site two, our flower bed data.
Laura says, "From the pie chart I can estimate that 55% of the soil is sand, 35% is clay, and 10% is silt." She's using the key and she's estimating roughly what proportion of the soil falls into each of those three categories.
Pie charts are drawn so that the largest percentage starts at the 12 o'clock mark and each segment gets progressively smaller from there in a clockwise direction.
You can see in our example that sand has the highest percentage of our three constituent parts.
So it's the one that starts at 12 o'clock.
Clay is the next largest, so that comes next and silt is the smallest.
So that finishes off the circle To know the size of the different pie chart segments in degrees, we calculate the segment value divided by the total value times 360, because there's 360 degrees in a circle.
You can then use a protractor to draw each segment.
So in our example, sand made up 55% of the soil sample at site two.
So we do 55 divided by 100, that's our percentage, times the 360, and that's the degrees of the circle, and that comes out to 198 degrees.
So I use my protractor to draw my segment to 190 degrees from that 12 o'clock position.
Proportional data does not have to be drawn using a pie chart, though it is the most common way it is shown.
A percentage bar divides a bar into proportional segments.
So here we've taken the idea of pie chart, but we've turned it into an oblong.
It's a bar instead.

You can also use something called a waffle chart.
You might be able to guess why it's called that.
This is a 10 by 10 grid with each square in the grid representing 1%.

So if we've got 55% sand, we will be shading 55% of the squares or 55 of the 100 squares in the colour for sand, which in this case is the purple colour.

Pie charts are not the only way to present proportional data.

This means geographers often use a triangular graph to show this data.
The data is read off three different axis lines.
We've got the X-axis, in this case that's going to be the silt; the Y-axis, in this case that's the sand; and the Z-axis, and that's the clay.
Soils are plotted onto the graph according to their structure.

Different sites can be plotted on the same graph and this helps geographers to actually compare the sites.
Here, you can see we've got four pink dots representing the four sites in our own investigation.
Maybe it's not surprising that those four sites are actually fairly close to each other on the triangular graph.

Well done if you recognise that it is option C.
Let's just check it on the graph together as well.
So we're expecting our sand to be 10%.
You can see that's where it falls on that Y-axis.
Our silt should come in at 50%.
Yep, there it is on the X-axis.
And our clay is at 40% and there it is on the Z-axis.
Well done if you got that.

So do take your time and make sure that you're using those axes correctly to plot your sites.
Here's an example of the kind of thing that you might have produced.
You will have your four plots onto your graph and it's a good idea to actually have them in a recognisable colour so they really stand out from the graph.
So your graph might look a little bit like this.
But as well as doing the plots, we've also gotta make sure that our graph is readable and correct.
Here's what your answer should include.
You need to have a title.

You also need to make sure you've got units on each axis.

Present your data then using your chosen data presentation techniques.

lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: relating to living organisms
relating to the interaction of substances
the process of being worn down by long exposure to the atmosphere

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are three types of weathering; biological, chemical and physical weathering.
Biological weathering is when rocks are broken up by the roots of plants or from animals burrowing into them.
Chemical weathering is when rocks are broken up by acids in rainwater or when air reacts with minerals in the rocks.
Physical weathering is when rocks are broken up by changes in temperature, such as when ice forces apart cracks in rock.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Students will be informed that erosion is the process of Earth’s surface, e.g. rock or soil, being worn away and transported from its original site, whereas weathering is the process of wearing or being worn by long exposure to the atmosphere.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Weathering and erosion are the same process.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the different types of weathering.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If teaching this lesson in person, you could bring in small rock samples or use a visual demonstration to show how weathering works. For example, use sugar cubes to illustrate chemical weathering by dissolving them in vinegar or place wet sponges in a freezer to mimic freeze-thaw weathering.

lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: rocks formed from cooled magma/lava
rocks formed from layers of compressed sediment
rocks formed due to intense heat and pressure
the structure of Earth’s crust and how it was formed
how something is spread out over a geographical area

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The UK has a rich and varied geology with igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks present.
England's lowland geology is dominated by sedimentary rocks, such as limestone.
Scotland's geology is dominated by metamorphic rocks with areas of igenous rock.
In the past, Britain was close to a plate boundary, and there was volcanic activity.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The UK was once a volcanically active region due to its position near tectonic plate boundaries millions of years ago. Evidence of past volcanic activity includes: the Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland and the volcanic rocks in Snowdonia.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The UK doesn't experience volcanic activity today, so volcanoes are not important to the UK's geological history.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the formation and distribution of rocks in the UK, and understand how past tectonic activity shaped the landscape.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use real-world examples and physical rock samples (if available) to help students connect abstract geological concepts to evidence.

lessons.lessonTitle: GIS: Visualising the geology of the UK
lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: rocks formed through the build up of sediments such as sandstone, limestone and chalk
rocks formed through volcanic processes, such as basalt, obsidian and granite
rocks that have changed due to heat and pressure, such as slate, gneiss and marble

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Understanding the UK’s geology is important, especially for building, mining and managing our energy and water supplies.
The British Geological Survey is a government-funded organisation that studies the UK’s geology, resources, and hazards.
GIS can be used to show the south-east to north-west pattern in the UK’s geology.
The UK’s varied geology leads to contrasting landscapes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Although many rocks formed during the same geological period will be similar, volcanic processes may be creating rocks at the same time as sedimentary rocks are being created. These rocks will be very different and create contrasting landscapes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All rocks formed during the same geological period will be similar.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use GIS to visualise and analyse the UK's geology and the way this creates contrasting landscapes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You may choose to project your use of the Geography Visualiser rather than using the video modelling in the slide deck.

lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: mining is the process of digging into the ground to remove natural resources
the process of removing natural resources from near the surface
the way money in a particular area is made and spent
fossil fuels are natural substances that were formed over millions of years from the buried remains of ancient organisms; they include coal, oil and gas
the improvement in people's quality of life within a country or region

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mining provides valuable materials like fossil fuels, stone, and metals.
Rare earth metals are vital for modern tech like phones and green energy.
Oil and gas are found in underground reservoirs, beneath land or sea.
Oil and gas take millions of years to form.
Fossil fuels and minerals support economies through jobs and exports.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Fossil fuels take millions of years to form – much longer than a human lifetime. We can’t just “make” more. Once we use them up, they’re gone. That’s why we need to balance using them with finding cleaner, renewable alternatives.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: If we run out of oil, we can just make more.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain why geological resources are important to the economy, and where they come from.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson can be made relatable by linking it to the technology students use. You could bring in real-world objects (like a smartphone or battery) and ask students to guess what materials it contains.

lessons.lessonTitle: The impacts of using geological resources
lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: the process of removing natural resources from the ground
natural substances that were formed over millions of years from the buried remains of ancient organisms; they include coal, oil and gas
harmful substances released into the environment
when something is able to continue over a long time

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Geological resources bring money, jobs, and materials we rely on daily.
Extraction harms landscapes, wildlife, and sometimes local communities.
Mining and fossil fuels create jobs and support national economies.
Fossil fuels pollute and add to global warming despite economic value.
Sustainable alternatives are growing but aren't yet fully replacing fossil fuels.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While they can cause environmental harm, they also provide essential materials and economic benefits. The key is understanding both advantages and disadvantages—which is what geographers evaluate.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Geological resources are all bad because they damage the environment.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using geological resources and explain how they affect people and the environment.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to think critically by weighing up the pros and cons, rather than assuming that resources are purely good or bad.

lessons.lessonTitle: Fieldwork: Planning a soil enquiry and collecting data
lessons.unitTitle: Rocks, weathering and soil: Why is geology important?

lessonKeywords.description: characteristics of soil, such as how large the soil particles are, or how large the pores (spaces) between the particles are
how porous soil structure is (i.e. the size and quantity of spaces between soil particles)
the movement of water from the surface to the lower soil layers

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Soil texture can potentially affect the rate of water infiltration.
A fieldwork enquiry can be used to find the extent to which soil texture effects infiltration.
Geographers can use a combination of data collection techniques to investigate the characteristics of soil.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Soil that is made-up of small particles has a structure where the particles can fit together more easily reducing the pore size between them.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Large soil particles means there are smaller pores between them.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can collect soil texture data on my school site.

We need to formulate an inquiry question.

Following that is the conclusion.

Soil type is likely to have a strong influence on the speed at which water moves through it.
A soil made up of large particles, such as a sandy soil, will have high porosity.
In other words, it will have large pores between the particles.
This means that water can infiltrate more easily and quickly through the soil.
A soil made up of small particles, such as a clay soil, will have a low porosity, so there'll be very small pores in between the particles.
This means that water takes a lot longer to infiltrate through the soil.
It will start off on the surface and very slowly move through.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are global inequalities in development.
There are physical/environmental causes of global inequality.
There are economic causes of global inequality.
There are historical/political causes of inequality.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Physical geography is a cause of inequality but human factors, past and present, are as influential in affecting the pattern of trade and development.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That the physical environment is the key cause of global inequalities.

And here we've got a visualization of Zambia's exports

452
00:22:53.220 --> 00:22:57.270
for 2022 by value, where the different exports

453
00:22:57.270 --> 00:23:00.840
are drawn to scale as boxes to represent them.

454
00:23:00.840 --> 00:23:03.903
What do you notice? What is it mostly selling?

455
00:23:12.660 --> 00:23:14.970
Okay, so we can see that raw copper

456
00:23:14.970 --> 00:23:17.550
is really important to Zambia,

457
00:23:17.550 --> 00:23:20.910
creating 44.5% of the value.

458
00:23:20.910 --> 00:23:22.770
We also have refined copper,

459
00:23:22.770 --> 00:23:24.630
which means copper that's been processed

460
00:23:24.630 --> 00:23:28.170
to an extent, making up almost another 20%.

461
00:23:28.170 --> 00:23:32.313
And gold, also very valuable to Zambia as an export.

462
00:23:33.780 --> 00:23:36.120
Now, copper actually makes up more than 60%

463
00:23:36.120 --> 00:23:37.980
of the value of Zambia's exports,

464
00:23:37.980 --> 00:23:39.300
as we can see between the raw

465
00:23:39.300 --> 00:23:41.280
and the slightly processed material.

466
00:23:41.280 --> 00:23:45.960
So, what we've got there, what the UN term it as,

467
00:23:45.960 --> 00:23:49.860
is overdependence on a single export,

468
00:23:49.860 --> 00:23:52.110
meaning its economy is particularly vulnerable

469
00:23:52.110 --> 00:23:53.580
to fluctuations in price.

470
00:23:53.580 --> 00:23:56.040
And we have a graph there showing the change

471
00:23:56.040 --> 00:24:00.000
in the price of copper per ton over time.

472
00:24:00.000 --> 00:24:01.620
Now, if the price of copper falls,

473
00:24:01.620 --> 00:24:04.080
the overall value of Zambia's export

474
00:24:04.080 --> 00:24:06.060
decreases significantly,

475
00:24:06.060 --> 00:24:10.268
which means it has less money to pay for imports,

476
00:24:10.268 --> 00:24:12.240
which is going to be damaging

477
00:24:12.240 --> 00:24:14.043
to economic development, clearly.

478
00:24:15.900 --> 00:24:20.340
Price fluctuation can result in a trade surplus

479
00:24:20.340 --> 00:24:22.530
or a trade deficit.

480
00:24:22.530 --> 00:24:24.330
Okay, so the value of exports,

481
00:24:24.330 --> 00:24:26.100
if it's larger than the value of imports,

482
00:24:26.100 --> 00:24:28.980
that might lead to a trade surplus,

483
00:24:28.980 --> 00:24:30.840
which would be good for the government.

484
00:24:30.840 --> 00:24:34.020
However, as mentioned, if the value of imports

485
00:24:34.020 --> 00:24:36.060
is greater than the value of exports,

486
00:24:36.060 --> 00:24:39.540
as we've just seen, as perhaps the price of copper falls,

487
00:24:39.540 --> 00:24:41.550
then the government and the country

488
00:24:41.550 --> 00:24:44.760
finds itself in a situation of trade deficit.

489
00:24:44.760 --> 00:24:46.530
What's happened in Zambia, as we've seen,

490
00:24:46.530 --> 00:24:49.770
years of trade deficit led to the Zambia government

491
00:24:49.770 --> 00:24:52.020
borrowing money and landing the country

492
00:24:52.020 --> 00:24:53.223
in a lot of debt.

493
00:24:54.390 --> 00:24:56.130
That becomes a problem over time

494
00:24:56.130 --> 00:24:58.710
because debt really limits development.

495
00:24:58.710 --> 00:25:01.230
Zambia's lenders demanded interest on the debt,

496
00:25:01.230 --> 00:25:04.140
meaning it has less money for public services

497
00:25:04.140 --> 00:25:05.700
and that has a knock on impact

498
00:25:05.700 --> 00:25:08.100
on the people that live in the country, clearly.

499
00:25:10.260 --> 00:25:12.300
True or false? Quick check for you here.

500
00:25:12.300 --> 00:25:13.680
The problem with an economy

501
00:25:13.680 --> 00:25:16.110
that depends on a single commodity

502
00:25:16.110 --> 00:25:18.510
is that the global price can fluctuate.

503
00:25:18.510 --> 00:25:20.943
Is that true or false, and why?

504
00:25:26.160 --> 00:25:27.960
That's right, it's true.

505
00:25:27.960 --> 00:25:30.180
What was your explanation of why?

506
00:25:30.180 --> 00:25:31.083
We had,

507
00:25:32.430 --> 00:25:33.620
commodities fall in price

508
00:25:33.620 --> 00:25:35.520
if the supply is greater than the demand

509
00:25:35.520 --> 00:25:37.710
within the global market.

510
00:25:37.710 --> 00:25:39.480
Low income countries that export

511
00:25:39.480 --> 00:25:41.250
just a handful of different commodities

512
00:25:41.250 --> 00:25:44.670
risk losing money if their global price falls.

513
00:25:44.670 --> 00:25:47.880
I'm sure you had an answer like that, well done.

514
00:25:47.880 --> 00:25:49.440
True or false?

515
00:25:49.440 --> 00:25:51.810
If the value of imports,

516
00:25:51.810 --> 00:25:53.700
so that's goods coming into the country,

517
00:25:53.700 --> 00:25:56.250
is greater than the value of exports,

518
00:25:56.250 --> 00:25:59.190
then a country has a trade surplus.

519
00:25:59.190 --> 00:26:02.193
Is that true or false, and why?

520
00:26:07.650 --> 00:26:09.120
That's false.

521
00:26:09.120 --> 00:26:11.463
What was your explanation about why?

522
00:26:15.870 --> 00:26:18.150
So, value of imports, if that's greater

523
00:26:18.150 --> 00:26:19.530
than the value of exports,

524
00:26:19.530 --> 00:26:22.080
that is in fact a trade deficit,

525
00:26:22.080 --> 00:26:24.090
not a trade surplus.

526
00:26:24.090 --> 00:26:26.220
And that deficit is a problem over time

527
00:26:26.220 --> 00:26:27.960
as it can lead to government borrowing

528
00:26:27.960 --> 00:26:30.030
and an increase in the debt.

529
00:26:30.030 --> 00:26:34.020
Many low income countries are seriously in debt.

530
00:26:34.020 --> 00:26:36.540
Well done if you got that one right.

531
00:26:36.540 --> 00:26:39.360
Now, we talked about what Zambia exports,

00:26:39.360 --> 00:26:42.090

533
00:26:42.090 --> 00:26:44.790
Here we have a different visualization.

And it shows us the countries that Zambia trades with.

535

And again, it's drawn to scale.

What can you tell about which countries

538
00:27:03.450 --> 00:27:05.670
Well, if you said to me Switzerland,

539
00:27:05.670 --> 00:27:09.300
China, and the Democratic Republic of Congo

540
00:27:09.300 --> 00:27:12.753
are where the exports go, you'd be absolutely right.

541
00:27:16.560 --> 00:27:18.360
China is clearly one of Zambia's

542
00:27:18.360 --> 00:27:20.850
most important trade partners.

543
00:27:20.850 --> 00:27:23.130
In recent decades, China has invested

544
00:27:23.130 --> 00:27:25.260
in Zambia's mineral industry

545
00:27:25.260 --> 00:27:27.690
to ensure that Chinese factories can continue

546
00:27:27.690 --> 00:27:30.180
to manufacture goods for export

547
00:27:30.180 --> 00:27:33.393
because they're really dependent on Zambia's copper.

548
00:27:35.970 --> 00:27:38.610
And further, China's gone further than that.

549
00:27:38.610 --> 00:27:40.320
China has lent Zambia money,

550
00:27:40.320 --> 00:27:41.850
so they've invested in businesses,

551
00:27:41.850 --> 00:27:44.160
but they've also lent the government money

552
00:27:44.160 --> 00:27:45.840
to improve its infrastructure,

553
00:27:45.840 --> 00:27:49.353
including its road network and building sports stadia.

554
00:27:50.580 --> 00:27:53.340
China's economic and political influence in Zambia,

555
00:27:53.340 --> 00:27:55.830
as we can see now, is pretty huge,

556
00:27:55.830 --> 00:28:00.180
and it's seen by other nations as this term neocolonialism.

557
00:28:00.180 --> 00:28:01.578
Why is that? What do you think?

558
00:28:01.578 --> 00:28:03.573
Why is that term used?

559
00:28:07.470 --> 00:28:11.970
Well, we've seen Zambia really relies on exporting copper

00:28:11.970 --> 00:28:14.793
and then China is one of its major trade partners.

00:28:16.020 --> 00:28:17.490
I just told you all about

how China actually has lent Zambia lots of money.

00:28:20.670 --> 00:28:23.950
So Zambia owes China billions of dollars now

and China's human rights record has been questioned.

00:28:29.340 --> 00:28:30.915
Zambia's workers have been exploited

566
00:28:30.915 --> 00:28:33.030
for working long hours and beyond that,

567
00:28:33.030 --> 00:28:34.950
health and safety rules have been ignored,

568
00:28:34.950 --> 00:28:37.650
leading to accidents in Zambian mines.

569
00:28:37.650 --> 00:28:39.930
So we can see that really big economic

00:28:39.930 --> 00:28:43.380
and political influence that China has over Zambia,

571
00:28:43.380 --> 00:28:46.503
not really benefiting Zambia and its people.

572
00:28:48.660 --> 00:28:50.940
So if I was to say to you, final check,

00:28:50.940 --> 00:28:53.250
which of the following are causes of a gap

00:28:53.250 --> 00:28:56.730
between the economic development of the UK and Zambia?

Which of those are causes?

00:29:03.480 --> 00:29:05.040
Well, if you said all four,

you'd be absolutely right, well done.

I've got a different visualization here for you,

which is in fact the UK,

so it's the UK's exports by value.

The UK sells most exports by value to the USA,

the Netherlands, Germany, and China.

And we've got the statistics there

Remember with that second one,

you just need to pick which one

you're going to have a go at,

historical, political, or economic causes.

You could talk about Nepal,

but I'm suggesting you might focus on Zambia.

Okay, how did we get on, then?

00:30:17.280 --> 00:30:18.450
Our first question,

what is the UK's largest export by value?

So we have machinery,

mechanical appliances, and parts is the correct answer.

00:30:27.210 --> 00:30:28.740
I'm sure you had that.

But when you went to describe three differences

I wonder what you chose.

00:30:37.230 --> 00:30:41.010
So, we have 60% of the value of Zambia's exports

00:30:41.010 --> 00:30:44.580
are based on copper, whereas only a small proportion,

less than .5% of the UK's exports are copper.

Zambia relies on a few primary products,

and overseen by the British during colonial rule,

railways were only built to support exports,

00:32:14.160 --> 00:32:18.753
So, colonialism is a key historical cause of inequality.

00:32:19.650 --> 00:32:22.530
So if you answered this question based on historical causes,

perhaps you had something similar,

00:32:24.090 --> 00:32:28.863
if you were going to answer linking to Zambia.

00:32:30.300 --> 00:32:33.690
I like the way they've used the word colonialism there.

00:32:33.690 --> 00:32:36.750
And we have a different answer here,

00:32:36.750 --> 00:32:38.340
which is all about economic causes.

So maybe you took up the economic mantle here

00:32:41.820 --> 00:32:43.590
and had a go at this one.

00:32:43.590 --> 00:32:46.440
Zambia is an LIC in southern Africa

00:32:46.440 --> 00:32:51.240
that depends on few primary sector exports.

Copper makes up more than 60% of the value of its exports,

00:32:54.510 --> 00:32:56.790

seen as neocolonialism,

00:33:37.500 --> 00:33:40.100
So, well done if your answer looked a bit like that.

673
00:33:41.880 --> 00:33:43.590
Let's sum up then, what have we covered today?

674
00:33:43.590 --> 00:33:44.640
We've covered quite a lot.

675
00:33:44.640 --> 00:33:46.860
Looking at these causes of global inequalities

00:33:46.860 --> 00:33:48.753
or the development gap.

677
00:33:49.710 --> 00:33:51.390
The physical geography of a country

678
00:33:51.390 --> 00:33:53.973
can affect its development in a number of ways.

679
00:33:55.080 --> 00:33:57.330
Arid and semi-arid climates, for example,

limit food production

00:33:59.100 --> 00:34:01.470
and infrastructure may be poorly developed

in mountainous regions.

However, physical factors interact

with a country's human geography

Colonialism, neocolonialism

and reliance on the export of a few primary products

are key causes of the limited economic development

of low income countries.

691
00:34:26.310 --> 00:34:28.980
Phew, we had a lot to do in that lesson, didn't we?

lessonKeywords.description: the study of population: its size, composition and change over time
the number of births for every 1000 people in a population per year
when a population grows in size as result of the birth rate being higher than the death rate
an age-sex graph used to present the structure of a population (that may resemble a pyramid)
a theoretical model that suggests how birth rate, death rate and total population change over time

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Countries at different levels of development have differences in their demographic characteristics.
The different demographic characteristics include birth rate or fertility rate, death rate and population structure.
A population pyramid enables us to compare population structure of different countries.
The economic impact of different population structures may be understaod by calculating the dependency ratio.
There are links between the stages of the Demographic Transition Model and the level of development.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: It is the proportion of the population that is small not the actual number of people. Some LICs and NEEs have large populations so there are millions of people who reach the age of 65 years plus.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That there are few people who live to 65 years and beyond in LICs and NEEs.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This topic provides the opportunity for students to practise interpreting bar graphs and line graphs; and link the data to the 'story' of a country's development. You may wish to set a research task using online resources.

lessons.lessonTitle: Strategies to reduce the development gap: Fairtrade, debt relief and aid

lessonKeywords.description: the buying and selling of goods and services between countries
a system that ensure producers in LICs and NEES get a fairer price for goods produced, improving their income and working conditions
when a bank or government tells another governnment that they do not have to pay back the money they owe
support (money, goods or services) given to improve the quality of life of a recipient
technology suited to the needs, skills, knowledge and wealth of local people in the environment in which they live

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Various strategies exist to reduce the development gap.
The global system of trade is not free or fair as trade blocs, tariffs and quotas hamper the flow of goods.
The Fairtrade movement aims to address some of the problems of the global trade system by supporting producers in LICs.
Debt relief enables the government in LICs to invest in public services and support the poorest.
International aid can support the development of essential infrastructure via the use of intermediate technology.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Fairtrade movement involves the trade in 300 different commodities and global networks of consumers as well as producers.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Fairtrade is small-scale and mostly based in the UK.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how Fairtrade, debt relief, aid and intermediate technology can reduce the global development gap.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There is a further opportunity to explore the benefits of intermediate technology in the Global pattern of resources unit, when teaching about an example of a local food, water or energy scheme.

lessons.lessonTitle: Using GIS maps to analyse links between inequality and migration

lessonKeywords.description: the Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite measure of development using income, life expectancy and education, ranging between 0 and 1
a data value supporting comparison within a data set, e.g. a category boundary or highest/lowest value for measures of development for different countries, such as HDI
in GIS, a read-only display of attribute information (e.g. text, images, charts) often linked to a location

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: GIS maps can be used to visualise and analyse inequalities in measures of development such as HDI.
Benchmarks are often used to compare inequalities in measures of development such as HDI.
GIS visualisations can be used to support analysis of reasons for migration.
GIS can be used to visualise and analyse migration trends over time, supported by configured pop-ups.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Chart axes appear to be comparable at first, the numbers on the vertical axis differ widely. It is therefore essential to look at the numbers carefully.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Chart axes for 'Immigration numbers trend' show numbers are similar for many countries.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use GIS maps to analyse links between inequality and migration.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The GIS knowledge and skills can be difficult at first and most errors will happen because students skip an important step. It's therefore important to rehearse the steps first yourself so that you can confidently demonstrate the steps as in the video. Encourage peer support, as appropriate.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

lessons.lessonTitle: Example of how tourism can reduce the development gap

lessonKeywords.description: feature of a place that makes people want to visit it or take part in an activity
way of life, especially general customs and beliefs
extensive area of land regarded as being visually and physically distinct
damage caused to water, air, etc. by  harmful substances or waste
when too many people visit a place, so that it is spoiled and life becomes difficult for people who live there

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Bali is an island province in Indonesia (an NEE) where international tourism has developed since the 1960s.
Tourism provides 60 per cent of Bali’s income, with many new jobs created.
Life expectancy in Bali is higher than average for Indonesia; Bali ranks fifth of 38 provinces for human development.
Tourism has some negative impacts, including eroding local culture, pollution and reduced water supplies.
The government plans to develop five new destinations elsewhere to address concerns about ‘overtourism’ in Bali.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Tourism has various positive and negative impacts - while the economy has grown and some public services have improved, others have declined (e.g. the water supply) and so many people visit Bali each year its environment has suffered in the South.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Tourism has only brought benefits to the island of Bali and its people.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how the growth in tourism has helped to reduce the development gap in Bali as well as concerns about overtourism.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Go online to find images of Bali's tourist attractions to help students picture this distant place. Using 'time hop' photography online can also be a great way to help students understand the pace of change.

lessonKeywords.description: the progress of a country in terms of wealth, use of technology and human welfare
a measure of goods and services produced by a country, including income earned abroad; may be divided by the total population to give ‘GNI per head’
average number of years an individual can expect to live at birth; worldwide this doubled from 1900 to 2021
a UN measure of development calculated using education, life expectancy and income data

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are global variations in economic development and quality of life.
There are a range of different measures of level of development.
There are limitations of both economic and social measures.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A country’s income is not equally divided by everyone who lives there. This is why GNI per head should be used along side other measures in order to understand differences in quality of life.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That everyone in a country with a high GNI is well off, with a good quality of life.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the different ways in which social and economic development is measured, and the limitations of individual economic and social measures used.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Skills: There is an opportunity to reinforce understanding of averages (mean, mode, median) and categorisation of data as quantitative or qualitative.

But I would say to you also, are there any issues with using this map to find out about economic development? And the hint is it uses two color families if you like.
So you've got the green family and the purple family.
The world appears to, at first glance, be divided into two groups.
So the rich, green group, and the poor, purple group.
Why is this a bit misleading? Well, almost half of all countries are in fact classified as middle income countries by the world banks.
So they're either lower-middle income or they're upper-middle income.
These countries are home to three quarters of the global population.
Is there also an issue with using GNI per head as a measure of wealth of countries worldwide? What do you think? Well, this is how it's calculated, isn't it? Gross national income divided by total population.

It doesn't tell us anything about how a country's income is actually distributed within that population.
So between its people.
So maybe that's not telling us very much about income development and perhaps what percentage of the population is living on the poverty line.
We don't know what's going on within each country.
So check for you here.
Gross national income per head is calculated by dividing the income of country by its population.
What type of average is this? And if you said it's the mean, well done.
True or false? The map of GNI per head shows us that the world divides into two categories: rich and poor.
Is that true or false? And if you said false, can you explain your answer? The answer we had was that World Bank uses GNI per head to categorize countries into four groups, high income, upper-middle income, lower-middle income, and low-income.
Three quarters of the global population lives in a middle income country.
So it's a gross simplification to talk about just rich and poor.
Two practice tasks for you then.
Can you calculate how many times larger the GNI per head is in Sweden than in Indonesia? And you've got a table of data there to use.
Secondly, how useful is GNI per head if you wanted to compare how wealth is distributed within Sweden and Indonesia? I'd like you to explain your answer to that second task.

73.

7 times larger than in Indonesia.

Well your answer might include something like this.
GNI per head is the mean average income within a population.

This is why it is not useful for comparing the distribution of wealth or income within the country.
So within those populations.
So if your answer looks something like that, well done.
Let's have a look at this second question then today.
What does social measures of development tell us? Well, social measures of development relate more directly to quality of life and we have a range of different measures which I'm going to talk us through.
So we've got birth rate, death rate, and within that a subset is infant mortality rate, life expectancy, people per doctor, literacy rate and access to safe water.

Firstly, let's have a think about birth rate and death rate.

We've got better social measures.

lessons.lessonTitle: Using GIS desire lines to visualise migration

lessonKeywords.description: a graphical technique using lines on a map to show the simple direction of movement from one place to another
the selection of data in a GIS layer which declutters a webmap to visualise spatial patterns more clearly
straight line routes which appear curved because they take the curvature of Earth into consideration
in GIS, a read-only display of attribute information (e.g. text, images, charts) often linked to a location

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Desire lines can be created using GIS to visualise migration.
Filters can be used in GIS to declutter a map showing many desire lines.
GIS desire lines can be configured to visualise migration proportionally.
GIS desire lines can be configured with pop-ups to improve visualisation.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Desire lines show a simple link between a source and destination; flow lines show the route taken between a source and destination.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Desire lines and flow lines are often confused.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use GIS desire lines to visualise migration.

teacherTips.teacherTip: No matter what your level of experience is with GIS, go through all the steps yourself first until you feel confident and fluent. Don't worry if you make a mistake, everybody does, even experienced practitioners!

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

lessons.lessonTitle: Strategies to reduce the development gap: industry and investment

lessonKeywords.description: the widening difference in standards of living and wellbeing between the world’s richest and poorest countries
the secondary economic sector, involving making goods from raw materials or other manufactured products (for example motor vehicles)
the tertiary economic sector, which includes tourism, banking, education and health
the provision of small-scale loans given to people in LICs to help them start a small business

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Various strategies exist to reduce the development gap.
The development of manufacturing industries can help to reduce the gap.
The development of services industries, including tourism, can contribute to economic development.
Foreign direct investment in infrastructure can promote economic growth.
Microfinance loans allow people to set up small businesses and become self-sufficient.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Microfinance loans can also support the development of new jobs in industry, at a smaller scale.
