lessons.lessonTitle: Using GIS to map the track of a tropical storm

lessonKeywords.description: a data value associated with a feature or variable measure (‘field’) in a GIS layer
in GIS, a read-only display of attribute information, often linked to a location
information which has been tied to a particular location (geolocated), using an agreed system such as latitude and longitude
information which is tied to a particular point in time, so that data can be time-enabled (also known as spatiotemporal data)

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Ready-made tropical storm layers can be configured to visualise spatial patterns more effectively, e.g. using filters.
Tropical storms can be analysed using pop-up data.
Georeferenced data about a particular tropical storm can be mapped using GIS and configured to show selected attributes.
A storm track can be visualised using temporal data, in a time-enabled GIS map.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Take students through each step and check for understanding very regularly.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: It is very easy to miss important small steps in GIS.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use and configure GIS to visualise the tracks of tropical storms.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Practise the procedural steps yourself first until you achieve fluency and feel confident. Don't worry if you make mistakes - everyone does even after years of experience!

lessons.unitTitle: Tectonic hazards: Why is Earth restless?

lessonKeywords.description: the chance of something occurring, such as an earthquake
saying exactly when, where and what will happen
identifying that something has just happened or is happening now

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Scientists can calculate the probability of an earthquake happening within an area in the future.
It is not currently possible to predict exactly when or where earthquakes will occur.
Earthquake detection can only provide seconds of warning.
Drop-cover-hold is practised during earthquake drills.
Base isolators, flexible building materials, strong shapes and mass dampers help create earthquake-resistant buildings.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Humans can calculate the probability of an earthquake happening within a region, over a long period of time. It is not possible to predict exactly when or where earthquakes will occur, or of what size.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Earthquakes can be predicted a few weeks or days before they happen so that people can evacuate.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain to what extent people can anticipate earthquakes and how they survive living in areas affected by earthquakes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To engage students you could introduce a simple earthquake drill "When I shout earthquake you need to drop to the floor, cover under the table and hold on." For even more suspense say that you may do this at any time for the rest of the unit.

lessons.unitTitle: Tectonic hazards: Why is Earth restless?

lessonKeywords.description: a series of large, powerful ocean waves caused by a sudden disturbance
to move something from its original position, e.g. ocean water
the basic systems in a country, such as transport and power supply

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A tsunami is a series of large, powerful ocean waves caused by a sudden disturbance.
Undersea earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and landslides can displace sufficient water to trigger a tsunami.
In 2018, a tsunami was caused by the collapse of the Anak Krakatau volcano in the Sunda Strait in Indonesia.
Tragically, the tsunami led to the deaths of over 430 people.
The impact was devastating due to insufficient warning systems, the Strait  funnelling the waves, and the time of day.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Tsunamis are caused by displacement of the ocean, not wind blowing over the surface. Tsunami waves don’t break, they come as a fast-moving wall of water, which can be far bigger and faster than a normal wave. They can also flood kilometres inland.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Tsunamis are just big waves.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how a tsunami occurs and what happened in the Sunda Strait in 2018.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Emphasising that the knowledge from the lesson could save their lives, can add importance to the content.

lessons.unitTitle: Tectonic hazards: Why is Earth restless?

lessonKeywords.description: the huge pieces that Earth’s surface is broken into
where two plates meet
fractures in Earth’s surface
the point deep underground where the tectonic plates first break

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Earthquakes are sudden, violent movements of the ground caused by tectonic plate movement.
Earthquakes usually happen on or near plate boundaries.
At a plate boundary two plates are locked together, yet moving in different directions.
When rock fractures at a plate boundary this causes an earthquake.
Small earthquakes can also occur far from plate boundaries.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There is not one fault but many, which make up a plate boundary and the rock is locked together across the two plates.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Plate boundaries are clean cuts through the ground which separate two plates.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe where earthquakes occur and explain how they happen.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Get up-to-date details of earthquakes in the UK and globally using the British Geological Survey and US Geological Survey websites.

lessons.unitTitle: Tectonic hazards: Why is Earth restless?

lessonKeywords.description: where two tectonic plates separate
consequences that relate to the way money is made, lost or spent
consequences that relate to people’s quality of life, e.g. healthcare
all the basic systems in a country, such as transport and power supply

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mount Nyiragongo is a volcano located in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on the East African Rift System.
On the 22nd May 2021, it began to erupt; this followed a deadly eruption in 2002, which reached the city of Goma.
When the eruption happened, lava poured down the sides of the volcano.
At least 450 000 people were displaced or evacuated due to the lava flows.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Mount Nyiragongo is on a constructive plate boundary known as the East African Rift System, where the African plate is splitting into the Nubian and Somali plates.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: There are no plate boundaries in Africa.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain why Mount Nyiragongo erupted and the impacts of the eruption.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It is worth researching the current state of the volcano to set the 2021 eruption in context, or asking students to find any updates for homework.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Primary effects happen directly as a result of an earthquake, for example broken gas pipes.

00:23:33.690 --> 00:23:37.770

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The theory of continental drift suggests that Earth’s continents were once joined together and later drifted apart.
Evidence for continental drift includes continents' jigsaw like shape, rock type and fossils matching across continents.
There are two types of crust; oceanic and continental crust.
Oceanic crust is dense but thin and continental crust is thicker and less dense.
Plates move by the processes of slab pull and ridge push.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: South America is a continent (land), whereas the South American plate also includes part of the Atlantic ocean.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: South America and the South American plate are the same thing.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use evidence to show that the continents have moved and explain how tectonic plate movement happens.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It is possible to model slab pull by using a chain or scarf hanging off the edge of a table. Let the students see how the weight of the item drags the rest of it down off the table.

Our keywords are: continent.
This is a large landmass on Earth.
There are seven, so we've got Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Oceania.
Are you familiar with those? We've now got tectonic plates.
So this term means large sections of the lithosphere that are on the move.
Density is our last keyword today, and this is the mass of something compared to its volume.
If you think it would be useful to note down any of those keywords and their definitions, feel free to pause the video and do that now.

So he would expect that actually the rock that the ground is made from, that would be the same across two continents, and also there would be the same species in both continents as well.
So you'd expect the continents if they had been joined together to be very samey, especially at the edges where these two continents meet.
You'd expect the same type of rock, same type of species of animals and plants to be in those two places before they were ripped apart.
So we've actually got some evidence here that this is the case.
So the bands of the same rock type match across some of the continents, and you can see that over here.
In addition, some types of fossils have been found across several continents.
So you can see here we've got a photograph of a fossil, and this is the Lystrosaurus fossil, and it's found in Africa, India, and Antarctica, suggesting that all of these locations were once connected.
Time for a quick check now.
Which species is found across the most continents? Is it A, Glossopteris? Is it B, Cynognathus? C, Lystrosaurus? Or D, Mesosaurus? Well done.
The Glossopteris.
So the theory of continental drift was put forward by Alfred Wegener in 1912.
He suggested that the Earth's continents were once joined together in a supercontinent called Pangaea and later drifted apart.
Can you see that on the animation on the left hand side? So we start with Pangaea and those continents slowly separate.
Scientists didn't believe him to start with, and it took a really, really long time for him to be believed.
It wasn't until the 1970s that the scientific community really accepted this theory, and the reason for that was that although Alfred Wegener had actually worked this out and decided this is probably what happened, there wasn't any evidence for really how this happened and how it worked.
Alfred Wegener didn't get to see his theories accepted by the scientific community and taught in schools.
It wasn't until the 1970s that the theory was really accepted.
Unfortunately, Alfred died in 1930, so a long, long time was required to gather the evidence and for the scientific community to actually really accept this actually could have happened.
Sofia asks, "How fast are the plates drifting or moving?" So the Earth's tectonic plates move towards or away from each other very slowly.
It varies between plates, but on average, the rate of movement is 1.

So that's about the speed your nails grow.
It is not fast.

The lithosphere is not one continuous layer.
It's broken up into the large sections called tectonic plates.

This is a section of tectonic plate covered by ocean.
It is relatively thin and it's dense.
The continental plate is a section of tectonic plate covered by land.
This is thicker and less dense.

This means that more molecules are in the same volume.
So where there are more molecules in the same volume, it is more dense, and where there are less molecules in the same volume, it is less dense.

This is the same for tectonic plates.

The new rock forms at the ocean ridges, cools and becomes denser over time.

Oceanic plate is dense but thin, and continental plate is thicker and less dense.
Plates move by the processes of slab pull and ridge push.
I hope that you enjoyed the lesson today and have learned lots.
I've certainly enjoyed learning with you, and I hope to see you next time.
Bye-bye.

so you've got some time to do this.

137
00:07:18.660 --> 00:07:22.620
Well done, everyone. Let's have a look at the answers.

138
00:07:22.620 --> 00:07:25.020
So the theory of continental drift

139
00:07:25.020 --> 00:07:28.710
was put forward by Alfred Wegener in 1912.

140
00:07:28.710 --> 00:07:30.600
He suggested that Earth's continents

141
00:07:30.600 --> 00:07:31.790
were once joined together

142
00:07:31.790 --> 00:07:34.470
in a supercontinent called Pangaea,

143
00:07:34.470 --> 00:07:36.690
and they later drifted apart.

144
00:07:36.690 --> 00:07:39.630
He thought this was because some continents,

145
00:07:39.630 --> 00:07:42.090
for example, Africa and South America,

146
00:07:42.090 --> 00:07:45.270
look like they fit together like puzzle pieces.

147
00:07:45.270 --> 00:07:48.690
Bands of the same rock type match across continents,

148
00:07:48.690 --> 00:07:53.253
and types of fossils found match across several continents.

149
00:07:54.180 --> 00:07:55.013
How did you do?

150
00:07:55.860 --> 00:07:57.150
Excellent work.

151
00:07:57.150 --> 00:07:58.830
Feel free to pause the video now

152
00:07:58.830 --> 00:08:00.730
and tweak your answers if you need to.

153
00:08:09.330 --> 00:08:11.550
Time to move on to the second part of our lesson now.

154
00:08:11.550 --> 00:08:13.743
This is tectonic plate movement.

155
00:08:15.600 --> 00:08:17.700
Sofia says, "There is a lot of evidence

156
00:08:17.700 --> 00:08:19.290
for continental drift,

157
00:08:19.290 --> 00:08:22.200
but how do the continents actually move?"

158
00:08:22.200 --> 00:08:24.510
This is exactly what the scientists wanted to know

159
00:08:24.510 --> 00:08:28.323
when Wegener proposed his theory back in 1912.

160
00:08:29.460 --> 00:08:31.710
So the upper mantle and crust combined

161
00:08:31.710 --> 00:08:33.873
make the rigid lithosphere.

162
00:08:35.400 --> 00:08:38.130
The lithosphere is not one continuous layer.

163
00:08:38.130 --> 00:08:40.050
It's broken up into the large sections

164
00:08:40.050 --> 00:08:41.613
called tectonic plates.

165
00:08:42.510 --> 00:08:45.330
Tectonic plates have two forms.

166
00:08:45.330 --> 00:08:47.730
We've got the oceanic plate.

167
00:08:47.730 --> 00:08:51.480
This is a section of tectonic plate covered by ocean.

168
00:08:51.480 --> 00:08:54.243
It is relatively thin and it's dense.

169
00:08:56.100 --> 00:09:00.030
The continental plate is a section of tectonic plate

170
00:09:00.030 --> 00:09:01.680
covered by land.

171
00:09:01.680 --> 00:09:05.430
This is thicker and less dense.

172
00:09:05.430 --> 00:09:07.350
It's worth noting at this point

173
00:09:07.350 --> 00:09:11.130
that we are not saying the whole plate.

174
00:09:11.130 --> 00:09:12.630
We're saying that oceanic plate

175
00:09:12.630 --> 00:09:15.540
is a section of tectonic plates,

176
00:09:15.540 --> 00:09:16.990
and the same for continental.

177
00:09:18.270 --> 00:09:22.260
This part of the South American plate is continental.

178
00:09:22.260 --> 00:09:26.850
However, this part of the South American plate is oceanic.

179
00:09:26.850 --> 00:09:31.650
So you can have one plate that has sections

180
00:09:31.650 --> 00:09:35.220
or a section that is continental

181
00:09:35.220 --> 00:09:39.960
and sections or a section which is oceanic.

182
00:09:39.960 --> 00:09:41.433
Time for a quick check now.

183
00:09:42.480 --> 00:09:45.337
Why is Jun's statement incorrect?

184
00:09:45.337 --> 00:09:47.877
"The African plate is a continental plate."

185
00:09:49.732 --> 00:09:51.533
Have a look at the map here to help you out.

186
00:09:57.360 --> 00:09:58.440
Well done.

187
00:09:58.440 --> 00:10:02.100
The African plate is made up of continental plate with land

188
00:10:02.100 --> 00:10:05.133
and oceanic plate where the seabed is.

189
00:10:07.170 --> 00:10:09.870
Another quick check. True or false?

190
00:10:09.870 --> 00:10:13.287
South America and the South American plate

191
00:10:13.287 --> 00:10:14.853
are the same thing.

192
00:10:21.030 --> 00:10:23.103
Well done. That is false.

193
00:10:24.135 --> 00:10:28.073
So South America is a continent, land,

194
00:10:29.400 --> 00:10:32.340
and the South American plate

195
00:10:32.340 --> 00:10:35.943
also includes part of the seabed of the Atlantic ocean.

196
00:10:37.020 --> 00:10:41.403
So the continent and the plate are two separate things.

197
00:10:42.330 --> 00:10:46.200
Density is the mass of something compared to its volume.

198
00:10:46.200 --> 00:10:48.933
So oceanic plates are more dense.

199
00:10:49.830 --> 00:10:54.780
This means that more molecules are in the same volume.

200
00:10:54.780 --> 00:10:57.270
So where there are more molecules in the same volume,

201
00:10:57.270 --> 00:10:59.160
it is more dense,

202
00:10:59.160 --> 00:11:03.330
and where there are less molecules in the same volume,

203
00:11:03.330 --> 00:11:05.040
it is less dense.

204
00:11:05.040 --> 00:11:08.130
So that would be the case for our continental plates,

205
00:11:08.130 --> 00:11:11.520
which are less dense, as you can see on the right here.

206
00:11:11.520 --> 00:11:14.880
Density affects how different materials interact,

207
00:11:14.880 --> 00:11:18.930
whether they sink or float in other substances.

208
00:11:18.930 --> 00:11:22.440
You can see here that wood is less dense than water,

209
00:11:22.440 --> 00:11:24.150
so it floats,

210
00:11:24.150 --> 00:11:28.500
whereas most metals are more dense, so sink in water.

211
00:11:28.500 --> 00:11:30.603
This is the same for tectonic plates.

212
00:11:32.280 --> 00:11:35.460
Where oceanic plates meet continental plates,

213
00:11:35.460 --> 00:11:39.030
the dense oceanic plate subducts, or sinks,

214
00:11:39.030 --> 00:11:40.233
into the mantle.

215
00:11:42.420 --> 00:11:45.275
This is the subduction zone I've circled here,

216
00:11:45.275 --> 00:11:47.475
and it's a really good key term to remember.

217
00:11:48.780 --> 00:11:50.430
As the oceanic plate subducts,

218
00:11:50.430 --> 00:11:52.680
it pulls the rest of the plate along with it.

219
00:11:54.030 --> 00:11:56.880
Jun asks, "How does that work?"

220
00:11:56.880 --> 00:12:00.210
Sofia says, "The weight of the oceanic plate

221
00:12:00.210 --> 00:12:02.340
drags the rest of the plate along,

222
00:12:02.340 --> 00:12:05.430
like the end of a heavy chain falling off a table."

223
00:12:05.430 --> 00:12:06.900
You can try this yourself

224
00:12:06.900 --> 00:12:08.580
with anything that you have lying around.

225
00:12:08.580 --> 00:12:11.430
So if you don't have a chain, might you have a necklace

226
00:12:11.430 --> 00:12:14.160
or even a scarf or something like that.

227
00:12:14.160 --> 00:12:15.720
Give it a go and see if it works.

228
00:12:15.720 --> 00:12:20.720
Does gravity pull the rest of that item off the table?

229
00:12:21.060 --> 00:12:23.010
I gave this a go myself with a scarf.

230
00:12:23.010 --> 00:12:25.310
I'll show you what it looked like. Here it is.

231
00:12:28.500 --> 00:12:30.930
This process is called slab pull.

232
00:12:30.930 --> 00:12:33.150
The slab part of this term

233
00:12:33.150 --> 00:12:35.943
refers to the slab of the tectonic plate

234
00:12:35.943 --> 00:12:38.490
that is sinking or subducting

235
00:12:38.490 --> 00:12:41.523
that you can see circled in turquoise here.

236
00:12:42.690 --> 00:12:46.890
The pull part of this term refers to the slab

237
00:12:46.890 --> 00:12:49.920
pulling the rest of the plate behind it.

238
00:12:49.920 --> 00:12:53.520
So it does make sense. I like a term that makes sense.

239
00:12:53.520 --> 00:12:56.790
Quick check time. What is slab pull?

240
00:12:56.790 --> 00:13:00.570
Is it A, a method of measuring plate movement speed;

241
00:13:00.570 --> 00:13:03.180
B, a type of volcanic eruption

242
00:13:03.180 --> 00:13:05.040
which occurs in the middle of a plate;

243
00:13:05.040 --> 00:13:09.270
or C, a process where dense oceanic plate

244
00:13:09.270 --> 00:13:11.550
sinks into the mantle?

245
00:13:11.550 --> 00:13:12.903
Which do you think?

246
00:13:18.810 --> 00:13:20.010
Well done.

247
00:13:20.010 --> 00:13:23.250
So C, a process where dense oceanic plate

248
00:13:23.250 --> 00:13:24.933
sinks into the mantle.

249
00:13:27.270 --> 00:13:29.940
Lucas says, "Okay, that makes sense

250
00:13:29.940 --> 00:13:33.030
for the oceanic plate on this side of the diagram,

251
00:13:33.030 --> 00:13:35.010
but what about the other one?

252
00:13:35.010 --> 00:13:36.417
What causes that to move?"

253
00:13:37.290 --> 00:13:39.240
And that's a really good question.

254
00:13:39.240 --> 00:13:41.850
So there is another process involved,

255
00:13:41.850 --> 00:13:43.350
and we'll talk about that now.

256
00:13:44.190 --> 00:13:47.280
At some boundaries new rock forms,

257
00:13:47.280 --> 00:13:50.010
pushing the tectonic plates apart.

258
00:13:50.010 --> 00:13:53.760
You can see where this is occurring on the diagram here,

259
00:13:53.760 --> 00:13:55.053
where it's been circled.

260
00:13:57.150 --> 00:13:59.160
So where this is happening,

261
00:13:59.160 --> 00:14:02.463
the mantle melts and forms magma.

262
00:14:03.420 --> 00:14:06.330
The magma rises through cracks in the plate

263
00:14:06.330 --> 00:14:08.043
and erupts as lava.

264
00:14:09.210 --> 00:14:11.220
The lava cools and hardens,

265
00:14:11.220 --> 00:14:16.113
becoming new rock which increases in density over time.

266
00:14:17.400 --> 00:14:19.650
The new rock forms at the ocean ridges,

267
00:14:19.650 --> 00:14:22.530
cools and becomes denser over time.

268
00:14:22.530 --> 00:14:26.640
As a result, it slides away from the top of the ridge.

269
00:14:26.640 --> 00:14:28.530
This makes sense, doesn't it?

270
00:14:28.530 --> 00:14:30.810
Where there's that ridge,

271
00:14:30.810 --> 00:14:32.550
as the rock gets denser,

272
00:14:32.550 --> 00:14:36.180
it slides down away from that ridge.

273
00:14:36.180 --> 00:14:39.783
So gravity's playing a role here. Makes sense.

274
00:14:40.770 --> 00:14:43.650
The process of new rock forming, cooling,

275
00:14:43.650 --> 00:14:47.370
and sliding away from the ridge pushes the plate apart.

276
00:14:47.370 --> 00:14:50.370
This is called ridge push.

277
00:14:50.370 --> 00:14:52.590
So the ridge part of this term

278
00:14:52.590 --> 00:14:55.950
refers to the less dense hot magma

279
00:14:55.950 --> 00:14:59.700
welling up and producing that ocean ridge.

280
00:14:59.700 --> 00:15:03.390
A ridge is that raised line

281
00:15:03.390 --> 00:15:05.673
where the two plates are separating.

282
00:15:08.040 --> 00:15:13.040
The push part is dense rock slides away

283
00:15:13.200 --> 00:15:15.420
due to the force of gravity

284
00:15:15.420 --> 00:15:19.143
and it pushes the rest of the plate along in front of it.

285
00:15:20.730 --> 00:15:22.230
Ridge push takes place

286
00:15:22.230 --> 00:15:24.573
where plates move away from each other.

287
00:15:27.720 --> 00:15:30.750
Laura has got another point she wants to make,

288
00:15:30.750 --> 00:15:33.907
and I wonder if any of you have this actually as well.

289
00:15:33.907 --> 00:15:35.460
"I have heard it was something to do

290
00:15:35.460 --> 00:15:38.760
with convection currents in the mantle."

291
00:15:38.760 --> 00:15:41.310
Now, this is an older theory

292
00:15:41.310 --> 00:15:43.950
about how plate movement happens.

293
00:15:43.950 --> 00:15:46.800
It's not one that scientists actually think

294
00:15:46.800 --> 00:15:49.140
is the main driver anymore at all.

295
00:15:49.140 --> 00:15:51.150
So the main driver of plate movement

296
00:15:51.150 --> 00:15:53.040
is thought to be slab pull,

297
00:15:53.040 --> 00:15:55.980
but ridge push also plays a role as well.

298
00:15:55.980 --> 00:15:57.780
Time for a quick check.

299
00:15:57.780 --> 00:16:00.783
Which plate is subducting at this plate boundary?

300
00:16:01.680 --> 00:16:03.980
Do you remember that subducting means sinking?

301
00:16:08.820 --> 00:16:10.713
Well done. It's the Nazca plate.

302
00:16:12.450 --> 00:16:16.923
Which process explains why the South American plate moves?

303
00:16:21.660 --> 00:16:26.480
Is it A, slab pull; B, ridge push;

304
00:16:26.480 --> 00:16:28.743
or C, convection currents?

305
00:16:36.060 --> 00:16:39.060
Well done. It's ridge push.

306
00:16:39.060 --> 00:16:40.290
You're correct.

307
00:16:40.290 --> 00:16:41.973
Time for our practice task now.

308
00:16:42.840 --> 00:16:45.120
Can you define the following key terms:

309
00:16:45.120 --> 00:16:47.493
oceanic plate and continental plate?

310
00:16:49.230 --> 00:16:51.570
Remember, when we're talking about oceanic

311
00:16:51.570 --> 00:16:53.010
and continental plates,

312
00:16:53.010 --> 00:16:56.313
we're talking about a section of plate, not the whole plate.

313
00:16:58.050 --> 00:16:58.953
Task two.

314
00:17:00.090 --> 00:17:01.500
Can you annotate a diagram

315
00:17:01.500 --> 00:17:05.010
to explain how slab pull moves the plates?

316
00:17:05.010 --> 00:17:07.890
I've put a diagram here to help you.

317
00:17:07.890 --> 00:17:09.360
And task three.

318
00:17:09.360 --> 00:17:11.190
Annotate a diagram to explain

319
00:17:11.190 --> 00:17:13.590
how ridge push moves the plates.

320
00:17:13.590 --> 00:17:15.900
Again, there's a diagram here to help you.

321
00:17:15.900 --> 00:17:17.400
Feel free to pause the video now

322
00:17:17.400 --> 00:17:20.013
to give yourself time to do this task.

323
00:17:27.660 --> 00:17:28.903
Well done. Brilliant.

324
00:17:28.903 --> 00:17:31.080
Let's have a look at some answers.

325
00:17:31.080 --> 00:17:33.000
Your answers may look like this.

326
00:17:33.000 --> 00:17:34.800
Define the following key terms.

327
00:17:34.800 --> 00:17:39.450
So oceanic plate is a section of plate covered by ocean,

328
00:17:39.450 --> 00:17:43.200
made up of relatively thin and dense material.

329
00:17:43.200 --> 00:17:45.480
So here we're really looking for that section of plate,

330
00:17:45.480 --> 00:17:47.070
not the whole plate.

331
00:17:47.070 --> 00:17:49.530
It's thin and dense material.

332
00:17:49.530 --> 00:17:52.680
Those two elements are really good to include as well.

333
00:17:52.680 --> 00:17:53.910
For the continental plate,

334
00:17:53.910 --> 00:17:56.190
this is a section of plate covered by land.

335
00:17:56.190 --> 00:17:58.830
Again, section of plate, not the whole plate,

336
00:17:58.830 --> 00:18:02.760
and it's made up of relatively thin and dense material.

337
00:18:02.760 --> 00:18:04.080
Feel free to pause the video

338
00:18:04.080 --> 00:18:05.883
to edit your own answers if needed.

339
00:18:12.300 --> 00:18:15.420
For task two, you had to annotate a diagram

340
00:18:15.420 --> 00:18:17.430
to explain slab pull.

341
00:18:17.430 --> 00:18:19.980
So our first annotation here says,

342
00:18:19.980 --> 00:18:24.483
dense oceanic plate or the slab sinks into the mantle.

343
00:18:25.740 --> 00:18:28.890
Our second annotation says that the slab

344
00:18:28.890 --> 00:18:31.323
pulls the rest of the plate behind it.

345
00:18:32.700 --> 00:18:35.253
Feel free to tweak your answer if you need to.

346
00:18:36.240 --> 00:18:40.350
Also, I would note that it's a good idea to have a title

347
00:18:40.350 --> 00:18:42.930
for that diagram as well as slab pull.

348
00:18:42.930 --> 00:18:44.700
Do make sure you've done that. I'm sure you have.

349
00:18:44.700 --> 00:18:47.010
For your ridge push diagram,

350
00:18:47.010 --> 00:18:48.450
these are the sorts of annotations

351
00:18:48.450 --> 00:18:50.130
I would expect you to include.

352
00:18:50.130 --> 00:18:51.750
So ridge push takes place

353
00:18:51.750 --> 00:18:54.030
where plates move away from each other.

354
00:18:54.030 --> 00:18:56.100
Have you linked that to the section on the diagram

355
00:18:56.100 --> 00:18:58.250
where you've got those arrows moving apart?

356
00:18:59.940 --> 00:19:03.510
Then we've got less dense hot magma wells up

357
00:19:03.510 --> 00:19:06.570
and produces an ocean ridge.

358
00:19:06.570 --> 00:19:11.070
So ocean ridge is a really key term to be including in this.

359
00:19:11.070 --> 00:19:12.633
Do make sure you've done that.

360
00:19:13.650 --> 00:19:14.940
And then denser rock

361
00:19:14.940 --> 00:19:17.820
slides away due to the force of gravity,

362
00:19:17.820 --> 00:19:20.883
which pushes the rest of the plate along in front of it.

363
00:19:23.130 --> 00:19:25.780
Feel free to edit your answers if you need to at all.

364
00:19:31.530 --> 00:19:34.590
Well done, everyone. Time for our summary now.

365
00:19:34.590 --> 00:19:36.000
The theory of continental drift

366
00:19:36.000 --> 00:19:38.880
suggests that Earth's continents were once joined together

367
00:19:38.880 --> 00:19:40.233
and later drifted apart.

368
00:19:41.250 --> 00:19:43.020
Evidence for continental drift

369
00:19:43.020 --> 00:19:46.440
includes the continents' jigsaw-like shape,

370
00:19:46.440 --> 00:19:50.193
matching rock types and fossils across continents.

371
00:19:51.180 --> 00:19:55.143
There are two types of plate: oceanic and continental.

372
00:19:56.280 --> 00:19:59.370
Oceanic plate is dense but thin,

373
00:19:59.370 --> 00:20:03.600
and continental plate is thicker and less dense.

374
00:20:03.600 --> 00:20:08.193
Plates move by the processes of slab pull and ridge push.

375
00:20:09.420 --> 00:20:11.310
I hope that you enjoyed the lesson today

376
00:20:11.310 --> 00:20:12.480
and have learned lots.

377
00:20:12.480 --> 00:20:14.520
I've certainly enjoyed learning with you,

378
00:20:14.520 --> 00:20:15.960
and I hope to see you next time.

379
00:20:15.960 --> 00:20:16.793
Bye-bye.

lessonKeywords.description: a very hot mix of lava, ash, gases and rock that flows rapidly down the side of the volcano
tiny pieces of volcanic rock and glass

all the basic systems in a country, such as transport and power supply

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Volcanic eruptions can lead to a range of hazards, such as pyroclastic flows, ash and lahars.
Pyroclastic flows are flows of hot volcanic gases, ash and rock.
Ash is made up of tiny pieces of volcanic rock and glass, this can damage lungs, machines, crops and buildings.
Lahars are mudflows caused by volcanic material mixed with water.
Mount Semeru (Java, Indonesia) erupted in 2021, triggering damaging pyroclastic flows, ashfall and lahars.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Ash, lahars and pyroclastic flows are all extremely dangerous volcanic hazards. Pyroclastic flows can reach speeds of 435 mph, which is faster than a car.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Lava is the only dangerous aspect to a volcanic eruption and you can just run out of the way.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain what pyroclastic flows, ash and lahars are and relate this to real life examples.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students enjoy imagining themselves experiencing a volcanic eruption. Try to set them up for the misconception above during discussion, this will make the learning more meaningful for them.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Stress had built up along the Sagaing faultline in central Myanmar and was released during the 2025 earthquake.
Myanmar is a low income country affected by conflict.
Few plans were in place and earthquake-resistant buildings were rare.
The 7.7 magnitude quake occurred close to large centres of population.
Many different organisations provided short-term aid for the millions of people who needed support.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Since many survivors had to stay in crowded shelters or sleep outside, the risk of diseases increased. In addition, strong aftershocks hit the area, damaging buildings that were already unstable.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: If someone survives and is not injured during the earthquake, they are then safe.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are two main types of volcano: composite and shield volcanoes.
Composite volcanoes are usually found at destructive plate boundaries and they are highly explosive volcanoes
Shield volcanoes are usually found at constructive plate boundaries.
Some eruptions are explosive, whereas others are effusive.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Magma is molten rock underground, whereas lava is molten rock above Earth's surface.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Lava and magma can be used interchangeably.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can name the key features of volcanoes and explain how composite and shield volcanoes are formed.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: One in twenty people lives close to an active volcano due to their fertile soils, tourist income and geothermal energy.
There are risks including: pyroclastic flows, ash and lahars.
Preparation such as public education as well as the monitoring of volcanoes can reduce risks to people living close by.
Short-term responses include local and international emergency services providing aid to people.
Long-term responses include infrastructure repair/rebuild in the months and years after the eruption.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: One in twenty people live close to an active volcano, as there are many attractive qualities to living there, e.g. fertile soils, tourist income and geothermal energy.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: People do not live on volcanoes because it is too dangerous.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain why people live near volcanoes and how to prepare for and respond to eruptions.

lessons.unitTitle: Tectonic hazards: Why is Earth restless?

lessonKeywords.description: the huge pieces that Earth’s crust is broken into are known as tectonic plates
where two tectonic plates meet is known as a plate boundary
a lot of mass packed into a small space

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are four main types of plate boundary: conservative, constructive, collision and destructive.
At a conservative plate boundary, the tectonic plates move past each other, causing earthquakes.
At a constructive plate boundary, the tectonic plates move apart, causing volcanic eruptions and earthquakes.
At collision plate boundaries, plates move together, causing earthquakes.
At destructive plate boundaries, plates move together, causing volcanoes and earthquakes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The water in the oceanic plate lowers the melting point, helping mantle rocks above to melt and form magma, not the subducting plate itself.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The oceanic plate subducts at a destructive plate margin and melts to form magma.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe what happens at plate boundaries, including the tectonic hazards that occur.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Focusing on the root words helps students to differentiate between the plate boundaries: conservative (land conserved), constructive (land constructed), collision (plates collide) and destructive (oceanic plate lost as it is subducted into mantle).

at destructive plate boundaries

two plates of different densities converge.

underneath the continental plate.

lower the melting points, so mantle rock above forms magma.

lessons.unitTitle: Tectonic hazards: Why is Earth restless?

lessonKeywords.description: a force pushing or pressing on a given area
density is the mass of something compared to its volume
the huge pieces that Earth’s crust is broken into
the point where two tectonic plates meet

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Earth is made up of four main layers: the inner core, outer core, mantle and crust.
Together the upper mantle and the crust form Earth’s rigid outer layer: the lithosphere.
The lithosphere is broken into large sections or tectonic plates.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur at plate boundaries.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Tectonic plates cover the whole world, this would mean they happen everywhere. The majority of earthquakes and volcanoes occur at plate boundaries (where two plates meet), though there are some which happen away from boundaries.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Earthquakes and volcanoes happen on tectonic plates.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the structure of Earth and how the pattern of earthquakes and volcanoes relate to Earth's tectonic plates.

teacherTips.teacherTip: A real or imaginary hardboiled egg can be used as a model: shell = crust, white = mantle and yolk = core, squeeze to crack the shell to show how the tectonic plates fit together. In addition, show students a globe and turn it round to the Pacific to demonstrate a Pacific centred map.

lessons.lessonTitle: Physical landscapes of the Middle East
lessons.unitTitle: The Middle East: How have natural resources shaped the Middle East?

lessonKeywords.description: the large scale processes that take place within Earth’s crust
a natural, raised part of Earth that is higher than a hill
an area of high, flat land
an area of land that is extremely dry and receives less than 25 centimetres of rain per year

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The Middle East lies at the crossroads of continents.
It has deserts, mountains, plateaux, and fertile valleys.
The Zagros and Taurus Mountains were formed by tectonic movement.
The Rub' al Khali is the largest sand desert in the Middle East.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Students will learn that the Middle East contains diverse landscapes including mountains, valleys, and fertile land.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Middle East is all desert.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can define the location and key landscapes of the Middle East.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Using a large wall map or interactive digital map will help students visualise the physical and political geography of the region.

lessons.lessonTitle: The greening of the Arabian Desert
lessons.unitTitle: The Middle East: How have natural resources shaped the Middle East?

lessonKeywords.description: the process by which fertile land becomes desert
the process of removing salt from seawater
able to continue over a long time

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Desertification is a major challenge in the region.
Desalination provides water for farming.
Tree planting projects aim to combat desert spread.
Vertical farming is used to grow food sustainably.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Plants can have special features, or adaptations, to help them survive in the desert. This, alongside new technology, means that plants can sustain life in the desert and overcome the issue of desertification.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: We cannot grow new plants in the desert, it is too dry.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the challenge of desertification and recognise the strategies to respond to it.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students may find it easier to grasp desertification when they can compare it to issues closer to home. Briefly mention how parts of southern Europe or areas in Africa are also affected by desertification. This helps them realise it's a global challenge—not just a distant issue in the Middle East.

lessons.lessonTitle: Climate change and environmental challenges in the Middle East
lessons.unitTitle: The Middle East: How have natural resources shaped the Middle East?

lessonKeywords.description: the large-scale and long-term change in the planet’s climate, including weather patterns and average temperatures
the process by which semi-arid land becomes drier and turns into desert
when there are not enough freshwater resources to meet the needs in a given area

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Rising temperatures make the region hotter and drier.
Water scarcity is worsening due to climate change, and this impacts food supplies.
Countries can use their natural resources to respond to climate change.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Climate change will continue to make the region hotter and drier, which will have consequences such as desertification, water scarcity and food shortages.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Middle East is already hot and dry, so climate change won’t really affect it.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how climate change affects the Middle East.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Try to make links between the impacts of climate change in the UK to support students in understanding the global scale of the issues surorunding climate change.

lessons.lessonTitle: History and legacy: Empires, borders and religion
lessons.unitTitle: The Middle East: How have natural resources shaped the Middle East?

lessonKeywords.description: the religion observed by many Jewish people, characterised by belief in one God and a religious life based on the Torah and the Talmud
the religion followed by Christians, based on the person and teachings of Jesus Christ
the religion followed by Muslims, centred on the belief in one God, Allah, and the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad
a group of countries or regions ruled by one leader or country
when one country takes control of all, or parts, of another country

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Judaism, Christianity and Islam began in the region.
Empires shaped borders in the Middle East.
Colonial rule created modern political borders.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Judaism is almost 2000 years older than Christianity.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Christianity is the oldest religion that originated in the Middle East.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how religion and historical empires have shaped the Middle East.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson requires sensitivity when taught as it touches on themes which are very controversial.  There are possibilities for a more in-depth analysis of modern-day conflict and the implications on borders, however, the way this is taught will be influenced by each school's context.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Dubai grew from a small port to a global city.

lessonKeywords.description: the movement from one place to another
when people choose to move, often for work or lifestyle
when people have to move, often due to war or natural disasters
a person who moves to another place for job opportunities

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The Middle East is a major source and destination for migrants.
Migration in the Middle East can be both voluntary or forced.
The Gulf States are a major destination for international migrants.
War has been a major cause of forced migration.
Migration stories reveal the personal impacts of conflict, work, and opportunity across the Middle East.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While war and displacement are significant in parts of the Middle East, the region is also a major destination for voluntary economic migration, especially to the Gulf States like the UAE, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All migration in the Middle East is forced due to conflict.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the causes and impacts of migration in the Middle East region.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to step into the shoes of real migrants. This helps them grasp the human emotions and challenges behind it.

lessonKeywords.description: a place that recieves less than 250 mm of precipitation a year
moving from place to place for resources or survival
special features that organisms have to help them survive in an environment
a spot of fertile land in a desert, where water is found
the process whereby water turns into vapour

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The desert has extreme heat and little rainfall.
The Bedouin live nomadic lifestyles, using camels for transport and relying on oases for water and farming.
Plants and animals have adptations that help them survive in the desert.
Camels store fat in their humps, fennec foxes have large ears to release heat, and oryx get moisture from plants.
Date palms have deep roots, cacti store water in thick stems, and acacia trees have small leaves to reduce water loss.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Camels store fat in their humps for energy, not water.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Camels store water in their humps.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how people, plants and animals have adapted to desert life.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Make sure students can link the adaptations to why they are needed. This will help students apply the concept of adaptations to different ecosystems.

We're going to start with our first learning cycle now, what is life like in the Arabian Desert? On this slide, we can see that there are four climate graphs from the Arabian Desert.

So the Arabian Desert is generally hot and dry.
Summer temperatures can reach up to 50 degrees Celsius, and winter temperatures are mild, averaging only about 20 degrees Celsius.
Most places are arid, receiving less than 250 millimeters of precipitation annually.
But there are seasonal variations in climate, and we saw that on those climate graphs.

Humans have inhabited the Arabian Desert for around 2.
6 million years, since the early Pleistocene times.
Now, this might sound surprising, but in the early Pleistocene, the desert wasn't always as dry as it is today.
During certain periods, the climate was wetter and greener with rivers, lakes, and vegetation that could support life.
Early humans were able to survive by using the natural resources around them, gathering plants, finding fresh water and herding animals.
But it was over time when the climate became more arid and the land changed.
Instead of leaving the desert behind, people learned how to live with these new conditions.
This is where we start to see the development of skills and knowledge that help desert communities thrive, such as knowing where to find water, how to raise animals like camels and goats, and how to move from place to place to follow seasonal patterns.
Living in the desert wasn't just about survival, it was about understanding the land, passing down knowledge through generations and building strong communities that work together.
These roots of desert life continue today with communities such as the Bedouins carrying forward traditions that stretch back thousands and even millions of years.
But due to the extreme climate and limited availability of natural resources, people who live in the desert cannot live in one place permanently.
They have to move from place to place, and this is called living a nomadic lifestyle.
In the image we can see nomadic people living in Jordan.
One of the most well-known nomadic communities in the Arabian Desert is the Bedouin community.

So we're going to have a think about some of the key features of the traditional Bedouin lifestyle.
So we need to start by imagining the vast desert, a place with extreme temperatures, little water, and long distances between towns.
In this challenging environment, the Bedouins have developed a lifestyle that is closely connected to the land, the climate, and one another.
One of the most distinctive features of the traditional Bedouin lifestyle is their homes.
Rather than permanent buildings, tents are used, often made from woven goat hair.
This material is ideal because it's strong, lightweight, and can breathe in hot weather whilst also providing shelter during sandstorms and cold desert nights.
These tents can be packed up quickly, making it really easy to move from place to place quite quickly.
Similarly, animal herding plays a central role in daily life.
Sheep, goats and camels are raised not just for food and milk, but also for materials like wool and leather.
Camels in particular are incredibly valuable in the desert.
Known as the ships of the desert, they can travel long distances without water and carry heavy loads, making them essential for transport and trade.
Now, traditionally people live and move together in groups known as tribes.
The close-knit communities offer support, protection, and a strong sense of identity.
Moving together across the desert, tribes rely on cooperation and shared knowledge, such as how to find water sources or navigate using the stars.
And lastly, trade is another key part of Bedouin history.
These communities have long been known as skilled traders, traveling across vast deserts to exchange goods such as spices, textiles, and livestock.
Alongside trade, storytelling has been highly valued.
Traditions are passed down through generations such as stories, poetries and songs to help preserve their history, culture, and teach important lessons.
What's remarkable about this is how well adapted it is to the natural environment, using limited resources efficiently whilst creating really strong social bonds and really rich cultural heritage.

lessons.lessonTitle: Climate and biomes of the Middle East
lessons.unitTitle: The Middle East: How have natural resources shaped the Middle East?

lessonKeywords.description: a large region of the world with places that have similar climates, vegetation and animals that have adapted to living there
an average of weather conditions in a place over a long period of time (usually 30 years or more)
a place that receives less than 250 mm of precipitation a year
a geographic information system (GIS) is a computer mapping system that captures and displays geographic data to help understand spatial patterns

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The region has desert, temperate, and Mediterranean biomes.
Hot, dry summers and low rainfall shape the land.
It is cooler and wetter in the north of the Middle East.
Climate affects where people live.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Middle East is so vast that it contains a number of different biomes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Middle East is all desert.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how climate and biomes differ across the Middle East.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use climate graphs and satellite images to help students visualise differences. Students may struggle with abstract biome names unless shown what these places actually look like.

lessons.lessonTitle: GIS: Visualising the physical and human geography of the Middle East
lessons.unitTitle: The Middle East: How have natural resources shaped the Middle East?

lessonKeywords.description: made up of features that people have built or changed in the environment including cities, roads and farmland
made up of natural features created by Earth, including mountains, rivers, deserts, coastlines and climate
how things are linked and affect each other

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The Middle East is a region of the world that spans parts of western Asia, north Africa and southeastern Europe.
The Middle East has diverse physical and human landscapes.
GIS can be used to identify countries within the Middle East.
GIS can be used to analyse the relation between physical and human landscapes in the Middle East.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Rivers often flow through different climate zones, therefore their source may be in a mountainous area with high rainfall totals, but they may then flow through arid areas to the sea.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Rivers can't flow through areas with very low rainfall totals.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use GIS to locate the Middle East and analyse how urban populations are related to rainfall totals.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pupils may choose different variables to investigate depending upon the previous topics they have studied.

lessons.unitTitle: Weather and climate: how do they vary?

lessonKeywords.description: the day to day condition of the atmosphere, e.g. sunny, snowing, warm etc.
an average of weather conditions (e.g. rain, sun, wind) in a place taken over a long period of time (usually 30 years or more).
shows the amount of precipitation and the temperature each month for a location.
water that falls from the sky as rain, snow, hail or sleet.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Weather is the day to day atmospheric conditions whereas climate is the average weather conditions over 30 years.
Weather can be seasonal which means our weather changes throughout the year, such as in the UK.
Climate graphs show us the precipitation and temperature of a place over a calendar year.
Analysing climate graphs can help us describe patterns of the climate.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Pupils will explore that weather is the short term changes in the atmosphere whereas climate is long term changes in the atmospheric patterns of a place.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that weather and climate are the same.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can understand the difference between weather and climate, and use climate graphs to compare different climates.

teacherTips.teacherTip: A great way to help students remember the difference between weather and climate is by using the phrase "weather is what we get, and climate is what we expect!"

lessons.unitTitle: Weather and climate: how do they vary?

lessonKeywords.description: a large-scale and long-term change in the planet’s climate, including weather patterns and average temperatures
the reason why something happens
gases in Earth's atmosphere that trap heat
the retention of heat in the atmosphere caused by the build up of greenhouse gases

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are both human and physical causes of climate change.
Volcanoes, sunspots and Earth's changing orbit around the sun can change the climate.
Human activity since the industrial revolution has been blamed for climate change.
Greenhouse gases absorb energy from long-wave radiation and re-emit it back into our atmosphere.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Students will recognise that our climate changes naturally and there are physical causes of this. Humans have intensified the process in recent years.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Climate change is entirely caused by humans.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I understand the physical and human causes of climate change.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Reinforce that climate change is not just caused by humans, and that we do expect climate to change naturally over time.

Hi, geographers, my name's Ms. Hoggett and I'm really excited you're here to learn some geography with me today.

Climate change, cause, greenhouse gas, and greenhouse effect.

lessonKeywords.description: the process of something changing from a liquid state to a gaseous state
water that falls from the sky as rain, snow, hail or sleet
conversion of a substance from solid to a gaseous form

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Relief rainfall occurs when warm moist air from the ocean rises up over mountains.
Convectional rainfall occurs when the sun heats up the land, when it cools and condenses it forms rainclouds.
Frontal rainfall occurs when a warm front meets a cold front.
The west of the UK is generally wetter than the east.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Students will be exposed to the three different types of rainfall: relief, convectional, frontal.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: There is only one type of rain; it is all the same.

lessonKeywords.description: A number representing the total number of carbon dioxide or other greenhouses gases that an individual, product, person, or country produces.
Making changes to suit different conditions.
If something is sustainable it is able to continue over a long time.
Actions to reduce or prevent something.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are a range of things we can do to measure our impact on the planet.
Living more sustainably can help tackle climate change.
We can mitigate against climate change by: planting trees, international agreements, and using alternative energy.
We can adapt to climate change by: adapting agriculture, considering water supply, and protecting the land from erosion.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Adaptation helps us cope with climate change, but it doesn’t stop the problem from getting worse. Mitigation helps slow down climate change. The best approach is to use both mitigation and adaptation.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: It's fine to adapt or mitigate, we don't need to do both.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how we can mitigate against and adapt to climate change.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It's useful to use real-world examples to make the distinction between adaptation and mitigation clear. For example, show images of wind farms or electric cars to represent mitigation and flood barriers or drought-resistant crops to illustrate adaptation.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hi, geographers.
My name's Ms. Hoggett, and I'm really excited you're here to learn some geography with me today.
I'm sure if you try your best, you're going to be absolutely fantastic.
Don't worry too much if you haven't studied this topic before.
I'm here to help you every step of the way.
So the title for today's lesson is Actions to Tackle Climate Change, and this sits within the unit, Weather and climate, how do they vary? Our learning outcome for today's lesson is that I can describe how we can mitigate against and adapt to climate change.
To help us through this lesson today, we have a number of keywords that are going to be really useful for us.
Carbon footprint, adaptation, sustainable and mitigation.
A carbon footprint is a number representing the total number of carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gases that an individual product, person, or country produces.
Adaptation is about making changes to suit different conditions.
Sustainable, if something is sustainable, it is able to carry on over a long time and mitigation, actions taken to reduce or prevent something.
So our key words for today, carbon footprint, adaptation, sustainable and mitigation are really going to help us in today's lesson.
This lesson is split into three learning cycles.
How can we measure our impact on the planet? How can we mitigate against climate change? And how can we adapt to climate change? And we're going to start with our first learning cycle now.
How can we measure our impact on the planet? Every decision we make has an impact on the environment.
This can be anything from what we eat to how we travel.
Scientists have developed tools to help us measure the impact we have on the planet.
One of these tools is called a carbon footprint.
A carbon footprint is a number often measured in tons, kilograms, or grams. It represents the total number of carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gases that an individual, product, person or country produces.
So we all have our own carbon footprint.
Let's check your understanding of the learning so far.
Which of these is not a unit of measurement used to measure carbon footprint.
A, tons, B, milliliters, or C, grams? Pause the video and have a go at answering this question.
Well done if you said B, milliliters.
Tons and grams are both ways that we can measure carbon footprint.
Now, calculating our carbon footprint is really important as it helps us to understand the impact that we are having on the planet.
The larger the carbon footprint, the more greenhouse gases are released and the larger the impact this has on climate change.
The foods we consume add different amounts to our carbon footprint.
You can see on the screen here that one serving of pasta released 75 grams of CO2 into the atmosphere.
One dairy latte is 350 grams of CO2 and one potato is 40 grams of CO2.
Now, I don't know about you, but I think I normally eat more than that in a day.
So we can see that we are having a significant impact with just our meals when we are looking at our carbon footprint.
So let's check our understanding.
Which of the following modes of transport would contribute most to your carbon footprint? Would it be A, walk, B, public transport, or C, car? And this is based on a typical 2.
5 kilometer or 1.
55 mile journey.
Well done if you said car.
If we were looking at public transport, then lots of people are sharing one vehicle, which means it's going to be lower.
But car, you're generally traveling individually or in small groups.
So the amount of carbon dioxide being released per person is higher.
Now, if something is sustainable, it's able to carry on over a long time.
Therefore a smaller carbon footprint is going to be more sustainable.
We want to try and live more sustainably because that can help us to tackle climate change.
Each government tries to do this by setting their own targets to reduce their carbon footprint as not every country releases the same amount of CO2.
If they did, we'd all have the same targets, but that's why we all have to have different.
So countries in Asia and North America produce the most carbon dioxide, whereas countries in Africa only produce about three to 4% of global carbon dioxide emissions.
And therefore it'd be unfair for countries in those continents to have the same targets for reducing CO2.
We are now gonna have a go at practicing what we've learned so far and considering your own carbon footprint.
So I'd like you to take the quiz to determine your carbon footprint.
We'll read through the questions together.
What is your main mode of transport? A, walking or cycling.
B, public transport.
C, petrol or diesel car.
D, flying.
How do you stay warm at home? A, I wear extra layers.
B, I put the heating on low.
C, the heating is on, or D, we have an open fire.
How do you use electricity at home? A, I turn off lights and appliances when not in use.
B, I sometimes forget, but I do try to be mindful.
C, I leave things on standby often.
D, I use a lot of different appliances at once.
How do you shop for clothes? A, I buy secondhand or upcycle.
B, I buy new clothes and make them last.
C, I buy new clothes frequently or D, I buy fast fashion regularly.
How often do you eat meat? A, never, I'm vegetarian or vegan.
B, once or twice a week.
C, most days or D, every meal.
How do you dispose of waste? A, I recycle and compost everything.
B, I recycle but I don't compost.
C, I throw away most things and occasionally recycle.
D, I don't recycle at all.
How do you use water? A, I take short showers and conserve water.
B, I try to be mindful, but sometimes waste water.
C, I take long showers and leave taps running.
D, I use water without considering my impact.
How often do you travel long distances? A, rarely, I mostly stay local.
B, occasionally I go for holidays or family visits.
C, frequently by car or train or D, regularly by airplane.
Pause the video and have a go at reflecting on your answers.
Well done for completing that quiz.
Let's see what it tells us about your carbon footprint.
So what letter did you mostly get? I'd like you to compare that to the size of your carbon footprint and the smaller your carbon footprint, the more sustainable your actions are.
So if you put mostly A, then you have a really sustainable and small carbon footprint.
It gets bigger if it was B, bigger again if it was C, and if it was mostly D, you know that you have quite a large carbon footprint and you are not living as sustainably as possible.
Well done for completing learning cycle one.
We are now ready to move on to learning cycle number two.
How can we mitigate against climate change? So mitigation strategies are the actions taken to reduce or prevent the effects of climate change.
Scientists, governments, and individuals can all help mitigate against climate change.
It's something that we can all do and we can work together on.
True or false, mitigation strategies are the actions taken to adapt to the effects of climate change.
Pause the video and have a go at answering this question.
Well done if you said false.
We now know that mitigation strategies are the actions taken to reduce or prevent the effects of climate change.
So it's the preventative rather than the adaptation which comes after.
So we've got another quick check for understanding.
Who can help mitigate against climate change? Is it A, scientists, B, governments, C, individuals, or D, all of the above.
Pause the video and have a go at answering this question.
Well done if you said all of the above.
We know that mitigation is something that we can all achieve if we work together.
Now there are three key strategies for mitigation, planting trees, international agreements, and renewable energy.
We are going to go through these one by one to understand them a little bit more.
So trees absorb carbon dioxide, CO2.
And planting trees helps remove more CO2 from the atmosphere reducing the negative impacts of the greenhouse effect.
Now we know that across the world people are trying to plant more trees all the time, and this is because it plays such an important part in mitigating against climate change.
Our second strategy is international agreements and this is where countries work together to help us meet global targets quicker.
Now, we've already said that every country has their own targets, but they're all working towards the shared goal, which is to mitigate against climate change.
And this was discussed in 2015 where 195 countries met in Paris to sign something that we call the Paris Agreement.
This agreement was aimed at limiting global warming to less than two degrees Celsius globally, ideally 1.
5 degrees Celsius by 2030.
So the targets that countries are putting in place are to meet this shared goal of reducing global warming to less than two degrees Celsius a year by 2030.
And finally, we can look at renewable energy sources, because by using renewable energy sources such as wind and solar, we are reducing our dependence on fossil fuels, like coal and oil.
Burning fossil fuels contributes a lot of CO2 to the atmosphere, and so we know that is adding to climate change.
So if we look at more sustainable strategies and renewable energy such as solar power, hydroelectric power and wind power, we know that we are working to mitigate against climate change.
Let's check your understanding.
Which of the below are not a strategy to mitigate against climate change? Is it A, international agreements, B, planting trees, C, growing drought resistant crops, or D, using renewable energy sources? Pause the video and have a go answering this question.
Well done if you said, C, growing drought resistant crops.
We've just discussed that international agreements, planting trees and using renewable energy sources are all strategies to help mitigate against climate change.
Good work geographers.
Let's practice what we've learned so far in this learning cycle.
So Lucas and Laura have written pledges of things they will do to mitigate against climate change.
Laura says, "I pledge to plant three trees in the next year." Well done, Laura, that's great.
And Lucas says, "I'm going to learn more about the Paris Agreement so that I can educate others." And that's fantastic because it's sharing that common goal.
So I'd like you to write a pledge for one thing you are doing to mitigate against climate change.
Pause the video and have a go at writing your pledge.
Well done for giving that a really good go.
Now there's lots and lots of things you could have pledged to do here, but here are some examples of what your answer may have included.
I pledge to recycle more to reduce waste, to cut down on carbon emissions created from landfill.
I will switch off lights and appliances when not in use to save energy and reduce my carbon footprint.
And I pledge to walk whenever possible or use public transport to reduce carbon emissions from vehicles.
So if you had anything similar to that, you've done a fantastic job, but you might have had other things too.
And that's also great.
Well done geographers, you've done fantastically.
And we've now reached the end of learning cycle two.
Now ready to move on to learning cycle number three.
How can we adapt to climate change? So adaptation involves making changes to suit different conditions.
And in this context, the different conditions are the changing climate.
So how can we make changes in our actions and our behavior to suit the new climate that we're experiencing? Sam says, "Some places are facing more droughts, stronger storms, or rising sea levels.
And Izzy says, "So we need to think about how we can adapt to the impact of these." Let's check your understanding of that.
So add in the missing word to Andeep's sentence.
What involves making changes to suit different conditions? Pause the video and think about the word that needs to go in that gap.
Well done if you said adaptation, as Andeep correctly says, "Adaptation involves making changes to suit different conditions." Now there are different strategies for adaptation in the same way that there was for mitigation, but this time we are looking at growing drought resistant crops, building flood defenses and managing water sources.
The changing climate means that farmers in the UK may have to change what crops they grow on their farms. Now vineyards are becoming more common in the UK because the warmer climate means we now have temperatures warm enough to grow grapes.
This isn't something that we experienced before.
So that's a strategy that we can put in place to adapt to climate change.
Likewise, to help increase water sources in areas prone to drought, people may collect rain water and store it.
This can be done individually as well as on much larger scales.
Now the velodrome of the London Olympic Park is designed to harvest rainwater.
You might have a water butt in your garden which collects rainwater and stores it.
And lastly, being an island nation, the UK is particularly vulnerable to flooding caused by rising sea levels.
At Dawlish Warren, in Devon, thousands of pounds have been spent on sea defenses to protect the landscape from erosion.
And you can see that in the image there.
Let's check your understanding.
Which of the below are not a strategy to adapt to climate change? Is it A, international agreements, B, managing water sources, C, growing drought resistant crops, or D building flood defenses? Pause the video and have a go answering that question.
Well done, if you said A, international agreements.
We discussed earlier that international agreements are an example of mitigation.
But as we've just seen, managing water sources, growing drought resistant crops and building flood defenses are all examples of ways we can adapt to climate change.
Now it's important that we actually do use adaptation and mitigation strategies together to respond to climate change.
This is important because mitigation actually slows down climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
And without mitigation, carbon dioxide levels will continue to rise.
But adaptation ensures that communities can cope with the impacts of climate change that are already happening.
So we need to take that mitigation and that adaptation together in order to have that best response.
So we're going to practice what we've learned so far, and I'd like you to firstly complete the table explaining why each method for adaptation is important.
So you can see there you've got your adaptation strategy such as growing drought resistant crops, building flood defenses, and managing water sources.
And then you have a space for explanation.
And the second part of this practice task is to explain why we should consider adaptation and mitigation strategies when trying to tackle climate change.
Pause the video and have a go at completing this practice task.
Well done for giving that a really good go geographers.
You've done fantastically today.
Let's check your answers and see what your table may have looked like.
So the adaptation strategy of growing drought resistant crops can be explained by saying, it ensures food supplies are maintained in regions affected by climate change, as it reduces the risk of crop failure.
Building flood defenses.
We could say it protects communities and ecosystems from damage caused by floods, reducing costs, and preventing loss of life.
And then lastly, for managing water sources, we could have said that it helps maintain a stable water supply for drinking, farming, and industry, ensuring long-term sustainability of water supplies.
Well done if you've got that one spot on.
For part two, which was, explain why we should consider adaptation and mitigation strategies when trying to tackle climate change, we could have said, we should consider both adaptation and mitigation strategies when tackling climate change because they help us deal with its effects in different ways.
Mitigation focuses on reducing the causes of climate change like cutting down greenhouse gas emissions by using renewable energy or planting more trees.
This helps slow down global warming.
Adaptation is about making changes to cope with the effects of climate change, like building flood defenses or growing drought resistant crops.
This is important because some of the effects of climate change are already happening.
So we need to be prepared.
Using both strategies together gives us the best chance of protecting people, the environment, and the economy.
So it is important and as we can see from this answer that we consider our response and use both adaptation and mitigation strategies when trying to tackle climate change.
Well done geographers, you've done brilliantly today.
So to summarize our lesson on actions to tackle climate change, we've got that we can use carbon footprints to measure our impact on the planet.
Living more sustainably can help tackle climate change.
We can mitigate against climate change by planting trees, international agreements and using alternative energy.
And adaptation to climate change includes adapting agriculture, considering water supply, and protecting the land from erosion.
Geographers, you've been absolutely fantastic today and you've done a brilliant job.
I look forward to seeing you in our next lesson, and I hope you have a great rest of your day.

Surface pressure charts are important

00:04:56.970 --> 00:05:00.180
Now weather can also be represented using symbols.

116
00:05:03.780 --> 00:05:05.340

00:05:07.590 --> 00:05:09.690

what these symbols represent based on what you already know.

How many did you get?

Let's see which ones we got right.

00:05:23.820 --> 00:05:26.580
Some commonly used weather symbols include

00:05:26.580 --> 00:05:30.030
a sunny day represented by a small yellow sun,

cloudy, represented by a single white cloud.

125
00:05:33.420 --> 00:05:35.880
If there's a light rain shower expected in the day,

00:05:35.880 --> 00:05:38.580
we might see a cloud with a little bit of rain

127
00:05:38.580 --> 00:05:40.230
and half a sun in the background.

128
00:05:41.550 --> 00:05:44.523
A gray cloud that says hail underneath represents hail,

129
00:05:45.390 --> 00:05:49.260
a white cloud with drizzle underneath represents drizzle,

130
00:05:49.260 --> 00:05:50.970
a gray cloud with a snowflake

00:05:50.970 --> 00:05:54.060
and a rain drop underneath represents sleet,

00:05:54.060 --> 00:05:56.820
but if it just has two snowflakes underneath,

00:06:00.240 --> 00:06:03.210
This box that says fog represents fog,

00:06:03.210 --> 00:06:05.550
if there's heavy rain, there'll be a dark gray cloud

00:06:05.550 --> 00:06:07.140
with two raindrops,

00:06:07.140 --> 00:06:09.240
and if there's thunder and lightning expected,

00:06:09.240 --> 00:06:13.470
we would see a lightning bolt in front of a gray cloud.

139
00:06:13.470 --> 00:06:16.383
So these are some of the commonly used weather symbols.

140
00:06:17.940 --> 00:06:19.950
Now weather forecasts are really useful

141
00:06:19.950 --> 00:06:22.680
as they help people know how to plan their day.

142
00:06:22.680 --> 00:06:24.780
Aisha says, "I packed sunglasses

00:06:24.780 --> 00:06:27.090
as I thought it would be a sunny day today,"

00:06:27.090 --> 00:06:29.850
but Lucas says, "Well, I packed my umbrella

00:06:29.850 --> 00:06:32.400
because the weather forecast predicted rain."

00:06:32.400 --> 00:06:35.610
So Lucas used the weather forecast to help prepare him

00:06:35.610 --> 00:06:38.430
with what he needed to take for the day.

00:06:38.430 --> 00:06:40.380
Sometimes this can impact people's jobs,

149
00:06:40.380 --> 00:06:43.260
particularly if they have jobs that work outside.

150
00:06:43.260 --> 00:06:46.293
So it can help people know how to prepare for their day.

00:06:48.780 --> 00:06:51.300
We are now gonna practice what we've learned so far.

So in the boxes, I'd like you to write the correct type

00:06:54.210 --> 00:06:56.403
of weather being shown by each symbol.

Pause the video and have a go at completing

00:06:59.730 --> 00:07:01.023
this practice task.

Let's check your answer.

So our first symbol, the yellow sun represents a sunny day,

00:07:15.240 --> 00:07:17.820
our white cloud is cloudy,

160
00:07:17.820 --> 00:07:20.970
then we have a light rain shower during the day,

00:07:20.970 --> 00:07:25.230
then we have hail, drizzle, we then have sleet,

heavy snow, fog, heavy rain and thunder.
