lessons.unitTitle: Cities: What are they like to live in?

lessonKeywords.description: the increase in the proportion of people living in towns and cities
when a population grows because births outnumber deaths
the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The urban hierarchy explains how settlements range from small villages to global cities based on size and function.
Urbanisation is the growth of urban areas and is a phenomenon experienced globally.
The location of the biggest cities in the world has changed over time from high to low and middle income countries..
The two main causes of urbanisation are rural to urban migration and natural increase.
In 2008, for the first time in world history, over 50% of the world's population lived in towns and cities.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Urbanisation is occurring fastest in low and middle income countries due to rapid population growth and rural to urban migration
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Urbanisation only happens in rich countries.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the process of urban growth and describe the distribution of cities around the world.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use Our World in Data to show interactive graphs on urban population growth. Let students explore how urbanisation rates differ between HICs, NICs, and LICs to visualise global trends and challenge misconceptions.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, my name is Mrs. Gray, and I'm so excited that you've decided to join me to learn geography today.
Today's lesson is in our unit of cities: what are they like to live in? And the title of today's lesson is The Growth of Cities.
By the end of the lesson, you will be able to explain the process of urban growth and describe the distribution of cities around the world.
There are some keywords that will come across in today's lesson.
They are urbanization, natural increase, and rural-to-urban migration.
Urbanization is an increase in the proportion of people living in towns and cities.
Natural increase is when a population grows because births outnumber deaths.
And rural-to-urban migration is the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities.
Today's lesson on the growth of cities is split into two learning cycles.
The first, how do cities grow and change? And the second learning cycle is where are the world's biggest cities? So let's take a look at the first learning cycle: How do cities grow and change? All settlements are different.
They are different sizes and have different functions.
One measure of size is population, the number of people that are living in that settlement.
Settlements can be ranked by size and function, by how big they are and how they work, what they're used for.
This is called the settlement hierarchy.
And this is an image of the settlement hierarchy.
So at the bottom there, we have a hamlet.
The next level up, a village.
The next level up, a town.
Then a city.
And at the very top, a global city.
Larger settlements offer more services and jobs than the smaller settlements.
A city functions as a regional center for commerce and industry, providing services not found elsewhere.
So a city has a large population, more varied jobs, different types of public transport, hospitals, schools, and entertainment.
Whereas a village has few people and a limited range of services.
For example, a few shops, or one or two schools.
So you can see a big difference there between the services provided by a city and by a village.
So a quick check now then.
Rank these settlements from largest to smallest.
So we have town, hamlet, city, village, global city.
So put them in order from the largest down to the smallest.
Pause the video, write down your answer, and then come back and let's see how you got on.
Okay.
How did you get on? Rank these settlements from the largest to smallest.
And the answer is: global city, then city, then town, then village, then hamlet.
The global city is the biggest settlement, and the hamlet is the smallest settlement.
Well done.
Now urban areas all over the world are growing.
We've got a line graph to have a little look at that.
Just take a minute to have a little look at that line graph.
See what you can see.
So this line graph shows the change in urban and rural population by percentage globally from 1980 to 2025.
And we can see the percentage of the population at the side.
And the urban population, the percentage of the population that's urban, is shown in blue.
And the percentage of the population that's rural is shown in pink.
So the proportion of people living in urban areas compared with rural areas is increasing.
And you can see that, can't you? Because the blue line is going up, so the proportion of people living in an urban area is increasing.
And at the same time, that rural line, the pink one, the proportion of people living in a rural area, is decreasing.
This is called urbanization, when the proportion of people living in urban areas compared to rural areas increases.
Now urbanization is not just happening in richer countries.
In 2008, for the first time in world history, over 50% of the world's population lived in towns and cities.
And you can see from that graph that that's continued to increase.
The gap has got wider, so we've got more people living in urban areas, well, proportion of people living in urban areas, than in rural areas, a higher proportion.
So one other check for us now then.
Why was 2008 a significant year for the world's population? Got a graph there for you to have a look at.
Is it A, over 50% of the world's population lived in urban areas? Is it B, over 50% of the world's population lived in rural areas? Or is it C, urbanization began to slow? So pause the video, write down your answer, and then come back and let's see how you got on.
Okay.
How did you get on? Why was 2008 a significant year for the world's population? And the answer is A, over 50% of the world's population lived in urban areas.
Did you get that right? Well done.
Now, urban areas grow for different reasons.
And there's two main reasons for urban growth are: rural-to-urban migration and natural increase.
And we're going to look at each of those two things now in a little bit more detail.
So rural-to-urban migration is when people move from the countryside to towns and cities.
So people move from countryside areas and live into towns and cities.
That's rural-to-urban migration.
They're migrating from a rural area into an urban area.
Rural-to-urban migration happens all over.
We can see here in London.
And we've got an example of people moving from the countryside into London.
So in the countryside surrounding it into London, which is the capital of the UK.
That's an example of where rural-to-urban migration is happening.
Motorways, airports, railways, and the Tube give easy access to jobs and services in London, which is a reason why people are wanting to live there.
You can see an image there of the Tube, which gives people the ability to transport easily from one place to another in London.
And you can see an OS map there of London.
You can see the airports is a little gray symbol with an airplane on.
That shows the airports.
And you can see lots and lots and lots of roads.
There's a very big road network.
The blue lines are motorways.
And then we can see the airroads or the green lines.
Lots and lots of transport in and around London.
Shops in a variety of industries also attract people to cities.
In London, banks, technology companies, the National Health Service, and the tourist industry are all really big employers, so lots of people want to move to London and live in London for access to all of those different jobs in all those different industries.
Another check for us now then.
True or false? Good transport links can encourage rural-to-urban migration.
Is that true or false? So pause the video, write down your answer, and then come back and let's see how you got on.
Okay.
How did you get on? True or false, good transport links can encourage rural-to-urban migration? That's true.
Why is it true? Good transport links lead to rural-to-urban migration because they give easy access to jobs and services, making an area more attractive for people to live and work.
Did you get that right? Well done.
So let's take a look at natural increase now then.
We've looked at rural-to-urban migration.
Now we're going to look at natural increase.
So natural increase is when there are more births than deaths, yeah? The birth rate is higher than the death rate.
And when that happens, when the birth rate is greater than the death rate, then the population gets bigger, yeah? Because more people are being born than are dying, and therefore there's going to be more people.
And that is called natural increase.
So another check now.

Is that true or false? Pause the video, write down your answer, and then come back and let's see how you got on.

Did you get that right?

Well done.

The location of the world's biggest mega cities

You can see some images of those two cities

Now, many are in MICs and LICs like China, India,

So there are five mistakes in that paragraph.

Urbanization in high-income countries started earlier.

In LICs and MICs, many people still live in rural areas,

00:20:13.830 --> 00:20:15.900

from high-income countries

lessons.lessonTitle: GIS: Visualising and analysing the growth of cities
lessons.unitTitle: Cities: What are they like to live in?

lessonKeywords.description: a city with a population over 10 million
a composite measure of development that gives a score between 0 and 1, based on indicators of health, education, and income
a background map or satellite image you can choose in GIS that lets you add other layers of information on top

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: GIS can be used to visualise cities around the world.
India and China now have a large number of megacities.
Cities with a lower HDI often have faster growth rates than cities with a higher HDI.
GIS can be used to analyse the growth of different cities around the world.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Cities are growing at different rates around the world. Often, cities in countries with a lower HDI are growing more rapidly than cities in countries with a higher HDI.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Cities are growing at the same rate everywhere around the world.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use GIS to visualise and analyse the growth of cities around the world.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pupils can study the cities which are referred to in other parts of your curriculum. This will help pupils make links with other topics of study.

lessonKeywords.description: the movement of water (through pipes or via canals or rivers) from areas of water surplus to areas of water deficit
when the demand for water exceeds the available amount during a certain period or when poor quality restricts its use
a measure used to assess the suitability of water for drinking and for supporting river ecosystems

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Changing demand and provision of water in the UK creates opportunities and challanges.
Demand for water is changing and there are issues matching supply to demand.
There is a need for water transfers within the UK to maintain supplies.
There are various causes of water pollution including agricultural runoff, industrial discharges and sewage spills.
Pollution management is needed to maintain water quality and protect the environment.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Few water systems link wastewater treatment plants to the supply system, with treated water going into covered reservoirs before the clean water network. Most release treated wastewater into rivers; from where it is abstracted downstream, later on.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Our wastewater is treated and sent straight to our taps, to drink.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how changing demand for water in the UK creates opportunities and challenges.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If you plan to study the water lessons, within the Global pattern of resources topic, you will have opportunites to reinforce the impact of water quality on water security. If not, this is the opportunity to discuss the link water quality and the environment with your future domestic consumers.

lessonKeywords.description: food grown without the use of artificial chemicals, such as fertiliser and pesticide
a measurement of all greenhouse gas emissions associated with a good or service (or lifestyle), expressed as tonnes (or kg) of carbon dioxide equivalent
an intensive farming system often involving high capital costs to maximise profits
the distance food is transported from the producer to consumers

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Changing demand for food in the UK creates opportunities and challenges.
There is growing demand for high-value food exports from LICs, seasonal food (all-year) and organic produce.
There is a move towards local food sourcing to reduce carbon footprints.
There is a trend towards agribusiness.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Organic farming does involve the use of fertiliser but not the use of artificial chemical fertiliser (e.g. derived from fossil fuels). For example, farmyard manure is a good source of nutrients for crops on an organic farm but so too is seaweed.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Organic farmers do not use fertiliser on their crops.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how changing demand for food in the UK creates opportunities and challenges.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Your students' understanding of agribusiness and the impacts of different methods of food production on the environment will be further developed, if you do the food option within the global resources topic. If not, this is a key lesson for help students understand their role as consumers.

lessonKeywords.description: natural sources of energy that will run out because they cannot be reproduced, such as fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas) and nuclear power (uranium)
the release of carbon into the atmosphere, contributing to the greenhouse effect and global warming
the combination of different energy sources used by a country or a region. The energy mix can change over time
natural sources of energy that will never run out, such as wind, water and solar energy

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Changing demand and provision of energy in the UK creates opportunities and challanges.
The energy mix in the UK is changing.
There are reduced domestic supplies of coal, gas and oil.
There are economic and environmental issues associated with energy exploitation.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Renewables and recyclables can have environmental consequences too, although they generally cause less harm than fossil fuels. These consequences can include impacts on biodiversity and the ability of ecosystems to absorb carbon dioxide.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Only the extraction and use of non-renewable energy has environmental consequences.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can discuss opportunities and challenges resulting from the UK's changing energy mix.

teacherTips.teacherTip: GIS offers excellent opportunities to identify and assess (e.g. measure change over time) environmental impacts of energy extraction and generation in the UK landscape.

lessons.lessonTitle: The importance of food, water and energy for human development

lessonKeywords.description: materials available in the environment (such as water, food and oil) that support our wants and needs
not consuming enough calories (or nutrients) to maintain a normal, active, healthy life
systems designed to protect public health, such as disposing of sewage and other waste products

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Food, water and energy affect economic and social well-being and are fundamental to human development.
There are global inequalities in the supply and consumption of: food, water and energy resources.
Around 10% of people worldwide face hunger; between 740-780 million people.
There is overlap between regions in which many face hunger and those in which many lack safe water and/or electricity.
Supply  (or lack of resources) limits consumption in some locations, as does poverty.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Having access to electricity means having an electricity source that can provide lighting and charge a phone or radio for 4 hours a day. In LICs, and some NEEs, electricity outages are part of daily life.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Access to electricity means 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the significance of food, water and energy to well-being and describe global inequalities in supply and consumption of these resources.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There will be opportunities to reinforce key ideas about inequality and resource management in later lessons looking at global resources; choose between food, water and energy for your students key focus.

lessons.lessonTitle: The tropical rainforest in the Democratic Republic of Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: areas of dense forest found close to the Equator where it is warm and there are high levels of rainfall
the complete removal of trees
anything that absorbs and stores more carbon dioxide than it releases
all the living things in an ecosystem or area

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The Congo is the world's second largest tropical rainforest.
The Congo rainforest is in the Congo Basin, which spans 6 countries.
Over 400 species of mammal live in the Congo, including gorillas and okapi.
32 billion tonnes of carbon is stored in trees and plants in the Congo rainforest.
Deforestation threatens biodiversity and local communities that depend on the forest.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Congo rainforest is found in the Congo Basin, which spans six countries in Africa: Cameroon, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That the Congo rainforest is only found in the DRC.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the importance of the Congo rainforest and the threats it faces.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Remember that several of the causes of deforestation can happen by legal means or illegally. For example, logging may be done by commercial companies or through illegal activity. Whether legal or illegal, they all contribute to the total deforestation experienced in the DRC each year.

lessons.lessonTitle: Climate change and the Democratic Republic of the Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: a large-scale and long-term change in the planet’s climate, including weather patterns and average temperatures
anything that absorbs and stores more carbon dioxide than it releases
all the living things in an ecosystem or area
the science and practice of cultivating soil and farming
not being able to regularly access enough safe and nutritious food to live, work and play

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Climate change is causing rising temperatures, extreme weather, and habitat loss in the DRC.
Deforestation is reducing the rainforest's ability to absorb carbon dioxide.
Flooding and droughts are affecting agriculture and food security.
The DRC's role in climate action is crucial for global environmental health.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Tropical rainforests are rich in biodiversity and play a crucial role in regulating Earth's climate as carbon sinks. Rainforests in Africa or Asia are as important as the Amazon in South America, so global climate action is needed to protect them.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That the most important rainforest to protect is the Amazon and that other rainforests are smaller so they don't matter as much.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how climate change is affecting the DRC and its people.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students could work in groups to do some research about organisations working to conserve the rainforest in the DRC. Then each group could give a presentation about their findings. Remind students to use trustworthy sources of data when researching online.

lessons.lessonTitle: Conservation in the Democratic Republic of Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: a large area of land protected by law to keep the natural environment safe
all the living things in an ecosystem or area
a species of plant or animal in danger of extinction
the illegal hunting or capturing of wild animals

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The DRC has several national parks that protect endangered species.
Virunga National Park is home to rare mountain gorillas but faces threats from poaching and conflict.
Conservation efforts must balance protecting nature with supporting local communities.
International organisations and local people are working to protect the rainforest and wildlife in the DRC.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Poaching happens on a daily basis all around the world as a means of organised illegal activity (but in some cases for survival). It can include any animal species, large or small, that has a perceived value in its meat, skin, or another biproduct.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That poaching only involves 'trophy' animals like elephants and wild cats.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe conservation efforts in the DRC and explain why they are important.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Watch out for National Park and 'national park'. Named parks such as Virunga National Park do have upper case letters as they are part of a proper noun, whereas national parks in general do not have any upper case letters.

lessons.lessonTitle: Population of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: the number of people living in a defined area, e.g. 300 people per square kilometre
a chart representing the population structure of a given location
the middle value of a set of data when all values are placed in numerical order
the number of live births per 1000 people per year
the average age a person will reach in a given location

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The DRC has a population distribution of around 45 people per square kilometre due to its sheer size.
Just over half of the people live in rural areas, but Kinshasa is one of the fastest-growing cities in the world.
Population pyramids represent the population structure of a given location.
The median age in the DRC is 18.8 years, however half of the population are under 15 years old.
High birth rates and low life expectancy impact population growth.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A population pyramid provides information about the structure of the population; the age and gender profile of the location represented. This can help governments with future planning.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Population pyramids only show us the total population size.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe where people live in the DRC and describe what the population structure of the DRC is like.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Compare the population pyramid of the DRC with population pyramids for other countries at various stages of development. Ask students what they notice, what is similar and what is different about the population structures of each country. Can they suggest reasons for the differences?

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of violence or suffering
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Depiction or discussion of famine, disease, natural disasters.

lessons.lessonTitle: A sustainable future for the Democratic Republic of Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: development that meets the needs of the present, without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
renewable energy is sources of energy that can be reused and will not be used up or run out
the careful protection of something

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The DRC has potential for sustainable development through renewable energy and responsible resource management.
Hydropower from the Congo River could provide electricity to millions.
Community-led conservation and fair trade practices can improve livelihoods.
International support and government policies will shape the country's future.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The government of the DRC has many departments focussed on a variety of areas from energy and industries to farming and conservation. The government makes policies and pledges in a number of contexts, not only in defence and military matters.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That the government of the DRC is only concerned with the military and defence and not with other important matters that affect the people.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can suggest ways the DRC can develop sustainably while protecting its environment and people.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could extend the task in Activity C to become group work or a whole class debate by putting students into groups which agree or disagree with the statement and asking them to put forward their reasoning.

lessons.lessonTitle: Physical landscapes of the Democratic Republic of Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: hydroelectric power generates electricity by using water
volcanic describes something that is created by a volcano
a valley is a long, low-lying area of land surrounded by hills or mountains
natural resources are those that come from Earth without human influence and can be used for human needs

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The DRC's physical geography includes mountains, lakes, rivers, and the Congo Basin.
The Congo River is the second longest river in Africa and is important for transport and hydroelectric power.
The Great Rift Valley runs through the eastern DRC, forming mountains and volcanoes.
Natural landscapes affect where people live and how they use resources.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The DRC and the Republic of Congo are two separate countries in central Africa. The Congo River forms part of the border between the countries; their capital cities Kinshasa and Brazzaville are located on oppposite banks of the river from each other.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That the Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighbouring country, the Republic of Congo, are the same country. Students can inadvertently shorten DRC to 'Congo' in verbal or written work.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify and explain the importance of the DRC's key physical features.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Give students a blank outline map of the DRC and ask them to annotate it or shade it to show key features of the physical landscape such as the Great Rift Valley and the Congo River.

lessons.lessonTitle: Colonial history and legacy of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: a country or area that is controlled by another country and has people living there from the controlling country
something handed down or passed on from an earlier generation
resources that come from Earth without human influence and can be used for human needs
the dividing lines between two countries
to use something for personal benefit

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The DRC was a former Belgian colony and has had multiple names over time including the Belgian Congo and Zaire.
King Leopold II exploited the country's natural resources and people, causing millions of deaths.
After independence in 1960, the DRC faced political instability and conflict.
Colonial borders and exploitation still affect the DRC today.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: History has shown that in many countries borders move, countries expand or shrink and the name of any given country is not fixed and permanent. These things are often the result of conflict or warfare which causes significant political change.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That countries are always the same shape and size, with the same borders and the same name throughout their history and that these aspects will never change.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the impact of colonial rule on the DRC and its lasting effects.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Read a passage from Conrad's 'Heart of darkness' to get pupils thinking about the impact of colonialism in the DRC.

lessons.lessonTitle: Resources in the Democratic Republic of Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: natural resources are those that come from Earth without human influence and can be used for human needs
mining is the process of digging into the ground to remove natural resources
the economy is the way money in a particular area is made and spent

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The DRC has abundant natural resources, including coltan, diamonds, and copper.
In the DRC, most mining occurs in the east and southeast of the country.
The natural resources of the DRC are essential for global industries, including technology and energy.
Many of the DRC's natural resources are owned by companies in other countries.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Some natural resources are found deep underground, like ores of some metals and fossil fuels. Others are not found underground, for example the rainforest trees that are used for timber or as a source of rubber, or water sources like lakes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That all natural resources are found deep underground and so need to be mined to extract them.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the DRC's natural resources and their role in the global economy.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Put the question to the class to think about whether they have used any items that could contain resources that originated in the DRC. Have they used any technology such as a mobile phone or computer? Could the components of their devices be linked to the DRC?

lessons.lessonTitle: Life in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: something to do with the countryside
something to do with a city or town
farming that provides enough food for the farmer and their family to live on, rather than for them to sell
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there for some time
jobs that are not officially recorded or regulated and do not involve the payment of taxes

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Life in the DRC varies greatly between rural villages and urban areas like Kinshasa.
Rural life relies on subsistence farming and small-scale trade.
Urban life includes a wide range of jobs, from informal market vendors to high-income professionals.
High-income careers exist in areas such as banking and the oil and mining industries.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Cities are often perceived to have better or more housing but this is not always the case. Inner city housing can be small and run down; people who move to cities may not find accomodation at all and may have to live in informal settlements.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That housing in cities is better / bigger / cheaper / more available than in rural areas.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can compare urban and rural life in the DRC.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There is opportunity for further research and comparison between the earnings of people in various industries of the DRC and people in the same industries and professions in other countries. Direct comparisons like this can be useful in making situations more tangible for students to understand.

lessons.lessonTitle: Climate and biomes of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: a large region of the world with places that have similar climates, vegetation and animals that have adapted to living there
a climate with consistently high temperatures, frequent high rainfall and a very short dry season, found in locations near the Equator
a biome that is predominantly grassland with scattered trees and shrubs, found in locations near the Equator
a biome where the land is either permanently or seasonally flooded or saturated

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The DRC has an equatorial climate with high temperatures and heavy rainfall.
The country is home to diverse biomes, including rainforest, savanna, and wetlands.
The climate creates opportunities and challenges for agriculture, wildlife, and human settlements.
Some areas face seasonal flooding, while others experience drought.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Heavy rainfall is experienced in some parts of the DRC such as rainforests whilst other parts such as savanna are very dry. Furthermore rainforests are depleting and savanna is expanding as global temperatures are rising, increasing risks of drought.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That places which experience rain, particularly heavy rain as in the DRC, musn't experience water scarcity or drought.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the climate and major biomes of the DRC.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Put students into groups and allocate each group either an animal or a crop of the DRC. Ask them to research and report on what makes their animal or crop suited to growth in the DRC climate, and exactly where and how it grows or lives. Examples include crops like cassava, or animals of the savanna.

Hi, there.
I'm Ms. Roberts, and this is a geography lesson from our unit of work all about the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
We are investigating the opportunities, as well as the challenges that are faced by that country.
In this lesson today, we are exploring the climate and the biomes that we can find in the DRC.
By the end of the lesson today, you will be able to describe what the climate is and what the major biomes of the DRC are.

So let's have a look at our keywords for today's lesson.
You have heard our first keyword today already, and that is biome.
Bio is to do with life, isn't it? To do with living things.
And a biome is a very large region of the world, and within that region, the places share a very similar climate and the vegetation and all of the animals that have adapted to living there are shared in that place.
So that's one biome.
For example, a rainforest.
Next we have equatorial climate.
Now, this is the climate of the DRC.

It rains and rains and rains all the time.
It may or may not include a very, very short dry season.
And this type of climate is only found in locations that are on or near the equator.
It's exclusive to that area.
We can't find this climate anywhere else, which is why it's called equatorial.
The next two keywords are both types of biomes.
We have the savanna, which is a grassland biome that has some scattered trees, some shrubs, and this is also found in locations that are near the equator.
And then secondly, we have wetlands.
There are a wide range of different types of wetlands, but the key thing about a wetland biome is that all of the land within it is either permanently flooded or permanently saturated, meaning wet, okay? And this is a type of land that's very, very wet.
We're not talking about rivers or lakes or seas here.
This is a biome, and it's saturated land.
Today's lesson has got two parts.
First of all, we need to investigate what the climate of the DRC is and what the biomes are.
So we're going to do that in the first half of the lesson.
In the second half of the lesson, we're going to think some more about the effects that climate has in the DRC.
So let's begin now by exploring the climate and biomes in some more detail.
The DRC is the second largest country in Africa.
I have put a circle around it there.
There are 13 countries in the world that sit on the equator.
You can see the equator there running through the north of the DRC.
Now, I'm not going to name the other 12 countries, but maybe after this lesson, you could go and find out what they are.
Due to this equatorial position being sat where it is with the equator running through it, the DRC is a location on Earth that experiences the equatorial climate.
This means that in this climate zone, the weather patterns are the same all year round.
There's no different seasons.
There's no spring, summer, autumn, winter.
And in the equatorial climate, there is frequent heavy rainfall.
If you look at this picture here, we can see some beautiful lush green trees, but what we can see even more is teems of rain coming down almost like sheets of water there.

And when they reach those places, the sun's rays spread out across a greater area.
Rays of light that comes straight from the sun to the equator travel a shorter distance.
And because of the curvature of the Earth, when they hit the equator and the land surrounding it, those rays of light have to focus a smaller area.
That's what creates this equatorial climate.
You can see the yellow at the top there that shows you how the heat from the sun, the solar radiation, is spread over a greater area nearer to the poles, whereas at the equator here in the middle, the solar radiation is more concentrated in a smaller area.

and we have areas of savanna.

537
00:29:27.803 --> 00:29:29.970
In the wetlands, those hippos, they love it.

538
00:29:29.970 --> 00:29:32.163
They love that rain creating all that mud.

539
00:29:33.660 --> 00:29:36.870
Humans, not so much.

540
00:29:36.870 --> 00:29:39.300
It can be very, very challenging,

541
00:29:39.300 --> 00:29:42.199
and this increasing of torrential rainfall

542
00:29:42.199 --> 00:29:43.950
can lead to flooding,

543
00:29:43.950 --> 00:29:48.950
which can have very serious impacts for human populations.

544
00:29:49.380 --> 00:29:54.180
And in 2024, the worst floods that had happened

545
00:29:54.180 --> 00:29:58.200
for many, many years happened in the DRC.

546
00:29:58.200 --> 00:30:01.680
The Congo River burst its banks.

547
00:30:01.680 --> 00:30:05.130
In fact, by January of 2024,

548
00:30:05.130 --> 00:30:06.390
which was three months

549
00:30:06.390 --> 00:30:09.780
after the torrential rainfall had started,

550
00:30:09.780 --> 00:30:14.780
it was reported that over 300 people had died

551
00:30:14.880 --> 00:30:17.283
as a result of the heavy rain and flooding.

552
00:30:18.720 --> 00:30:20.640
More than half the country

553
00:30:20.640 --> 00:30:23.793
had been forced to evacuate from their own homes.

554
00:30:24.870 --> 00:30:26.910
There was also extensive damage

555
00:30:26.910 --> 00:30:30.300
to very important public community places

556
00:30:30.300 --> 00:30:34.860
like schools and markets and health centers.

557
00:30:34.860 --> 00:30:37.800
And helping to recover from the floods

558
00:30:37.800 --> 00:30:40.350
was being made even more challenging

559
00:30:40.350 --> 00:30:44.160
because roads have been damaged and destroyed by the floods.

560
00:30:44.160 --> 00:30:47.700
These torrential downpours are accompanied

561
00:30:47.700 --> 00:30:50.760
by ever-increasing temperatures,

562
00:30:50.760 --> 00:30:55.760
which is also not very good for the human populations.

563
00:30:56.880 --> 00:31:01.530
Extremely high temperatures can lead to water scarcity,

564
00:31:01.530 --> 00:31:03.333
or worse, to drought.

565
00:31:05.460 --> 00:31:08.550
The extent of areas in the DRC

566
00:31:08.550 --> 00:31:11.850
that are at risk of drought are expanding,

567
00:31:11.850 --> 00:31:15.300
and that's because of the increasing temperatures.

568
00:31:15.300 --> 00:31:18.030
The temperatures are increasing,

569
00:31:18.030 --> 00:31:22.503
the rainforest is shrinking, and the savanna is expanding.

570
00:31:23.970 --> 00:31:28.970
A report published in 2022 by a charity called WaterAid

571
00:31:29.940 --> 00:31:34.940
warned that up to 40% of land was already being impacted

572
00:31:35.843 --> 00:31:37.753
by drought in the DRC

573
00:31:38.937 --> 00:31:41.370
and that, over the coming decade,

574
00:31:41.370 --> 00:31:43.953
this was only going to increase.

575
00:31:45.390 --> 00:31:48.270
What a great contrast to see

576
00:31:48.270 --> 00:31:51.450
how excessive rainfall and flooding

577
00:31:51.450 --> 00:31:53.520
can affect people in the same country

578
00:31:53.520 --> 00:31:57.543
just as much as a lack of water and drought can.

579
00:31:58.920 --> 00:32:02.880
Izzy and Sam have been talking about this situation.

580
00:32:02.880 --> 00:32:06.030
I'm not quite sure if they're both right though.

581
00:32:06.030 --> 00:32:07.890
So read what they say

582
00:32:07.890 --> 00:32:10.743
and decide who you think is correct.

583
00:32:17.700 --> 00:32:22.500
I think that Izzy is actually correct in this case.

584
00:32:22.500 --> 00:32:24.150
And the reason I think that

585
00:32:24.150 --> 00:32:28.350
is because the savanna is expanding,

586
00:32:28.350 --> 00:32:31.410
and more and more areas of the DRC

587
00:32:31.410 --> 00:32:33.930
are becoming at risk of drought every year.

588
00:32:33.930 --> 00:32:37.923
And that's due to rising global temperatures.

589
00:32:39.030 --> 00:32:41.040
It's time for some activities now

590
00:32:41.040 --> 00:32:43.413
to finish off this lesson together.

591
00:32:44.460 --> 00:32:46.620
First of all, in task one,

592
00:32:46.620 --> 00:32:49.470
I have produced a table of data for you.

593
00:32:49.470 --> 00:32:53.490
The table shows some crops that are produced in the DRC

594
00:32:53.490 --> 00:32:55.950
and tells you the average production

595
00:32:55.950 --> 00:32:59.520
in millions of tons per year for each crop.

596
00:32:59.520 --> 00:33:03.030
I would like you to put that information

into a bar chart, please.

598
00:33:08.220 --> 00:33:11.310
Secondly, I would like you to explain

599
00:33:11.310 --> 00:33:14.790
how the equatorial climate of the DRC

600
00:33:14.790 --> 00:33:18.330
presents both opportunities and challenges

601
00:33:18.330 --> 00:33:21.693
for the people and the wildlife of the DRC.

602
00:33:23.100 --> 00:33:26.460
You can pause the video while you complete the activities,

603
00:33:26.460 --> 00:33:27.930
and then when you come back,

604
00:33:27.930 --> 00:33:31.023
I will share some examples with you.

605
00:33:32.070 --> 00:33:33.603
I hope you enjoy the task.

606
00:33:37.878 --> 00:33:40.961
Okay, task one, here is my bar chart.

607
00:33:41.850 --> 00:33:44.760
On the Y-axis, the vertical axis,

608
00:33:44.760 --> 00:33:48.510
I have the numbers representing the millions of tons.

609
00:33:48.510 --> 00:33:51.368
And on the X-axis, the horizontal axis,

610
00:33:51.368 --> 00:33:54.960
I have the types of crop labeled palm oil,

611
00:33:54.960 --> 00:33:57.570
plantain, maize, and cassava,

612
00:33:57.570 --> 00:34:00.786
and it's clear to see there a glance from the graph

613
00:34:00.786 --> 00:34:03.851
that cassava is by far and away

614
00:34:03.851 --> 00:34:07.800
the most highly produced crop in the DRC

615
00:34:07.800 --> 00:34:09.933
from these crops that are shown.

00:34:11.160 --> 00:34:15.600
Secondly, to explain how that climate has an impact,

00:34:15.600 --> 00:34:18.487
you may have had ideas like this.

00:34:18.487 --> 00:34:22.290
"The DRC experiences an equatorial climate.

00:34:22.290 --> 00:34:25.470
This means that biomes like tropical rainforests

620
00:34:25.470 --> 00:34:28.260
cover wide areas of the country.

621
00:34:28.260 --> 00:34:30.900
The climate is also good for crop growth,

622
00:34:30.900 --> 00:34:33.243
especially cassava and cocoa.

623
00:34:34.890 --> 00:34:36.510
The equatorial climate means

624
00:34:36.510 --> 00:34:39.570
that there is frequent heavy rainfall.

625
00:34:39.570 --> 00:34:42.510
When this happens for a long period of time,

626
00:34:42.510 --> 00:34:47.130
rivers can reach capacity or even burst their banks.

00:34:47.130 --> 00:34:52.130
In 2024, 300 people died and lots more were left homeless

when the Congo River flooded a large area

00:34:56.820 --> 00:34:58.980
due to heavy rainfall."

630
00:34:58.980 --> 00:35:00.993
Did you have similar ideas?

631
00:35:01.920 --> 00:35:04.350
Well done for completing these activities

and well done for listening so well

00:35:15.240 --> 00:35:19.110
The DRC has an equatorial climate

The country is home to diverse biomes,

I hope you have enjoyed learning

and I look forward to seeing you again next time

for another lesson from this units of work

lessons.lessonTitle: The impact of resource exploitation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: things that come from Earth without human influence and can be used for human needs
using something or someone for  personal benefit
the complete removal of trees for any reason
cutting down trees as a product for economic gain
dishonest behaviour by people in a position of power for personal gain

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mining and logging have led to deforestation and environmental destruction.
Many workers, including children, face unsafe conditions in mines.
The wealth from natural resources does not benefit most people in the DRC.
Resource exploitation has fueled conflict and corruption.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Logging is the use of trees as a natural resource for their wood and can happen legally or illegaly. Deforestation is the cutting down of trees for many reasons, often to make space for other activities such as mining, road building or farming.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That deforestation and logging are the same thing.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the environmental, social and economic impacts of resource exploitation in the DRC.

teacherTips.teacherTip: In the UK, the minimum age to work is 13. Ask the class if anybody has a job yet, for example they may do a paper round. How do they balance that with their school work, do they find it difficult? Ask those who do not have a job if they would like one, when do they think will start working, why?

lessons.lessonTitle: GIS: Visualising the physical and human geography of the DRC
lessons.unitTitle: The Democratic Republic of the Congo: What are its opportunities and challenges?

lessonKeywords.description: to form a mental or physical image of something, making it easier to understand
a geographic information system (GIS) is a computer mapping system that captures, and displays geographic data to help understand spatial patterns
a visual representation of geographic data on a digital map, such as population density, income levels, or land use

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The DRC is a country in central Africa and is one of the largest countries in Africa.
The DRC is largely landlocked, it has a very small stretch of coastline to the west.
Different layers of data on a GIS help us visualise the human geography of the DRC.
Different layers of data on a GIS help us visualise the physical geography of the DRC.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The DRC is a very large country. It's position on the equator means that it often appears smaller than it really is on some world maps.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The DRC is a relatively small country.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use a geographic information system (GIS) to visualise the human and physical geography of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There is ample opportunity to expand or reduce the use of GIS in this lesson to suit the needs of your class.

lessons.lessonTitle: Developing unconventional oil/gas sources in sensitive or remote areas

lessonKeywords.description: sources of oil and gas that are relatively difficult to extract because the oil and gas is trapped and cannot flow freely towards an oil well or a gas well
whether what is in a supply of water (e.g. its chemical or biological contents) make it suitable for a particular kind of use

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Unconventional sources of oil and gas include shale gas and tar sands.
Unconventional sources of oil and gas are increasingly being exploited.
There are environmental costs associated with developing new unconventional oil and gas sources.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In fact fracking fluid includes toxic chemicals and sand as well as water, which can have serious environmental impacts if they get into groundwater or are spilled. The wastewater left over from fracking also needs to be stored carefully.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Fracking only uses water which means its environmental impacts are harmless.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the environmental costs associated with developing unconventional sources of oil and gas - oil from tar sands and gas from shale.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Watching a video to show the processes involved in converting tar sands to oil and extracting gas from shale rocks can help students understand the challenges involved in making use of unconventional oil and gas sources.

lessons.lessonTitle: Developing conventional oil/gas sources in sensitive or remote areas

lessonKeywords.description: sources of oil and gas that are relatively easy to extract because the oil and gas can flow freely towards an oil well or a gas well
able to generate enough money to cover its costs and remain profitable
a known amount of oil or gas that can be taken from underground and used

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The world’s continuing reliance on fossil fuels increases pressure to exploit new areas.
There are economic benefits of developing conventional oil and gas sources in ecologically-sensitive and isolated areas.
There are economic costs of developing conventional oil and gas sources in ecologically-sensitive and isolated areas.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In fact, just because a reserve exists doesn't mean that it will be technically or economically viable. Reserves that are in remote locations or in challenging conditions may have high development costs, especially if oil prices fall.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: If you find oil or gas underground, it is always worth extracting it.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the economic costs and benefits of developing conventional sources of oil and gas in ecologically-sensitive and isolated areas.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Using Google Earth or similar applications to really demonstrate the remoteness of sites like ExxonMobil's Point Thomson reservoir helps students to grasp the logistical difficulties involved in extracting oil and gas from Alaska's North Slope.

lessons.lessonTitle: Changing attitudes to unsustainable energy consumption

lessonKeywords.description: the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere by an individual, product, process, country, etc
the impact of a person or community on the environment, expressed as the amount of land required to sustain their use of natural resources
balancing the amount of greenhouse gases emitted into the atmosphere with the amount removed from it

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by an individual or activity.
In some developed countries, there are changing attitudes to unsustainable energy consumption.
Environmental concerns, economic interests and education are responsible for changing attitudes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Although carbon footprints and ecological footprints both provide comparable measures of human impacts on the environment, carbon footprints measure greenhouse gas emissions while ecological footprints measure the total demand on Earth’s resources.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Carbon footprints and ecological footprints measure the same thing.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain ways in which attitudes to unsustainable energy consumption are changing.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There are several carboon footprint and ecological footprint calculators online, such as the WWF Footprint Calculator and the Global Footprint Network Calculator.

lessonKeywords.description: the amount of energy that is needed to power daily activities
energy efficiency means using technology that needs less energy to perform the same task
energy conservation involves changing people's behaviour in ways that mean they use less energy

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Reducing reliance on fossil fuels presents major technical challenges.
Energy efficiency and conservation can reduce demand and help finite energy supplies to last longer.
Energy efficiency and energy conservation can help to reduce carbon emissions.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In fact, energy efficiency is about using technology to do the same task but with less use of energy, while energy conservation is about changing people's behaviour so they use less energy.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Energy efficiency and energy conservation mean the same thing.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how energy efficiency and energy conservation in transport and in the home can reduce demand for finite energy resources and reduce carbon emissions.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students could carry out a review of energy efficient technology in the school and make suggestions for how energy conservation could be improved within the school day.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, my name's Mr. March, and I'm here today to teach you all about reducing demand on fossil fuels.
So grab everything that you need for today's lesson, and let's get going.
So by the end of today's lesson, you will be able to explain how energy efficiency and energy conservation in transport and in the home can reduce demand for finite energy resources and reduce carbon emissions.
There are three key terms for today's lesson, and those are demand, efficiency, and finally, conservation.
Demand refers to the amount of energy that is needed to power daily activities.
Efficiency refers to using technology that needs less energy to perform the same task.
And energy conservation involves changing people's behavior in ways that mean they use less energy.
There are three learning cycles for today's lesson, and we're gonna start with learning cycle one, which is all about reducing energy demand.
So the demand for energy is increasing.
That much is clear.
The graph in front of you does a great job in illustrating that point because if we look at the beginning of the graph in 1800 and compare it to 2023, we can see how energy consumption is increasing year on year.
So let's study the graph in a little bit more detail.
It says: What sources of energy are most important globally, renewables or non-renewables? Now, you may like to pause the video here to study that graph in a bit more detail and come up with the answer yourself.
So the answer we were looking for, as Sofia says, is that non-renewables make up around 80%, and those include oil, coal, and natural gas.
What does this mean, though, for carbon emissions, and why should we care? Once again, you may like to pause the video here whilst you consider your answer to that question.
Well, the reason that we should care is, once again, Sofia says that carbon emissions will go up instead of reducing.
And why is that such a big problem? As Sam says, that means more global warming.
There is a clear relationship and link between the amount of carbon emissions being released into the atmosphere and our average global temperature.
So Sofia and Sam are absolutely right, burning fossil fuels is the main cause of increased carbon emissions.
And increased carbon emissions are the cause of increasing global temperatures, which is driving climate changes around the world.
So as long as increased demand for energy is met by increased use of fossil fuels, then carbon emissions will continue to increase, all other conditions being equal.
Globally, most countries have agreed to reduce the amount of carbon they emit to meet targets.
So how is this to be achieved given increased energy demand? So why don't we just swap to renewable energy, as Lucas so correctly says? It seems like an obvious switch.
Then we can meet rising demand without increasing carbon emissions.
The switch to renewables is happening, but it's happening too slowly, so fossil fuels are being used to actually meet this extra demand for energy.
And why is the switch to renewables not happening fast enough? Well, it's not happening fast enough because of the demand for energy is rising very quickly as living standards rise in developing and emerging countries and as rapid population growth continues in some developing countries.
As living standards rise, people can afford things that consume more energy, such as cars, fridges, and air conditioning.
And as population sizes increase, there are more people to consume energy.
Alongside this, renewables take a long time to build, such as wind farms, hydroelectric power, and solar farms. And the best places to build them are often not where existing power facilities are actually located, so there needs to be a whole new infrastructure around them to connect them to where energy is consumed.
Fossil fuel lock-in is all about the existing fossil fuel power stations, pipelines, and all the factories and facilities that are built to run on fossil fuel energy.
These were built to last for decades, and it's not cheap or easy to actually just replace them.
In many countries, fossil fuels may be cheaper than renewables.
Indonesia, with its large coal reserves, for example, which makes it economically and politically hard to transition to renewables, which would mean more expensive energy for ordinary people and businesses.
Renewables like wind only produce power when it's windy, and solar only produces energy when there's enough sunlight, and renewable energy can be challenging to store.
Meanwhile, fossil fuels are much more reliable in the sense that they will generate energy whenever you need it.
There is often a certain amount of political opposition to the renewables in many, many different democracies because politicians recognize that large numbers of people are wary about paying more for energy.
And some sectors are hard for renewables to replace non-renewables, especially transport, which relies heavily on oil.
And heating in homes and businesses also relies heavily on gas and coal, as well as some very high-energy-use industries such as steel and cement production.
So energy efficiency and energy conservation both work to actually try to bring down or decrease the energy demand.
Energy efficiency uses technology which reduces the amount of energy needed to do something.
For example, LED light bulbs use less energy to provide light than traditional incandescent bulbs.
Meanwhile, energy conservation encourages people to change their behavior, to behave in a way that uses less energy.
For example, trying to encourage people to use bicycles, which reduces energy used for transportation, for example.
Time now for a learning check, and it says: True or false? Energy efficiency and energy conservation mean the same thing.
What you need to do then is pause the video here whilst you consider and then select your answer.
And the correct answer was false.
Now, once again, I'd like you to pause the video whilst you consider as to why or how this statement is false.
And the reason it's false is that energy efficiency is about using technology to do the same task but with less use of energy.
Meanwhile, energy conservation is about changing people's behavior so that they use less energy.
Really, really well done if you were able to get those two answers correct.
Our next learning check says: Which two of the following are examples of energy efficiency? So what you need to do then is read through the four statements, pause the video whilst you consider, and then select your two answers.
And the correct answers were home insulation and B, LED light bulbs.
So home insulation is energy efficiency because by reducing the amount of heat that is lost from a house, it means a smaller amount of energy is required to keep the house just as warm as before the insulation was installed.
And LED light bulbs are energy efficiency because they use a smaller amount of energy to provide as much or more light as a traditional incandescent light bulb.
Using public transport instead of driving your own car is a behavioral change that reduces energy use.
One bus uses a lot less fossil fuel to run than if everyone on the bus drove their own individual car to achieve their journey.
And washing clothes at a lower temperature than usual is a change in behavior.
Once again, energy conservation, which reduces the amount of energy used to heat water in the washing machine.
So really well done if you were able to select A and B as the correct answers.
So we're on now to our two practice tasks for our first learning cycle, and the first one says to, while using examples, explain the difference between energy efficiency and energy conservation.
The second question says to explain how energy efficiency and energy conservation can help to reduce carbon emissions.
So what I'd like you to do then right now is pause the video here whilst you attempt these two practice tasks.
Best of luck.
And now for some feedback.
So, your answer may have looked something like this: Energy efficiency is about using technology to do the same task but with less use of energy.
An example would be an aerodynamic lorry, which uses less energy to carry the same load the same distance as a standard lorry because it has less wind resistance.
Energy conservation is about changing people's behavior so that they use less energy.
An example would be encouraging people to use public transport rather than drive individual cars.
The second question, once again, your answer may have included something like this: Currently, carbon emissions are increasing because there is increasing demand for energy globally and 80% of that energy is coming from fossil fuels, which release carbon emissions when they're burned.
Currently, the switch to renewable energy is not happening fast enough to meet increasing demand.
In the meantime, energy efficiency and energy conservation reduce demand for energy.
In some sectors, such as housing and transportation, that can really reduce carbon emissions.
So really well done if you were able to include anything like that in your own answer.
We're on now to our second learning cycle, which is all about energy efficiency and conservation in transport.
The aim of energy efficiency in transportation is to actually reduce the amount of fuel being used without reducing travel.
And this can be done through fuel-efficient vehicles, and these go further on less fuel due to improved engines, better aerodynamics, and less weight.
What about hybrid and EVs, electric vehicles? Electric vehicles are much more efficient at converting energy from their batteries, in the case of an electric vehicle, into motion than petrol or diesel engines.
And thereby, by being more energy efficient, they're of course using less energy to begin with.
Furthermore, with energy-efficient public transport.
Making trains, buses, and trams more energy efficient reduces the amount of fossil fuel needed for the same journey.
It also makes public transport much more energy efficient than traveling by private car.
So a quick learning check.
It says: True or false? Electric vehicles, or EVs, are not an example of energy efficiency because they do not use fossil fuels.
So what I need you to do right now then is pause the video here whilst you consider and then select your answer.
And the answer was false.
Now, once again, I'd like you to pause the video whilst you consider as to why this statement then is false.
And the reason it's false is that energy efficiency in transportation means using less energy to complete the same task, so driving the same distance, for example.
EVs are much more efficient at converting energy into motion than petrol or diesel, petrol or diesel engines, which lose as much as 80% of energy as heat.
So really, really well done if you were able to identify those two correct answers.
The aim of energy conservation in transportation is to switch people to lower-energy transportation or just to reduce how much or how often people travel in the first place, and how can that actually be achieved? Well, we can try to encourage people to drive less.
For example, we can encourage people to walk to work or cycle to work instead of driving.
Working from home instead of actually making that commute, that trip to work, will of course bring down the amount of energy needed.
Also encouraging car sharing, so using one car rather than two or three to get to different destinations.
And finally, encouraging the use of public transport.
So once again, trying to limit the number of journeys being taken by individuals in cars.
The same is true in terms of encouraging people to actually fly less.

lessons.lessonTitle: Global patterns of energy use and causes of variations

lessonKeywords.description: differences or changes in something, for example variations in energy use between countries means differences in the amounts and types of energy that different countries use
the growth of a country’s wealth, leading to better jobs, higher incomes and improved living standards
the different types of jobs and industries in an economy, divided into primary (e.g. farming), secondary (e.g. manufacturing), tertiary (services) and quaternary (e.g. research)

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are variations (inequalities) in the global pattern of energy use.
Level of economic development is a cause of variations in the global pattern of energy use.
Demand from different economic sectors cause variations in energy use.
Energy poverty has negative economic, social and environmental implications.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While people in hot countries may need to use less energy on heating, energy use depends most on how developed a country is - developed countries use more energy per person because they have more industries, transport and technology.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Hot countries use less energy because it is warm all year so they do not need to heat their houses.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the global pattern of energy use and explain reasons for the variations in energy use per person.

teacherTips.teacherTip: An interesting development in recent years is that some developed countries are starting to see reductions in their energy use per person, which includes the UK and Canada. Students could explore reasons (e.g. energy efficiency, vehicle electrification) and consider whether this trend will continue.

lessonKeywords.description: visible damage to a landscape caused by human activities such as mining or construction
the release of carbon into the atmosphere, contributing to the greenhouse effect and global warming

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Energy extraction has environmental consequences.
Mining and drilling can have environmental impacts, such as landscape scarring, oil spills and carbon emissions.
Renewable energy can have landscape impacts including from HEP flooding and land use for wind turbines and solar panels.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Renewables and recyclables can have environmental consequences too, although they generally cause less harm than fossil fuels. These consequences can include impacts on biodiversity and the ability of ecosystems to absorb carbon dioxide.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Only the extraction and use of non-renewable energy has environmental consequences.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain environmental impacts associated with non-renewable, renewable and recyclable energy extraction and use.

teacherTips.teacherTip: GIS offers excellent opportunities to identify landscape scarring and measure the impact of changes in landscapes due to energy extraction and production over time.

lessonKeywords.description: the amount of something (e.g. oil) that is available to buy
how much of something (e.g. oil) that people want to buy
how well (or badly) countries get along with each other, which can affect trading relationships of supply and demand
a period when economies stop growing temporarily and people spend less

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Oil production and the price of oil change over time.
Political factors, such as conflicts and changing diplomatic relations, affect oil supply and oil prices.
Economic factors, such as recessions and booms and under and over supply, affect oil supply and oil prices.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Although oil prices may decrease if demand decreases, oil-producing countries can increase the price of oil by reducing the amount of oil they supply. This requires oil-producing countries to work together to reduce supply.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: If demand for oil decreases then oil prices will always decrease too.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how changing international relations and economic factors can affect oil supply and oil prices.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Practising interpreting oil price and oil production data is a very useful skill for students to develop, and can usually be linked to current news events.

Demand refers to how much of something, for example, oil that people want to buy.

lessons.lessonTitle: Costs and benefits to fossil fuel alternatives

lessonKeywords.description: the combination of different energy sources used by a country or a region. The energy mix can change over time
the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price
the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere by an individual, product, process, country, etc

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The UK's energy mix has diversified in response to policies of reducing carbon emissions and improving energy security.
2020 was the UK's first year in which more electricity came from alternatives to fossil fuels than from non-renewables.
Alternatives to fossil fuels can reduce carbon emissions, improve energy security and diversify the energy mix.
Alternatives to fossil fuels include biofuels, wind, solar, HEP and future technologies such as hydrogen.
Alternatives to fossil fuels have both benefits and costs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Even if all your electricity comes from renewables, other parts of your lifestyle (like the manufacture of the clothes you wear, the food you eat, the technology you use) still produce carbon emissions elsewhere — often in other countries.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: If you got your electricity from 100% renewable energy sources, then your carbon footprint would be zero.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can assess the costs and benefits of alternatives to fossil fuels.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The UK's National Grid: Live service (grid.iamkate.com) provides a dashboard of live data on the UK's electricity generation and consumption, which could be a useful resource for students to explore in relation to energy mix and alternatives to fossil fuels.

lessons.lessonTitle: Classification of energy – non-renewable, renewable and recyclable

lessonKeywords.description: a natural source of energy that will run out because it cannot be reproduced, such as coal, oil and natural gas
a natural source of energy that will never run out, such as flows of wind, water and solar energy
sources of energy that can be reused and so will last into the future, such as biofuels and nuclear energy

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Energy sources can be classified as non-renewable, renewable and recyclable.
Non-renewable energy resources include fossil fuels: coal, oil and gas.
Renewable energy resources include flows of solar, wind and HEP.
Recyclable energy resources include nuclear and biofuels.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Renewable energy comes from natural processes that are constantly renewed, so they never run out. Recyclable energy comes from resources that are often finite (they can run out) but which can be reprocessed or reused to extend their use.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Recyclable energy is the same as renewable energy.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can classify sources of energy into non-renewable, renewable and recyclable energy.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Understanding what makes nuclear power and biofuels recyclable is sometimes challenging for students: YouTube videos about the process of generating nuclear power (and reprocessing spent nuclear fuel), and of turning biofuels into energy sources work well in consolidating understanding here.

lessons.lessonTitle: Distribution of oil reserves, factors affecting growth of oil consumption

lessonKeywords.description: locations where oil is found in significant amounts
the process by which an economy is transformed from primarily agricultural to one based on manufacturing and industry
nations with social or business activities in the process of rapid growth and industrialisation

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The global demand for oil is increasing.
Oil reserves and production are unevenly distributed.
Oil consumption is growing due to rising per capita GDP and rapid industrialisation in emerging countries.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Oil consumption varies based on industrialisation, population size, and economic factors.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All countries consume oil at the same rate.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how oil reserves and production are unevenly distributed and that oil consumption is increasing.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Interestingly, as development increases, countries use more energy and oil. That is, until the country reaches a high level of development whereby oil consumption falls off. Students could explore reasons for this (e.g. energy efficiency, vehicle electrification, rise of renewable energy).

lessons.lessonTitle: Factors affecting access to energy resources

lessonKeywords.description: the ability to use a resource in a way that benefits people
the type, structure and layers of rock found beneath Earth’s surface
the amount of a fossil fuel that has been discovered and can be extracted and sold
hydraulic fracturing (fracking) is a method used to extract gas or oil from shale rock formations deep underground

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Access to energy resources is not evenly distributed.
Access to energy resources is affected by physical resources, such as geology, accessibility, climate and landscape.
Access to energy resources is affected by access to technology.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Some countries lack the infrastructure or funding to develop their resources, even if they are accessible, while in other cases a country might have resources that require advanced and expensive technology to access.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: If a country has fossil fuels underground, it can easily use them.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how access to energy resources is affected by physical resources and access to technology.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use this topic to refresh and develop students' skills in use and interpretation of world maps showing the distribution of energy resources.

lessons.lessonTitle: Plant and animal adaptations in tropical rainforests

lessonKeywords.description: the variety of species found in a habitat
a feature or behaviour that helps an animal or plant survive in its environment
the natural place where a plant or animal lives and grows

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Tropical rainforests are home to a wide variety of plants and animals.
Plants are adapted to the physical conditions in tropical rainforests, for example, drip tips and buttress roots.
Animals are well adapted to the physical conditions in tropical rainforests.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Plants and animals face different challenges in the different habitats of the tropical rainforest. For example, plants on the forest floor have to have adaptations for low light levels.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The challenges faced by plants and animals in the canopy layer are the same as challenges on the forest floor.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how plants and animals in tropical rainforests are well adapted to the physical conditions.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Virtual reality tours of the tropical rainforest will allow students to better understand the adaptations of plants and animals living in each layer of the tropical rainforest. BBC Earth's 'The "busy" life of the sloth' is an engaging way into this topic, for example.

lessonKeywords.description: a measure of how many different species live in an ecosystem
large-scale removal or clearing of forests
farmers that grow only enough food for themselves

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The majority of Indonesia’s rainforests are located in Borneo, Papua and Sumatra.
Causes of deforestation in Indonesia include subsistence and commercial farming, logging, energy and population growth.
Impacts of deforestation in Indonesia include erosion, pollution, habitat loss, carbon emissions, economic development.
