lessonKeywords.description: the movement of water (through pipes or along rivers) from areas of water surplus to areas of water deficit
the industrial conversion of saltwater into freshwater, commonly in arid or semi-arid areas

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Different strategies can be used to increase water supply.
Strategies to increase water supply include diverting supplies, increasing storage and desalination
The California State water project is a large-scale water transfer scheme with advantages and disadvantages.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Although dams and reservoirs do provide a reliable and easily-controllable source of water, this supply is not guaranteed. Over time, sediment will build up and reduce the capacity of the reservoir. Also, reservoirs can dry up during droughts.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Dams and reservoirs guarantee a reliable water supply for many years into the future.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe different strategies used to increase water supply and outline the advantages and disadvantages of California's water project.

teacherTips.teacherTip: ArcGIS Online provides a wide array of useful layers related to water supply, including for example location of desalination plants in Saudi Arabia.

lessonKeywords.description: organic matter, from plants or animals, used as a fuel source to produce energy. A biofuel is biomass converted into a liquid or gas fuel which can be used in place of oil and natural gas
the process of using moving water to generate electricity: also known as hydroelectric power (HEP)
the release of carbon into the atmosphere, contributing to the greenhouse effect and global warming
able to generate enough money to cover its costs and remain profitable

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Different strategies can be used to increase energy supply.
Strategies to increase energy supply include developing renewable and non-renewable sources of energy.
The USA is developing new sources of oil and gas in Alaska, which has advantages and disadvantages.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Renewable energy comes from sources that don’t run out or are quickly renewed. Because plants are quickly replaced, biomass is a renewable energy source. Also, biomass is carbon neutral as CO2 released is the same CO2 absorbed during plant growth.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Biomass is not a renewable source of energy because carbon dioxide is released when it is burned.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can assess strategies used to increase energy supply and use an example to support my answer.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Understanding nuclear power and biomass is sometimes challenging for students: YouTube videos about the process of generating nuclear power (and reprocessing spent nuclear fuel), and of turning biofuels into energy sources work well in consolidating understanding here.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, my name is Mr. March, and I'm here today to teach you all about strategies to increase energy supply.
So grab everything that you need for today's lesson and let's get going.
So by the end of today's lesson, you will be able to assess strategies used to increase energy supply and use an example to support your answer.
There are four key terms for today's lesson.
Those are carbon emissions, biomass, hydro, and, finally, viable.
Carbon emissions refers to the release of carbon into the atmosphere, contributing to the greenhouse effect and global warming.
Biomass refers to organic matter from plants and animals used as a fuel source to produce energy.
A biofuel is a biomass converted into a liquid or gas fuel, which can be used in place of oil and natural gas.
Hydro refers to the process of using moving water to generate electricity, also known as hydroelectric power or HEP.
And finally, viable, refers to being able to generate enough money to cover its costs and remain profitable.
There are two learning cycles for today's lesson.
I'm gonna start with learning cycle one, which is all about strategies for increasing energy supply.
So we're gonna start today's lesson with a really interesting graph.
Now, this graph on the right-hand side is showing global energy consumption by source.
And what does this graph actually tell us? Well, first of all, what is it telling us in terms of energy demand? We can see the graph beginning in 1800, all the way up to 2023.
What is it telling us about energy demand? Also, what is it telling us about what sources of energy are being used to actually meet that demand? Now, you may like to pause the video here whilst you really study that graph to try to answer those two questions, or perhaps, even better, have a discussion with someone near you.
So let's now start with that first question.
What did you come up with? Well, Lucas also has an answer.
Lucas says that demand has increased rapidly over the last 70 years or so.
From 30,000 terawatt hours to 180,000 terawatt hours.
And indeed, if we look at the graph, you can see that sudden increase really in the last 70 years.
What about in terms of the sources of energy, the types of energy sources that are being used to meet this demand? Well, again, Lucas says a really good answer.
We can see that renewables have grown as a source of energy, but I'd estimate that around 80% of energy is still coming from fossil fuels, such as oil and coal.
So really, really well done if you're able to identify the same answers that Lucas has just come up with.
Now, realistically, there are two main strategies for trying to increase energy supply.
The first of which is to increase the supply of non-renewable, so fossil fuels for example.
And the second is to increase the supply of renewable energy types, such as solar and wind.
Non-renewable, as I just said, include fossil fuels.
And now my question to you is, why are most countries looking to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels? Now, once again, you may like to pause the video here whilst you consider your own answer to that question or better still, once again, have a discussion with someone new.
Now, increasing fossil fuel energy supply has many, many different disadvantages.
And it really comes back to this question right here, which is why are most countries looking to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels? Well, really it comes back to increasing carbon emissions is the main problem with increasing the energy supply by supplying more fossil fuels.
Adding more carbon dioxide to the atmosphere will intensify the rate of global warming and therefore the impacts of climate change, which is why international agreements have instead been made that set targets for each country to reduce their emissions in the hope of avoiding the worst where climate change impacts are concerned.
Energy security is about achieving a reliable supply of energy that meets people's needs.
For many countries, increasing the supply of fossil fuel energy reduces energy security because these supplies have to be imported.
Furthermore, reserves are running out.
As the easy-to-access oil, gas, and coal are used up, countries have to spend more money getting remaining, less accessible supplies until those too are used up.
Non-renewable energy is finite.
Next, we have air pollution.
Now, air pollution is a major problem in many cities around the world.
Caused at least in part by burning fossil fuels for transportation and energy generation.
Meeting rising demand for more petrol and diesel cars, for example, adds to the air pollution problem, and it's often severe health impacts.
Developing new sources of fossil fuels is often in areas that have previously not been developed because of their remoteness, challenging conditions, or environmental sensitivity, such as the Arctic for example.
As we will see in the second part of this lesson, drilling for oil and gas in such conditions poses high risks for habitats and species.
In the same way, clearing forest to mine coal or extract oil from tar sands deposits can have very severe environmental impacts.
And finally, there's also a high cost to developing new sources of fossil fuel energy in remote locations, such as the cost of building pipelines to transport the oil.
Now let's look at developing renewable sources of energy.
Biomass, hydro, solar, and wind are all renewable sources of energy.
Renewable means the energy comes from sources that don't run out or are quickly renewed or replaced.
And now, as we can see on the graphic on the right-hand side, renewables now generate over 50% of the UK's electricity.
And when we compare that with 1990, we can see the vast increase in that electricity generation.
So let's now look at the advantages of using biomass.
Well, first of all, it's carbon neutral.
The carbon released when biomass is burnt is offset by the carbon that's absorbed as the plant is actually growing.
Biofuels can also be mixed with petrol and diesel, which can keep transportation costs lower at times of high oil prices.
Growing biofuels would reduce a country's need to import petrol and diesel, increasing energy security.
And finally, renewables can power electric vehicles.
But for petrol and diesel vehicles, then biofuels provide a carbon neutral option.
And what about the disadvantages then? Well, rainforest is often cleared unfortunately, to grow crops for biofuels.
Deforestation causes habitat destruction and increases atmospheric CO2.
Also, the amount of energy available for biofuels is lower than that we can get from fossil fuels.
So very, very large areas of land would need to be cleared to replace fossil fuel use.
Growing biofuels can also reduce the land available for growing food, leading once again to an increase in food prices.
Also, biofuels often require a lot of water, which can stress ecosystems, and can also lead to land degradation, as well as damaging habitats.
Time now for a learning check.
It says true or false.
Burning biomass for energy is a renewable source of energy because plants regrow quickly.
So what you need to do right now then is pause a video here whilst you consider, and then select your answer.
And the correct answer was true.
Now, once again, I'd like you to pause the video here whilst you consider as to why that statement is true.
And the reason it's true is that renewable energy comes from sources that don't run out or are quickly renewed.
Because plants are quickly replaced, biomass is a renewable energy source.
Also, plants absorb CO2 as they grow, which is released when they burn.
So they're also carbon neutral as well.
Really, really well done if you're able to get those two answers correct.
So let's now look at the advantages of using hydro.
First of all, there are zero carbon emissions when generating electricity.
Hydro is a clean renewable source of electricity.
Furthermore, hydro plants are very expensive to build, but they do last a long time once built and actually have very low maintenance costs.
It supports energy security by reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels, although not all countries actually have the large rivers that are required for really effective hydro projects.
And finally, hydro is reliable and predictable and can also be used to store renewable energy.
This makes it great for balancing energy supply from intermittent renewables such as solar and wind, which only generate electricity when the sun is shining and when the wind is blowing.
And what about the disadvantages then of using hydro? Well, first of all, dams and reservoirs are very expensive to build, around $5 billion for a one-gigawatt dam and hydro plant.
Flooding land for reservoirs can mean loss of farmland and displacement of communities that would've lived there.
And not all countries have the large river systems required for large scale hydro.
So the potential for hydro may actually be limited.
Dams can disrupt river ecosystems and affect fish migrations while flooding river valleys for reservoirs can cause deforestation as well as habitat loss.
Moving on to solar and again the advantages.
Well, first of all, it generates electricity, once again, without any carbon emissions.
The costs of solar power have fallen dramatically and households can actually add solar panels to roofs to reduce energy costs.

And it's also good for balancing a country's energy mix, especially for higher latitudes, in summer, when days are really long and potential for solar is at its highest.
But what about the disadvantages? Well, although costs have reduced significantly with regards to solar power generation, the cost of installation can still be too high for homes, school buildings, offices, et cetera.
There is often opposition to large scale solar farms because of the big impact they have on farming as well as natural habitats.
Solar only works in daylight and is best in summer in higher latitudes, while power is actually still needed 247 and all year round.
So it's only really truly effective perhaps during those summer months.
Manufacture of solar panels include toxic chemicals, and systems to recycle panels safely after they stop working are not yet fully developed.
So it's not 100% environmentally friendly.
So let's now have a look at the advantages of using wind power.
So first of all, there are zero carbon emissions when generating electricity.
Wind is a clean, renewable energy source.
Wind farms can be built offshore, so in the sea, so they don't actually take up land area.
And the UK has some of the world's best offshore wind resources in the North Sea.
Wind energy is now one of the cheapest sources of electricity in countries like the UK.
And wind supports energy security by reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels.
Wind can also be combined with solar to balance supply, for example, at night when solar power isn't actually working.
And what about the disadvantages then of wind turbines? Well, once again, they are expensive to build, especially for offshore wind farms, which need underwater foundations as well as cables to the shore.
Furthermore, turbines have a big impact on landscapes and can be noisy, which leads to local opposition to wind farms, especially if they're on shore.
Furthermore, no power if there's no wind, which means other sources of power or power backups will always be needed.
And finally, turbines can actually kill birds and bats if they fly into the blades.
Turbine construction also disturbs habitats on shore and offshore, for example, seabeds.
Time for our next learning check.
It says, which two of the following are costs associated with both solar and wind energy? So you can see you've got four different options on the screen there.
What you need to do is pause the video here whilst you read through those four options and select what you think are the two correct answers.
And the two correct answers are, A, landscape impacts, which are often opposed locally.
And C, intermittent supply, rather than always being available.
Really well done if you're able to select A and C as the correct answers.
Let's now look at nuclear power, 'cause nuclear power requires uranium, which is a non-renewable resource.
It is finite.
It will run out.
As a result, nuclear power is classed as a non-renewable energy source.
Aisha says though, "I thought nuclear fuel could be recycled and used again." Well, it is possible to recover uranium from spent fuel rods and use it again, but it is expensive and not all countries are able to do this.
So let's now look at the advantages of using nuclear power.
First of all, it's a low carbon source of electricity.
No, CO2 is actually released during power generation.
Nuclear power stations can be built in a wide range of locations.
All they need is really lots of water for cooling.
So by coast, by rivers are usually greater locations for nuclear power stations.
And a low risk of tectonic hazards is also really, really important consideration.
Building nuclear power plants is very, very expensive, but once they're running, the cost of power is low.
Nuclear power could replace fossil fuels because nuclear power reactions produce an enormous amount of energy.
And finally, nuclear power is 24/7 and isn't dependent on weather.
So it's ideal for balancing less reliable supply from perhaps wind and solar energy.
And what about the disadvantages then of using nuclear power? Well, first of all, it's very expensive to build, and construction can take many, many years.

lessons.lessonTitle: Global patterns of energy consumption and supply

lessonKeywords.description: a measure of how much of something people want to buy
the ability of a country to ensure a reliable, affordable and uninterrupted supply of energy to meet its needs now and in the future
the amount of something that is bought and used
the amount of something that is available to buy

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Demand for energy resources is rising globally.
Globally, there are areas of surplus (security) and deficit (insecurity).
Impacts of energy insecurity include exploration in sensitive areas, economic and environmental costs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Although supplies of energy from solar and wind can be variable, renewables diversify a country's energy supply and reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels. Overeliance on imported fossil fuels is a bigger cause of energy insecurity.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Renewables make a country less energy secure because they’re unreliable.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can interpret patterns in global energy security and describe the impacts of energy insecurity on people and economies.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The Our World in Data website has a wide range of excellent maps and other resources related to energy consumption and production.

lessonKeywords.description: the growth of a country’s wealth, leading to better jobs, higher incomes and improved living standards
the ability to use a resource in a way that benefits people
the amount of a fossil fuel that has been discovered and can be extracted and sold

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Energy consumption is increasing due to economic development and technology.
Energy consumption is increasing due to population increase.
Physical, technological, economic and political factors affect energy supply.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: This is one reason for the growing demand for energy, but economic development is another factor that affects demand. As people become richer, their consumption of energy increases, e.g. instead of using bicycles for transport, people use mopeds.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Rising demand for energy is simply down to the world's growing population.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain reasons for increasing energy consumption and factors that affect energy supply.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ofgem publishes typical energy usage figures with descriptions of the user groups which can be useful for developing students' understanding of factors that increase energy consumption.

So by the end of today's lesson, you will be able to explain reasons for increasing energy consumption and factors that affect energy supply.
There are three key words for today's lesson.
Those are "economic development," "access," and finally, "reserve." "Economic development" refers to the growth of a country's wealth, leading to better jobs, higher income, and improved living standards.
"Access" refers to the ability to use a resource in a way that benefits people.
And finally, "reserve" refers to the amount of a fossil fuel that has been discovered and can be extracted and sold.

For example, fridges, air conditioners, laptops, which all use energy.
And finally, urbanization, people moving to cities with economic development, these go hand in hand.

So we can really begin to understand how energy consumption and increasing development really do go hand in hand.

29 billion in the mid-2080s, and we can see what it's currently at today in 2025, up and around eight billion.

lessonKeywords.description: the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere by an individual, product, process, country, etc.
energy efficiency means using technology that needs less energy to perform the same task
energy conservation involves changing people's behaviour in ways that mean they use less energy

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Many countries are taking action to use energy more sustainably.

Togo provides examples of local renewable energy schemes using solar power.

lessons.unitTitle: Forest biomes: why are forests so important?

lessonKeywords.description: all the living things in an ecosystem or area
the complete removal of trees
the natural home or environment of an animal, plant or other organism
the function or purpose of a particular area

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Costa Rica is a small country in central America which once experienced the highest rate of deforestation in the world.
Costa Rica was the first tropical country in the world to reverse deforestation.
Wildlife corridors enable species such as the jaguar to move through the rainforest undetected.
National parks, selective logging, small-scale agroforestry and ecotourism have protected the rainforest.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There are many approaches to preventing and even reversing deforestation not just one, for example national parks, selective logging, small-scale agroforestry and ecotourism.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Stopping deforestation just means preventing the felling of trees.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how tropical rainforests can be protected using the example of Costa Rica.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There is the potential to use GIS to compare forested area over time.

00:11:41.040 --> 00:11:45.243

00:11:46.500 --> 00:11:49.560

00:11:49.560 --> 00:11:51.630

lessons.unitTitle: Forest biomes: why are forests so important?

lessonKeywords.description: A large region of the world with places that have similar climates, vegetation and animals that have adapted to living there.
Imaginary lines on Earth showing position north or south of the Equator, measured in degrees.
Half of Earth, usually divided into the Northern or Southern hemisphere by the Equator, or Eastern and Western hemispheres by the prime meridian.
Energy radiated from the sun via electromagnetic waves.
The process by which green plants and certain bacteria create glucose from sunlight, water and CO2.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The boreal forest is the world's largest land-based biome.
The boreal forest is also known as the taiga; they are found at high latitudes.
There is little rainfall in the boreal biome due to the high latitudes and temperature.
Boreal forests contain many coniferous trees which are normally evergreen and so don’t drop their leaves.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Coniferous trees produce cones and are normally evergreen (don't lose their leaves in autumn). Some evergreen trees are not coniferous, e.g. holly.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Evergreen and coniferous trees are the same.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can locate boreal forests and explain their climate and adaptations.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If any trees are visible from the window or are well known to students locally, these can be discussed alongside christmas trees to relate the coniferous, evergreen, deciduous definitions to students' own lives.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Temperate forests are distributed across Europe, Asia and North America, within the temperate climate zone.
The temperate forests have an average annual temperature of 10 degrees Celsius.
There are four layers in a temperate deciduous forest; the canopy, sub-canopy, herb layer and the ground layer.
The nutrient cycle means the soil in the temperate deciduous forest is nutrient rich.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Temperate deciduous forests have more nutrient rich soil than other forests as trees lose their leaves, meaning there is a lot of leaf litter and the climate is not too cold for decomposers.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Rainforests must have the most nutritious soil as they have such a lot of plants and such tall trees.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Global temperatures are increasing because of climate change.
Forests remove carbon dioxide from Earth's atmosphere and replace it with oxygen.
Deforestation is a major contributor to climate change.
Climate change can cause changes to species in a forest; the spread of pests and diseases and more and worse wildfires.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The greenhouse effect is a natural process that is essential for life on Earth. Without it, our planet would be too cold to sustain most life forms.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The greenhouse effect has a negative impact.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how deforestation contributes to climate change and how climate change impacts forests.

teacherTips.teacherTip: A homework task linked to this topic could involve students calculating their own carbon footprint using an online calculator.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Sustainable management of the forests is vital for the health of Earth and for future generations.
Reforestation and afforestation schemes help absorb carbon dioxide and improve biodiversity.
Agroforestry can help people farm more sustainably and reduce forest clearance.
Stronger laws and the use of technology help to combat deforestation and illegal logging.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The forests should be fenced off and guarded to stop illegal logging.

lessons.unitTitle: Forest biomes: why are forests so important?

lessonKeywords.description: a large area full of trees
the natural home or environment of an animal, plant or other organism
the increase in Earth's average temperature over a long period of time
a large region of the world with places that have similar climates, vegetation and animals that have adapted to living there
an average of weather conditions (e.g. rain, sun, wind) in a place, taken over a long period of time (usually 30 years or more)

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Forests have a range of important functions and benefits.
There are different types of forest across the world, e.g. tropical rainforests, boreal forests and temperate forests.
Different types of forests are located in specific parts of the world.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Different forests have unique characteristics and ecosystems. The boreal forest, for example, is characterised by its cold climate and coniferous trees.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All forests are the same.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain why forests are important and describe the global distribution of different types of forest.

teacherTips.teacherTip: A nice way to help students understand biome locations is to describe how the vegetation would change if you walked north from the equator.

lessons.unitTitle: Forest biomes: why are forests so important?

lessonKeywords.description: the increase in Earth's average temperature over a long period of time
the natural home or environment of an animal, plant or other organism
the world’s largest land biome, found in the northern hemisphere
anything that absorbs and stores more carbon dioxide than it releases

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Wildfires are uncontrolled fires that spread fast through vegetation, e.g. forests, grasslands or shrublands.
Wildfires have both natural and human causes.
Climate change is making the conditions needed for wildfires to spread more likely.
The carbon dioxide emitted from wildfires was a huge contribution to carbon emissions in 2022.
The 2022 Siberian wildfires had devastating impacts on people and the environment.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Wildfires can be ignited by natural (e.g. lightning) or human causes (e.g. campfires).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Wildfires are all ignited naturally.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can say why wildfires occur and talk about the impact of the Siberian wildfires.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There is potential to relate this content to the increased wildfire risk in the UK. A HW research task to create a poster on "How to avoid accidental wildfires" could be beneficial.

lessons.unitTitle: Forest biomes: why are forests so important?

lessonKeywords.description: People who are the original inhabitants of a place, rather than people who moved there from elsewhere.
Related to the making of money from buying or selling things.
The way money in a particular area is made and spent.
The process of Earth’s surface, e.g. rock or soil, being worn away and transported from its original site.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Indigenous peoples have been living in tropical rainforests for thousands of years.
People use rainforests in a variety of ways including farming, mining, medicine and homes.
Deforestation is rapidly reducing the size of rainforests to make way for human activity.
Deforestation has negative impacts: loss of carbon sinks, loss of habitats, soil erosion and the displacement of people.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Many products grown/extracted from the rainforest are exported and used by people all over the world.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Only people that live in/near the rainforest use it.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe different ways people use tropical rainforests and explain the impacts of deforestation.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There is the potential to discuss what jobs students would want in the rainforest.

270
00:13:43.860 --> 00:13:45.690
You can see this in the diagram,

271
00:13:45.690 --> 00:13:47.823
with our leaf on the right-hand side.

272
00:13:48.900 --> 00:13:52.323
Deforestation is a major cause of global warming.

273
00:13:53.160 --> 00:13:56.430
In 2022, deforestation in the Amazon

274
00:13:56.430 --> 00:13:57.750
resulted in the release

275
00:13:57.750 --> 00:14:02.160
of over the equivalent of 1 billion tons

276
00:14:02.160 --> 00:14:04.020
of carbon dioxide,

277
00:14:04.020 --> 00:14:07.650
about the same as all the cars in the USA

278
00:14:07.650 --> 00:14:10.410
driving for a whole year,

00:14:10.410 --> 00:14:12.240
and that was just the Amazon,

00:14:12.240 --> 00:14:15.723
not rainforest across the world, just the Amazon.

00:14:17.130 --> 00:14:18.990

00:14:18.990 --> 00:14:21.990
to 10% of known species on Earth,

00:14:26.370 --> 00:14:28.530

00:14:28.530 --> 00:14:30.780

00:14:32.160 --> 00:14:34.680

00:14:34.680 --> 00:14:36.780

00:14:36.780 --> 00:14:38.850

00:14:38.850 --> 00:14:41.523
and that's mainly due to habitat loss.

00:14:42.480 --> 00:14:44.490
We're going to do a check for understanding now.

292
00:14:44.490 --> 00:14:46.650
Is it true or false?

00:14:46.650 --> 00:14:49.923
Deforestation is a major cause of climate change.

00:14:55.240 --> 00:14:57.330

295
00:14:57.330 --> 00:14:59.670
Trees absorb carbon dioxide from the air

296
00:14:59.670 --> 00:15:02.223
and therefore reduce the effects of global warming.

297
00:15:03.240 --> 00:15:05.760
We're moving on to soil erosion now.

298
00:15:05.760 --> 00:15:08.100
Soil erosion is caused by deforestation

299
00:15:08.100 --> 00:15:11.370
because leaves and branches and trees

300
00:15:11.370 --> 00:15:14.310
slow the journey of the rain to the forest floor,

301
00:15:14.310 --> 00:15:16.773
and the tree roots hold the soil together.

302
00:15:18.510 --> 00:15:20.040
Without those trees,

303
00:15:20.040 --> 00:15:22.920
the rain can erode away the thin layer of soil

304
00:15:22.920 --> 00:15:25.620
really easily, because the rain gets the forest floor

305
00:15:25.620 --> 00:15:28.680
really fast, so it has more power and energy,

306
00:15:28.680 --> 00:15:32.010
and then also there's nothing holding that soil together,

307
00:15:32.010 --> 00:15:33.690
so it's really easily washed away.

308
00:15:33.690 --> 00:15:36.030
There's nothing resisting that.

309
00:15:36.030 --> 00:15:38.370
This means that plants cannot grow in the future,

00:15:38.370 --> 00:15:41.190
as there's no nutrients left in the soil.

311
00:15:41.190 --> 00:15:43.020
So if you do cut down the rainforest,

00:15:43.020 --> 00:15:45.300
if deforestation does occur,

00:15:45.300 --> 00:15:48.360
then it's not as simple as just planting some trees

00:15:48.360 --> 00:15:49.530
to replace it

00:15:49.530 --> 00:15:51.660
because actually those trees won't grow well

00:15:51.660 --> 00:15:53.790
because there isn't the nutrients in the soil

Conflict over land between Indigenous groups,

local people, environmentalists,

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mangroves are shrubs and trees which grow in coastal waters.
Mangroves help protect the land from flooding, caused by tropical storms and tidal surges.
The Sundarbans in India and Bangladesh are an example of a mangrove forest.
Mangroves face a variety of threats including coastal developments, farming and sea level rise.
The impacts of mangrove loss include: coastal flooding, loss of biodiversity, resources and income.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Mangroves provide many services, including flood protection for settlements inland and nurseries for young fish (who may be caught for food when they have grown and left the protection of the mangroves).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Removing mangroves on the coast will not affect people inland or out at sea.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the role of mangrove forests and talk about the impact of forest loss in the Sundarbans.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There is potential for students to research the actions people are taking to protect the mangroves as homework.

lessons.unitTitle: Forest biomes: why are forests so important?

lessonKeywords.description: a large region of the world with places that have similar climates, vegetation and animals

energy radiated from the sun via electromagnetic waves

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Tropical rainforests are located in the tropical climate zone.
Tropical rainforests are home to millions of species of plants, animals, insects, birds and humans.
There are four layers to the forest; the emergents, the canopy, the understory and the forest floor.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In tropical rainforests it is hot, this heat actually causes the rain by creating a lot of evaporation and rising air, which then cools and condenses to form clouds which rain.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Topical rainforests are cold and wet.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe and explain the location of tropical rainforests and identify their key features.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Every time you can it is good to emphasise that the climate of the rainforest is hot, potentially ask the students to imagine how they would feel if they were in a rainforest, what they would wear etc. This helps remove misconceptions before they arise.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Animals such as squirrels, hedgehogs, and birds, such as nightingales, can be found in temperate deciduous forests.
Plants such as oak trees, beech trees and bluebells can be found in temperate deciduous forests.
Animals and plants adapt to living in seasonal conditions in different ways.

lessons.unitTitle: Anthropocene: What is the impact of humans on the world?

lessonKeywords.description: the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere at a given time, measured in parts per million (ppm)
long cylinders of ice drilled from glaciers or ice sheets

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Atmospheric CO₂ levels have risen steeply since the industrial revolution.
Ice core data shows a sharp increase in greenhouse gases linked to human activity.
Biodiversity loss is happening faster than natural extinction rates.
Plastics and radioactive elements form geological markers of human impact.
Land cover change is visible from satellites and historical maps.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Microplastics are found in the ocean, soil, rock and animals.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Microplastics are only found in the ocean.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe and evaluate key evidence that shows how humans have altered Earth's systems.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Get students to look out the window and ask what evidence they can see of human impact on the environment.

lessons.unitTitle: Anthropocene: What is the impact of humans on the world?

lessonKeywords.description: tiny particles held in the air such as dust, ash and soot
data that is collected by geographers themselves in the field
data that has been collected by someone else but not necessarily an expert in that topic area

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Though most air pollution is not visible to the naked eye, particulate matter can be captured using simple methods.
Questionnaires are a good way of gauging public opinion about an issue.
Secondary data can support the primary data that is collected in the field.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Though geographers often use secondary data that has been researched and produced by experts, it does not have to be: it can come from other students.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Secondary data has to have been collected by an expert in the data and the topic area.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can collect data about air pollution as part of a fieldwork enquiry.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students might like to look into how researchers collect particulate matter data and how that method compares to the one they will be using.

lessonKeywords.description: a statistical test that shows the strength of any correlation between two variables
enquiries that focus on a small area such as a street or a park
enquiries that focus on a large area such as a city or a whole country

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Statistical tests are used by geographers to find patterns in data sets that are not obvious in their raw form.
Conclusions can be strengthened by combining the results of different data sets together.
The scale at which geographers collect data can have a significant influence over the type of conclusions they make.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: You have to know how to interpret the results of statistical tests to use them in geographical enquiries.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You have to be good at maths to be able to use statistical tests in geographical enquiries.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can analyse and reflect on my air pollution data to create meaningful conclusions and an evaluation.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Model the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient calculations in real time with students so you can ensure that no student gets lost in the process.

lessonKeywords.description: data that is made up of words
data that is made up of numbers
a form of shading that uses one colour where the greatest density of something is shown by the darkest shade of that colour
using colour conventions in data presentation to represent certain ideas

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Qualitative data can be presented in interesting ways, such as word clouds and proportional speech bubbles.
Choropleth shading on a map can be used to show the level of air pollution.
Emoji icons can be used to show the strength of agreement or favourability.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The colours geographers use are often associated with social conventions such as red being negative and green being positive.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The colours geographers use in their data presentation are always randomly chosen.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can present qualitative and quantitative air pollution data.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To better grasp the concept of choropleth shading, show students applied examples that they may see regularly such as rainfall maps in weather forecasts.

lessons.unitTitle: Anthropocene: What is the impact of humans on the world?

lessonKeywords.description: natural substances that were formed over millions of years ago from the buried remains of ancient organisms. They include coal, oil and gas
energy sources, such as fossil fuels, that cannot be replaced and will eventually run out
sources of energy that can be reused and will not be used up or run out
reducing the amount of carbon dioxide (CO₂) released into the atmosphere from processes such as burning fossil fuels

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Fossil fuels release large amounts of carbon dioxide when burned.
Fossil fuels are non-renewable and contribute to climate change.
Some countries rely heavily on fossil fuels for energy and income.
Moving away from fossil fuels requires investment and new technology.
There is disagreement about how quickly fossil fuels should be phased out.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Over 80% of global energy still comes from coal, oil, and gas.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: We are sourcing more energy from renewables than fossil fuels.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain why fossil fuels are being phased out and what challenges this creates.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask students if they have seen any of the measures which are helping us to reach net zero, electric cars, wind turbines, etc.

lessons.unitTitle: Anthropocene: What is the impact of humans on the world?

lessonKeywords.description: global deal made in 2015 where nearly every country agreed to work together to limit global warming
taking action to reduce or prevent the effects of something
a person who belongs to a country and has rights and responsibilities there
steps taken by people, governments, and organisations to reduce climate change and its effects
(non-governmental organisation) is a group that works independently from governments to help with social or environmental issues

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Climate change is a global issue that requires international cooperation.
Agreements like the Paris Accord aim to reduce global emissions.
Some countries pollute more and have greater responsibility to act.
Not all countries agree on climate targets or financial commitments.
NGOs and citizens can influence climate action at different levels.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: North America and Europe have contributed the most to total CO₂ emissions, mainly because they industrialised first (in the 1800s).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: China has contributed most to CO₂ emissions.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how global cooperation is needed to solve environmental problems.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Show students the Greta Thunberg "how dare you" speech which is available on YouTube.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Plastic pollution harms marine life and spreads through ocean currents.
Overfishing reduces fish populations and disrupts marine food chains.
Climate change warms oceans and causes coral bleaching.
Oil spills and chemical pollution damage marine ecosystems.
Rising sea levels and acidification threaten coastal and ocean habitats.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Ocean acidification is when the ocean absorbs extra carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air, which makes the water more acidic.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Ocean acidification is when water is polluted from human activities on land.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the main threats to oceans and how they affect marine environments.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask students to do some extra research on the 1996 Milford Haven Oil spill, looking at the causes and effects.

lessons.unitTitle: Anthropocene: What is the impact of humans on the world?

lessonKeywords.description: the complete removal of trees
plants, animals, or other organisms that are brought into a new environment, usually by humans, where they don't naturally belong
all the living things in an ecosystem or area
a natural environment where the plants and animals interact within it

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Deforestation reduces habitats and threatens species survival.
Pollution from agriculture and industry harms ecosystems.
Climate change alters ecosystems and species distributions.
Invasive species introduced by humans disrupt native ecosystems.
Biodiversity loss reduces ecosystem resilience and services.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While some introductions are intentional (e.g. for pest control or landscaping), many invasive species are introduced accidentally, such as via ballast water in ships or hitchhiking on imported goods.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Invasive species are always introduced by humans intentionally.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how human activity changes ecosystems and reduces biodiversity.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask students to research an animal which has become extinct in the last 50 years and share findings as a class.

lessons.unitTitle: Anthropocene: What is the impact of humans on the world?

lessonKeywords.description: material or substance that can break down naturally over time by the action of bacteria, fungi or other living organisms
tiny pieces of plastic, usually smaller than five millimetres, that either come from the breakdown of larger plastic items or are made that size
a large area of the ocean where plastic and other waste collects, trapped by circular ocean currents

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Most plastic is made from fossil fuels and is not biodegradable.
Plastic production has grown rapidly since the 1950s.
Plastic waste pollutes land, rivers, and oceans.
Microplastics enter food chains and may harm human health.
Wildlife can be injured or killed by plastic waste.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Plastic is not biodegradable, it just breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces and eventually turns into microplastics (tiny plastic pieces, smaller than 5 mm).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Plastic will eventually biodegrade, even if it takes hundreds of years.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the causes, scale, and impacts of plastic pollution on people and the environment.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask students to think of how they could use less plastic (for example using refillable water bottles).

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Sustainability means meeting today's needs without harming future generations.
Reducing waste and reusing materials helps conserve resources.
Choosing local and seasonal food reduces environmental footprints.
Sustainable transport reduces carbon emissions and pollution.
Individuals, communities and governments all play a role in sustainability.

to reduce their carbon footprint since 2006.

00:13:24.210 --> 00:13:25.710
in the UK.

263
00:13:25.710 --> 00:13:26.820
So what they're doing,

00:13:26.820 --> 00:13:29.010
residents have installed solar panels,

improved home insulation,

and held local events to share ideas on saving energy.

00:13:39.180 --> 00:13:41.790
and shows how a whole community can come together

269
00:13:41.790 --> 00:13:44.073
to create a more sustainable future.

00:13:47.310 --> 00:13:49.530
Okay, let's check our understanding.

00:13:49.530 --> 00:13:51.450
Building a more sustainable future

is just the responsibility of communities.

00:14:09.240 --> 00:14:11.850
Building a more sustainable future takes action

275
00:14:11.850 --> 00:14:14.100
from all levels of society,

276
00:14:14.100 --> 00:14:17.223
individuals, community, and government.

277
00:14:19.620 --> 00:14:22.890
Okay, we're on to our final task for this lesson.

278
00:14:22.890 --> 00:14:25.260
So what I would like you to do is imagine

00:14:25.260 --> 00:14:28.290
you've been asked to design a village of the future,

280
00:14:28.290 --> 00:14:30.150
one that's environmentally friendly,

00:14:30.150 --> 00:14:33.990
and ready to face the challenges of the Anthropocene.

282

Your job is to plan a sustainable community

00:14:36.690 --> 00:14:38.460
that protects the planet

or drawing of your village,

287
00:14:46.380 --> 00:14:49.530
so make sure that you label some of the key features,

288
00:14:49.530 --> 00:14:51.330
and then a written explanation

289
00:14:51.330 --> 00:14:54.660
explaining how your village is sustainable.

290

So when you are thinking about your village plan,

food and water, and areas for green space and nature.

00:15:06.960 --> 00:15:09.933

295
00:15:20.070 --> 00:15:22.680
So, I'll go through some of the sustainable features

296
00:15:22.680 --> 00:15:23.730
of the village.

297
00:15:23.730 --> 00:15:27.240
So there are recycling bins placed around the village.

298
00:15:27.240 --> 00:15:30.570
There's areas for green space for people to go walking.

299
00:15:30.570 --> 00:15:32.670
Wind turbines are used for energy.

300
00:15:32.670 --> 00:15:36.783
Lots of bikes and paths and public transport.

301
00:15:37.860 --> 00:15:39.660
And there's also community gardens

302
00:15:39.660 --> 00:15:41.973
for people to grow their own food.

303
00:15:43.980 --> 00:15:45.390
So here's my explanation

304
00:15:45.390 --> 00:15:48.870
of how EcoHaven aims to be sustainable:

305
00:15:48.870 --> 00:15:52.020

00:15:52.020 --> 00:15:55.650

307
00:15:55.650 --> 00:15:57.330

and a monthly clothes swap to reuse clothes.

Local farmers supply food through a weekly market

00:16:10.170 --> 00:16:11.400
and there are shared gardens

where people grow fruit and vegetables.

Rainwater is collected in tanks

00:16:23.250 --> 00:16:25.650

lessons.unitTitle: Anthropocene: What is the impact of humans on the world?

lessonKeywords.description: when people use more resources than Earth can replace
the mass production and sale of cheaply made clothing that is not worn often and is quickly replaced
the exchange of goods, money and services between countries
electronic waste
resources that come from Earth without human influence and can be used for human needs

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: High levels of consumption increase demand for natural resources.
Global trade increases the environmental footprint of consumption.
Richer countries consume more per person than poorer countries.
Waste from overconsumption contributes to pollution and emissions.
Fast fashion and electronics create growing environmental problems.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Incinerating waste releases toxic gases and carbon emissions.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Incinerarting waste is good for the environment.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how resource use and consumption patterns affect the planet.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask students to think about how could they reduce their consumption (for example buy less clothes or buy clothes from a second hand source).

lessons.unitTitle: Anthropocene: What is the impact of humans on the world?

lessonKeywords.description: a computer program that uses maths and science to predict how Earth’s climate might change in the future
a severe weather event or any weather significantly different from the average
when people have regular access to enough safe, nutritious food to live healthy lives
moving from one place to another with the intention of staying there

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Climate models predict rising temperatures and more extreme weather.
Sea levels are expected to rise due to melting ice and thermal expansion.
Some regions may face drought, while others experience more flooding.
Climate change may increase migration and conflict over resources.
Actions taken now will influence how severe future climate change becomes.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The planet is getting hotter. Some places are going to get hotter whereas some places are going to get wetter.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Climate change is going to cause the planet to get hotter and drier.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how the climate may change in the future and what the impacts could be.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask students what extreme weather they have experienced and build on the fact it is more likely due to climate change.

lessons.unitTitle: Anthropocene: What is the impact of humans on the world?

lessonKeywords.description: the layer of gases that surrounds Earth. It includes the oxygen we need to breathe, so it is essential for life on Earth
includes all the water on Earth, such as oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers, groundwater, and water vapour in the atmosphere
the solid parts of Earth, including the crust, mantle, and core, as well as rocks, soil, mountains, and other landforms
life on Earth, encompassing all living organisms (plants, animals, bacteria, etc.) and the ecosystems they form
proposed geological epoch that marks when human activity has had a significant impact on Earth

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Human activity affects Earth's physical systems.
Population increase has significantly increased the human impact on Earth's physical systems.
Industrialisation significantly increased the human impact on Earth's systems.
The Anthropocene is a term used to describe a new geological age shaped by humans.
The term "Anthropocene" is debated by scientists.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Anthropocene is a proposed geological epoch that marks the period in Earth’s history during which human activity has had a significant impact on Earth.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Anthropocene is the period of Earth’s history from when homosapiens first evolved.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the meaning of the term 'Anthropocene' and can explain why it is debated by scientists.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask students what impact they have had on Earth.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Alternative energy sources include renewable energy sources and nuclear power.

lessons.lessonTitle: UK landscapes - the role of geology and past processes

lessonKeywords.description: an area shaped by physical and human processes
rocks formed when molten magma cools and solidifies
rocks made from compacted sediment layers over time
rocks changed by intense heat and/or pressure
the study of the Earth and its physical structure

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The UK has upland and lowland landscapes and river systems.
Geology affects the shape and type of UK landscapes.
Tectonic activity has helped form upland and lowland areas.
Glacial erosion and deposition shaped upland and lowland landscapes.
Geology is the study of the Earth.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Glaciers shaped many upland landscapes during the last Ice Age, but the original formation of mountains like those in Scotland and the Lake District was caused by tectonic activity millions of years ago.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Upland areas in the UK were created by glaciers.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how geology, tectonics and glaciation have influenced the UK's upland and lowland landscapes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There are opportunities to relate landscapes mentioned in this lesson to OS map extracts and to map skills.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, my name's Mrs. Hormigo, and I'm going to be teaching you today.
I hope you're going to enjoy the lesson and learn lots.
Let's get started.
Today's lesson looks at the UK's landscapes and how geology and past processes have shaped them.
By the end of the lesson, you'll be able to explain how geology, tectonics, and glaciation have influenced the UK's upland and lowland landscapes.
There are five key words for today's lesson, landscape, an area shaped by physical and human processes, igneous rocks, rocks that are formed when molten magma cools and solidifies, sedimentary rocks, rocks made from compacted sediment layers over time, metamorphic rocks, rocks that have been changed by intense heat and or pressure, and geology, the study of the earth and its physical structure.
There are three learning cycles for today's lesson.
The physical geography of the UK is our first, the second is the influence of geology and tectonic activity, and the third is the impact of glacial processes.
Let's get started on our first learning cycle, the physical geography of the UK.
The UK you may well know has many diverse physical landscapes.
You may have had an opportunity to visit many of these.
You'll see from these images here that we have steep mountains, coastal cliffs, and rolling hills and flat fertile plains.
This is a relief map and it shows the areas that are upland and lowland in the UK.
We can see this using the key, so the more dark orangy brownie colors show areas of high land, so upland, and the bluey greeny colors show lower land.
Where's the highest and lowest land in the UK? Have a chat to your partner and see if you can work that out.
So the upland areas are highland areas with steep slopes and rocky terrain, and we can see if you look at this map that a large proportion of these are found in the north and the west of the UK.
These include the Scottish Highlands, Eryri, and the Pennines.
The characteristics you would expect to find in these upland areas are steep gradients, thin soils, and a cooler, wetter climate, and they're largely made from harder, more resistant rocks, for example, igneous and metamorphic, and we'll come back to that a little bit later.
Lowlands are flatter, lower areas with softer ground and deeper soils, and these are largely found in the south and the east of the UK.
For example, we have the Fens in East Anglia, the Thames valley, and the Weald, an area between the North and South Downs in the southeast of the UK.
The characteristics of these areas are flat terrain, deep, fertile soils, and a warmer, drier climate, and they're made from softer sedimentary rocks, for example, chalk and clay.
Quick check now for you.
Which of these are upland areas of the UK? Eryri, the Weald, the Pennines, or Scottish Highlands? Pause the video and come back when you've made your decision.
I hope you correctly identified that it was Eryri, the Pennines, and the Scottish Highlands that were upland areas of the UK.
A second check now.
Which of these are lowland areas of the UK? Is it Eryri, the Weald, Pennines, or the Fens? Pause the video and come back when you've made your decision.
I hope you identified the Weald and the Fens as the examples of lowland areas of the UK.
Well done.
Rivers have played a major role in shaping the UK's landscapes as well.
They've done this by eroding, transporting, and depositing material over time.
This map shows four key rivers in the UK, the River Trent in the Midlands, the River Tyne in the northeast of England, the River Severn, which flows through Wales and England, and the River Thames, which starts in the Cotswolds and flows out to the North Sea through London.
In upland areas, rivers erode steep V-shaped valleys and waterfalls.
In lowland areas, rivers deposit materials, forming floodplains, meanders, and estuaries.
Check for you now.
Which of these features are caused by river erosion, floodplain, waterfall, estuary, or a V-shaped valley? Pause the video and come back when you've made your decision.
I hope you correctly identified that a waterfall and a V-shaped valley are erosional land forms that are found in upland areas due to the vertical erosion of the land by the rivers as they work their way down from the source towards the middle and the lower course.
First task for you now.
On your outline map of the UK, can you shade and label two upland areas and one lowland area, and then around the map, can you annotate it with key characteristics of upland and lowland areas? Pause the video and come back when you've had a go at this.
Your map will be similar to this one.
On your map, you should have identified two upland areas, and I've chosen Northwest Highlands in Scotland and the Lake District in northwest England, and for my lowland area, the Fens in East Anglia.
Then surrounding that, we've got the annotations, so for the upland areas I've put that they have steep gradients, thin soil, and cooler, wetter climates, and they're formed from hard, resistant igneous and metamorphic rocks.
And then for the lowland areas, they are flatter terrain and they have a warmer, drier climate, and the underlying geology are sedimentary rocks.
Well done if yours is similar to this one.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Rock types have distinctive physical and chemical characteristics.
Igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks are found in the UK.
Igneous rocks form from cooling molten magma.
Sedimentary rocks form from accumulated sediments.
Metamorphic rocks change due to heat and/or pressure.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Metamorphic rocks are created by heat and pressure acting on sedimentary and igneous rocks.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Rocks do not change once they are formed.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, geographers.
My name's Mrs. Hormigo, and I'm looking forward to teaching you today.
I hope you're going to enjoy the lesson and learn lots.
Let's get started.
Today's lesson looks at the varied geology of the UK.
And by the end of the lesson, you'll be able to describe the characteristics and the distribution of rock types in the UK.
There are five keywords for today's lesson.
Igneous rocks, rocks formed from the cooling of molten magma.
Sedimentary rocks, rocks formed from accumulated sediments.
Metamorphic rocks, rocks changed by heat and/or pressure.
And chalk, a soft white sedimentary rock found in southern England.
And granite, a hard igneous rock found in upland UK areas.
There are two learning cycles for today's lesson.
The first is the UK's main rock types and their characteristics.
The second is the distribution of the UK's main rock types.
Let's get started with our first and have a look at the main rock types found in the UK and consider their characteristics.
The UK is made up of a variety of rock types, each formed in different ways over millions of years.
And we can see here, looking at this geology map, the different colors represent the different types of rocks.
We can see that across the UK there are many different colors on that map.
Izzy says, did you know that the rocks beneath your feet could be up to 3 billion years old and completely different from those in another part of the UK.
So there are three main types of rock in the UK.
Igneous rocks, sedimentary rocks, and metamorphic rocks.
And this map here shows us the distribution of these three different types of rocks.
Each type has its own distinctive physical and chemical characteristics, and their distribution in the UK is also distinctive.
Looking at that map, we can see that igneous and metamorphic rocks tend to be in the northwest of the UK, and sedimentary rocks are in central and southern areas.
Igneous rocks are linked to volcanic activity, and they form when magma or lava cools and hardens and forms crystals.
Lava cools on the surface, and this happens quickly, forming small crystals.
And we call this extrusive igneous rock.
Magma cools underground, and it cools more slowly, and it forms large crystals, which we call intrusive igneous rock.
Now let's consider the main characteristics of igneous rock.
So it's made, as we've said, from interlocking crystals that vary in size depending on the type of rock.
They're usually very hard and resistant to erosion.
There are no fossils due to the extreme temperatures found in the molten rock from which it forms. It can be intrusive, which form large crystals, or extrusive, which form small crystals.
And usually it's impermeable.
Quick check for you now.
Which of these are common characteristics of igneous rock? Impermeable, easily eroded, or made of interlocking crystals.
Pause the video and come back when you've had a go.
I hope you correctly identified impermeable and made of interlocking crystals as the common characteristics of igneous rock.
Igneous rock is in fact hard and resistant to erosion.
So B is definitely not correct.
Sedimentary rock is made from layers of sediment, sand, mud, and dead plants and animals.
Over time, these layers are compressed and compacted to form rock.
Examples that we have include limestone, which is formed from marine shells, coral, and other sea creature remains that build up over time under the sea and are compressed and compacted to form rock.
And chalk, which is a type of limestone which is formed from microscopic plankton.
And finally, sandstone, formed from sand particles.
Let's look at the main characteristics of sedimentary rocks.
They're layered and usually softer than igneous rocks.
And that's because the sediment is laid down in layers and then compacted and compressed to form the rock.
Often more easily eroded.
They may contain fossils, as they're made from organic material.
Often underlie lowland areas in the UK.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Physical processes shape landforms through interaction with geology.
Weathering, rivers and slope processes shape the land.
Climate affects the formation of landscapes over time.
Human activity also changes how landscapes look and function.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Weathering breaks down rocks in place without movement, while erosion involves the removal and transport of that material by wind, water, ice, or gravity.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Weathering and erosion are the same process.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how distinctive upland and lowland landscapes result from physical processes and human activity.

lessons.lessonTitle: Location and physical characteristics of cold environments

lessonKeywords.description: environments found at higher latitudes and higher altitudes; they include polar, tundra and alpine biomes
a global land area that is characterised by its plants, animals and climate
the angular distance of a place north or south of Earth's Equator

the average weather conditions of a place over a long period of time, typically 30 years or more

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Cold environments (polar and tundra) and located at high latitudes close to the poles.
Cold environments have distinctive physical characteristics.
The climate influences other physical characteristics of cold environments.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While some areas of coastal tundra does receive a substantial quantity of precipitation, in reality most cold environment regions are extremely dry, with some areas receiving less than 250 mm of precipitation per year - defining them as deserts.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Cold environments receive a lot of precipitation (in this case snowfall).

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the location and physical characteristics of cold environments.

lessons.lessonTitle: The interdependence of biotic and abiotic components in cold environments

lessonKeywords.description: the living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. plants, animals)
the non-living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. water, nutrients)
the connections between different components of the environment, where each component depends on or influences the others
the transfer of water to the atmosphere through evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Cold environment ecosystems exhibit interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people.
Food chains and food webs show how biotic and abiotic components are interdependent in a cold environment.
Nutrient cycles show how biotic and abiotic components are interdependent in a cold environment.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Soil is classed as an abiotic component because soil itself is non-living.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Soil is a biotic component of ecosystems because it contains living organisms.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how biotic and abiotic components in a cold environment such as soil, climate, animals, plants and people are interdependent.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If pupils have a good understanding of nutrient cycles from studying ecosystems earlier in the course, then it is appropriate to challenge them to explain how the nutrient cycle of cold environments change in response to environmental change, such as a reduction in rainfall or removal of vegetation.

lessons.lessonTitle: Development opportunities and challenges in Northern Canada

lessonKeywords.description: the people that originally lived and may continue to live in a particular country or region
the process of removing valuable minerals from the earth
the business of attracting and taking care of visitors to a place
a thick subsurface layer of soil that remains frozen throughout the year, occurring chiefly in polar regions

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Northern Canada is an example of a cold environment.
There are opportunities for development in Northern Canada (mineral extraction, energy, fishing, tourism).
There are challenges for developing in Northern Canada (extreme temperatures, inaccessibility, provision of buildings).

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While challenging, development is possible in cold environments with proper planning and technology.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Cold environments cannot support any form of development.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain opportunities and challenges of developing cold environments in Northern Canada.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Set students the task of developing a fact file on this case study for homework, which they can then use for revision closer to the exam.

lessonKeywords.description: using resources in a way that means future generations will still be able to use them in the same way
a measure of how many different species live in an ecosystem
protection and management of natural resources to prevent damage and maintain biodiversity

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Cold environments are at risk from economic development.
Cold environments are valuable as wilderness areas and these fragile environments should be protected.
Strategies are used to balance economic development and conservation in cold environments.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Many valuable resources are found in cold environments (albeit difficult to access), such as fossil fuels and minerals. Timber in polar and tundra regions is not found there. These are treeless areas. Timber is found further south in the taiga biome.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The only valuable resource in cold environments is timber.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how cold environments are at risk from economic development and how they can be protected.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use GIS tools to analyse areas that have been mined and their impact on the environment. Students could map tundra or polar areas, identify regions most affected by mining or fossil fuel extraction and correlate them with changes in local biodiversity.

lessons.lessonTitle: Plant and animal adaptations in cold environments

lessonKeywords.description: evolutionary changes that improve an organism’s chance of survival in its environment
a state that certain animals enter to save energy during periods of unfavourable weather conditions or food shortages
the variety of different types of life found in a particular area
a community of living organisms and their interactions with their environment

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Cold environments are home to a variety of plants and animals.
Animals in cold environments are well adapted to the physical conditions.
Plants in cold environments are well adapted to the physical conditions.
There are issues related to biodiversity in cold environments.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Only two polar or tundra species enter full hibernation - the grizzly bear and arctic ground squirrel. Many other animals migrate to find food and warmth, while others are highly adapted to remain active and survive the extremely cold winters.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That due to the extreme cold climate, particularly during the winter months, that all animals must hibernate to save energy.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how plants and animals are well adapted to the physical conditions in cold environments and that there are issues related to biodiversity.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Watching short clips from wildlife programmes about animal and plant adaptations in the cold environment as a class helps to reinforce understanding of the link between challenges and adaptations.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Hot deserts are home to a variety of plants and animals.
Plants in hot deserts are well adapted to the physical conditions.
Animals in hot deserts are well adapted to the physical conditions.
There are issues related to biodiversity in hot deserts.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: A camel's hump does not hold water at all – it actually stores fat. The camel uses it as nourishment when food is scarce. If a camel uses the fat inside the hump, the hump will become limp and droop, but with food and rest the hump will normalise.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A camel's hump stores water.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain that plants and animals are well adapted to the physical conditions in hot deserts and that there are issues related to biodiversity.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Short clips from wildlife programmes about animal and plant adaptations in the hot desert help reinforce learning. Episode 4 of Planet Earth 2 has several good examples.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Desertification is a serious threat in hot desert environments.
There are several causes of desertification including climate change, population growth and removal of fuelwood.
There are several strategies used to reduce the risk of desertification including soil management and tree planting.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Desertification can occur in any fertile land that becomes increasingly arid, not just in deserts.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Desertification only occurs in existing deserts.

lessons.lessonTitle: The interdependence of biotic and abiotic components in hot deserts

lessonKeywords.description: the living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. plants, animals)
the non-living elements of an ecosystem (e.g. water, nutrients)
the connections between different components of the environment, where each component depends on or influences the others
the transfer of water to the atmosphere through evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Hot desert ecosystems exhibit interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people.
Food chains and food webs show how biotic and abiotic components are interdependent in a hot desert.
Nutrient cycles show how biotic and abiotic components are interdependent in hot desert.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Litter in the nutrient cycle is considered abiotic because it consists of non-living organic material, such as dead leaves and decomposing matter. Although it originated from living organisms, once it becomes litter, it is classified as non-living.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Litter in the nutrient cycle is considered biotic.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how biotic and abiotic components in a hot desert such as soil, climate, animals, plants and people are interdependent.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If pupils have a strong understanding of nutrient cycles from studying ecosystems earlier in the course, then it is appropriate to challenge them to explain how the nutrient cycle of hot deserts changes in response to environmental change, such as a reduction in rainfall or removal of vegetation.

lessons.lessonTitle: Development opportunities and challenges in the Kalahari Desert

lessonKeywords.description: a climate with little to no rainfall
the people or animals that originally lived and may continue to live in a particular country or region
the process of removing valuable minerals from the earth
the business of attracting and taking care of visitors to a place

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The Kalahari Desert is an example of a hot desert.
There are opportunities for development in the Kalahari Desert (mineral extraction, energy, farming, tourism).
There are challenges for developing hot desert environments in the Kalahari (extreme temperatures, water supply).

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Deserts can have significant opportunities for economic development, for example mineral extraction, solar energy, tourism and irrigated farming.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Hot deserts are barren, lifeless areas with no real economic potential.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the opportunities and challenges of developing hot desert environments in the Kalahari Desert.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Set students the task of developing a fact file on this case study for homework, which they can then use for revision closer to the exam.

lessons.lessonTitle: Location and physical characteristics of hot deserts

lessonKeywords.description: arid areas experiencing low rainfall, generally below 250 mm/year, and high summer temperatures
a global land area that is characterised by its plants, animals and climate
the average weather conditions of a place over a long period of time, typically 30 years or more

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Hot desert ecosystems are located at roughly 30°N and 30°S of the Equator.
Hot desert ecosystems have distinctive physical characteristics.
The climate influences other physical characteristics of hot deserts.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While some deserts are exceptionally dry, a region can experience up to 250 mm of rain each year and still be categorised as a desert.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: It never rains in hot deserts.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the location and physical characteristics of hot deserts.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The physical characteristics of deserts can vary significantly: show students a range of desert landscapes and use GIS to explore desert surfaces - from sand dunes to desert pavements.
