lessonKeywords.description: the pattern of where people do and do not live
the average number of people that live within a square kilometre

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are 76 cities in the UK and the majority of these are in England.
Population is unevenly distributed in the UK.
Population density varies between the countries of the UK and areas within them.
Human and physical factors can explain the differences in population distribution.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Population density is a spatial pattern of population whereas population density is the ratio of people to a defined space.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils can mix up population distribution and population density.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can locate major cities of the UK and describe and explain the UK's uneven population distribution.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pupils are likely to have some prior knowledge about the location of UK cities but using an atlas for Task A would scaffold it for those needing additional support.

lessons.lessonTitle: Economic opportunities and environmental impacts in rural areas
lessons.unitTitle: Liverpool: changes in a UK city

lessonKeywords.description: planned initiative designed to attract tourists such as new attractions, improvements to infrastructure, promotion of sustainable tourism and the development of tourism-related businesses
increase the spread of commercial activities, for example, by creating new enterprises on a farm such as a shop or a B&B

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Economic challenges from the decline in farming have led to new economic opportunities in rural areas.
Tourism projects and rural diversification support the local multiplier effect which strengthens the local economy.
An example of a tourism project in Eden is the Herdwick Stones and of rural diversification, Waterside House.
Economic opportunities have environmental impacts which can be positive and negative.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Environmental impacts from development can be negative, but they can also be positive, such as increased environmental awareness and reduced use of agricultural chemicals.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Environmental impacts from economic development are always negative.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify ways in which rural areas generate income through tourism projects and rural diversification, and recognise the environmental impacts of these opportunities.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Add a local component to this by finding an example of a local development which had some arguments around environmental impact within it. Or set up conflict more generally with a debate around the following motion: "This House would prioritise environmental protection over economic growth".

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, my name is Mr. March, and I'm here today to teach you all about economic opportunities and environmental impacts in rural areas.
So grab everything that you need for today's lesson and let's get going.
By the end of today's lesson, you will be able to identify ways in which rural areas generate income through tourism projects and rural diversification, and recognize the environmental impacts of these opportunities.
There are two key terms for today's lesson, and those are tourism project and rural diversification.
Tourism project refers to planned initiatives designed to attract tourists, such as new attractions, improvements to infrastructure, promotion of sustainable tourism, and the development of tourism-related businesses.
Rural diversification refers to the increase in the spread of commercial activities, for example, by creating new enterprises on a farm such as a shop or a B&B.
There are two learning cycles for today's lesson.
We're going to start with learning cycle one, which is all about economic opportunities in Eden.
Cumbria is the third largest county by area in England, and it's located in the northwest of England and borders Scotland, as you can see on the map on the right hand side of the screen.
Now, until 2023, there were six districts in the county of Cumbria, and the most rural of which, which means countryside, the most countryside-dominant of those districts was Eden.
And you can see Eden marked on that map on the right hand side, and you can see that it is the largest district which makes up the county of Cumbria.
England's largest national park is called the Lake District, and it covers 40% of Cumbria.
Ullswater is a lake in the Eden area of Cumbria and is within the Lake District National Park.
Now, evidence of extensive agriculture can be seen by the network of fields.
Sheep farming is also commonplace in these hills, and you can see that in the image in front of you.
So on the left hand side, we've got that map showing the location of Ullswater Lake.
And on the right hand side then you can see that image of Ullswater Lake, but also the array of different fields, which is again showing us sheep farming and really the agricultural nature of this landscape.
Eden's economy has changed significantly then over the past 50 years.
It was traditionally reliant on agriculture and other forms of primary industry.
Whilst they are still important, this sector has actually reduced significantly due to increased global competition as well as mechanization.
This economic change has brought about challenges to the local area; however, it has also presented some real significant economic opportunities through the following: tourism projects, as well as rural diversification.
Tourism projects in the form of different initiatives which are trying to attract tourists to the area to then spend money, but also rural diversification through the form of increasing the spread of different commercial activities.
So a quick learning check.
It says, true or false? Economic change only creates challenges.
So what I'd like you to do right now then is pause the video here whilst you consider and then select your answer.
And the correct answer was false.
Now, once again, I'd like you to pause the video here whilst you consider as to why or how this statement then is false.
And the reason it's false is because while economic change can lead to a number of different challenges, it's true, but it also presents many opportunities.
In an agricultural area, these opportunities may be relating to tourism projects as well as rural diversification.
So really well done if you were able to identify those two correct answers.
Tourism projects are funded in a variety of different ways, and one way is through the local council, which can give them small grants of £500 for tourism projects which are designed to add value to the visitor experience.
Examples in Eden include the following.
So Herdwick Stones, sculptures along the Ullswater Way, which celebrate shepherding in the area, as well as Hoff Beck information panel, which again promotes a walk along the stream with information about the different biodiversity in the area, as well as other attractions.
All these things then try to improve the visitor experience and perhaps try to attract more tourists in the future.
Rural diversification is often undertaken by farmers looking for new and different sources of income, and there's a great many different ways in which this can actually be achieved, the first of which is a farm shop, placing a shop on their farm to sell the produce that they and perhaps other local farmers are selling.
It creates income, it creates jobs, and it makes best use of that local produce that they are creating themselves, but also bed and breakfasts or B&Bs and glamping, you know, trying to tap into that tourism trade and trying to tap into and really take advantage of the beautiful scenery in their local area and the tourists that it's already attracting.
And finally, leisure activities such as fishing, quad biking, mazes, as well as petting zoos.
Once again, trying to tap into and create a larger tourism industry in the local area where it can generate income and jobs for themselves.
Rural diversification can be achieved by opening farm shops, as I said just a moment ago.
Some farms sell produce directly to local residents and tourists.
For example, they may sell meat, vegetables, and produce their farm or those nearby.
Open PYO, pick-your-own fields of fruit and vegetables.
So people can literally come to their farm and pick strawberries or pick raspberries, pick vegetables, and they can pay for that service and also pay for the produce as well.
Farm shops also include cafes where once again they can generate an income by selling teas and coffees as well as cakes, homemade cakes, which again add to the revenue stream of that farm.
Rural diversification can be achieved by providing accommodation too.
Many farms now add to their income through providing accommodation to tourists.
They can convert those old barns into holiday cottages.
They can turn fields into campsites.
They can use unused farmhouse bedrooms into B&B rooms. They can host events, for example, weddings in the countryside is always a big attraction for people, particularly those people living in the city looking for that glamorous, scenic wedding.
Some add facilities such as swimming pools, spas, and playgrounds.
It's about making best use of that beautiful landscape that they live in to try to generate more income for their business, for their farm.
Rural diversification can also be achieved by providing leisure activities.
For example, farms often have land which can be used for activities other than the arable or dairy farming that they're known for.
Tours to learn about farming and rural skills, horse riding and other sporting activities, attractions such as mazes and animal encounters, as well as hosting local events such as craft fairs or barn dances.
So it's once again trying to diversify, trying to generate new ways of making money.
Waterside House is a fantastic example of a working farm with sheep and cattle on the shores of Ullswater Lake.
And you can see that there identified on the map on the right hand side.
Now currently it employs 12 people and has diversified a number of different ways.
It now provides leisure activities through the form of paddleboarding, boat hire, as well as an art gallery, but also it's providing accommodation through tent and caravan pitches, glamping, holiday cottages, as well as onsite facilities such as a shop, a play park, and a cafe.
So when you look at all those different points there, you really try to see just how much it's diversified its ability to generate income and revenue streams for the farm.
Time once again for a learning check, and it says to complete the following facts about tourism projects and rural diversification in the Ullswater area.
So what you need to do right now then is pause the video here whilst you read through those four different statements and do your best to complete the facts.
Best of luck.
And the answers.
So A was Herdwick Stones and Hoff Beck information panel are examples of tourism projects.
B was rural diversification is often undertaken by farmers looking to increase their income.
C was examples of rural diversification include farm shops, accommodation, and leisure activities.
And D was Waterside House is an example of a working farm which has diversified to provide accommodation and leisure activities.
Really well done if you were able to complete those following facts.
Rural diversification and tourism projects aim to keep money local through providing jobs, which leads to increased spending and a stronger economy.
And this all links back to something that we need to know about, which is called the local multiplier effect.
But how does that work? Well, it starts with increased spending via perhaps tourism.
Money then enters the local economy, perhaps as a result of a tourist staying at a B&B or a tourist paying for something at a cafe.
Either way, money is then entering the local economy from somewhere else in the country.
Demand then increases for different commodities and different services in that area.
And more jobs are created, which thereby provides income for those local people.
So that local multiplier effect is all well and good in theory, but how does it actually work? Well, the tourism projects of Herdwick Stones and Hoff Beck information panel as well as rural diversification seen at Waterside House do benefit the local economy, and they do so in the following ways.
The attractions encourage more people to visit the area.
Tourists then spend money in local shops, on accommodation, as well as in restaurants.
The income of local residents increases, so demand for local services and amenities actually grows, and more jobs are created and more money is added to the local economy.
So you can see how by creating and developing this tourism industry, it really goes some way to supporting and developing the local economy.
Time once again for a learning check.
And you can see on the screen in front of you, you've got that local multiplier effect that we just went through.
What you need to do then is pause the video here whilst you try to fill those two gaps that you can see in front of you.
Best of luck.
And the answers were: so rural diversification and tourism projects aim to keep money local through providing jobs, which leads to increased spending and a stronger economy.
And the final gap that you needed to fill was demand increases for services.
So really well done if you were able to identify those two correct answers.
On now to our one and only practice question, and it's a really interesting one.
It says, you are a farmer looking to increase your income through rural diversification.
You have submitted a plan to the local council for approval, and you can see that plan there in front of you.
On the left hand side, you've got the current farm yard and fields.
On the right hand side then is your proposed redevelopment.
An application form needs to be submitted alongside the plans, and you need to then complete the following two questions.
The first one is to describe the rural diversification you wish to gain planning approval for.
And the second one is then to explain how your plans for rural diversification will actually go to support the local economy.
So please then pause the video here whilst you attempt these two practice questions.
Best of luck.
In terms of feedback then, your answer may have included the following for the first question.
So I've said that I plan to redevelop my farm to include holiday accommodation, leisure facilities, and a farm shop.
The accommodation will involve converting disused barns into holiday cottages and providing pitches for tents and caravans.
Onsite facilities will include a shower block and a children's playground.
The redevelopment will also feature the creation of a farm shop offering local produce.
In addition, a jetty will be constructed on Ullswater to support water-based leisure activities such as paddle boarding.
The second question, again, your answer may have included the following.
I've said that these plans will provide a boost through the local multiplier effect.
The conversion of disused barns and development of the field will create construction jobs, while the ongoing operation of the farm, farm shop I should say, holiday cottages, and campsite will generate permanent employment.
Tourists attracted by the new facilities will spend money both on site and in nearby attractions.
This increased spending will stimulate further demand, creating more jobs and encouraging the growth of local amenities and services.
As a result, additional income will circulate within the community.
So really well done if you were able to include anything like that in your own answer.
We're on now to our second and final learning cycle, and it's all about environmental impacts of economic opportunities.
So it's important to assess the environmental impacts of these tourism projects and rural diversification alongside the undoubted economic benefits.
What might the environmental impacts of these approaches to rural diversification actually be? Now, you may like to pause the video here whilst you consider your own answer to that question, or perhaps even better, have a discussion with someone near you.
So environmental impacts can certainly be positive and negative.
Let's start by looking at the positive impacts of these different developments.
First of all, it will cause a reduced pressure on agricultural land.
It also encourages land stewardship.
And finally, it develops environmental awareness.
What are the negatives though? Well, it undoubtedly causes habitat disturbance through different construction projects and more tourists visiting the area.
There's also increased waste and water demand.
There's also soil compaction and erosion, once again from tourists visiting the area.
And finally, there's carbon emissions from the increased traffic from once again the increased tourism.
So in terms of the positive environmental impacts, these include the following.
There is reduced pressure on agricultural land and intensive agricultural practices.
For example, fertilizer use is actually reduced.
There's also land stewardship, so ecotourism and conservation projects can actually encourage native species recovery as well as protection.

lessons.lessonTitle: Liverpool CBD and inner city: challenges and opportunities from decline
lessons.unitTitle: Liverpool: changes in a UK city

lessonKeywords.description: decline in importance of the industrial sector, for example, the closure of factories
reduction in the population of an area, typically involving out-migration following deindustrialisation
areas with a high concentration of students, typically in sub-divided rental properties
the upgrading of areas (typically housing) often in the inner city, making them more desirable but often more expensive

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Deindustrialisation in the 20th century triggered depopulation in Liverpool's CBD and inner city.
The CBD and inner city experienced decline from the 1930s to 1990s followed by growth due to regeneration efforts.
Decline in the CBD and inner city led to challenges including dereliction, unemployment and economic recession.
21st century economic and population growth led to significant investment in the CBD.
Studentification, gentrification and e-commernce have brought challenges and opportunities.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Whilst regeneration in Liverpool has been very positive for the CBD and inner city overall, it has brought a number of challenges such as negative impacts of studentification, gentrification and e-commerce developments.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Regeneration only brings positive impacts.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how 20th century decline in Liverpool’s CBD and inner city led to challenges and opportunities for the population and economy.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Bring inner city Liverpool during the slum clearances of the 1960s and 1970s to life by adding further images of the city at this time.

lessons.lessonTitle: Consequences of interdependence of Liverpool and accessible rural areas
lessons.unitTitle: Liverpool: changes in a UK city

lessonKeywords.description: a place, often a town or village, where people live and then travel to other places, normally a city, for work
easy to get to and from
close ties or links between two or more entities or areas

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Cities are interdependent with accessible rural areas. An example of this is Liverpool and the village of Aughton.
Interdependence involves flows of goods, services and labour between urban and accessible rural areas.
Interdependence leads to economic, social and environmental benefits for Aughton and Liverpool.
Interdependence leads to economic, social and environmental costs for Aughton and Liverpool.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Rural areas can offer the residents of urban areas a source of labour and produce. They can provide jobs in industries such as agriculture and opportunities for recreation and leisure.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Urban areas have more facilities and services than rural areas. As a result, rural areas can offer cities little in return.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify ways in which Liverpool and Aughton are interdependent and categorise costs and benefits for both places (social, economic or environmental).

teacherTips.teacherTip: Google Street View provides good opportunities for further investigating the functions of villages like Aughton.

lessons.lessonTitle: Liverpool suburbs and rural-urban fringe: challenges and opportunities of growth
lessons.unitTitle: Liverpool: changes in a UK city

lessonKeywords.description: the outward movement of businesses and administrative organisations from the city centre to the outskirts or beyond
the physical outward expansion of a city into the surrounding countryside
land that is protected from development and surrounds major English cities

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Between 1931 and 2021, population in some local authorities in the Liverpool City Region grew, e.g. Halton.
The 1960s saw decentralisation from the declining CBD and inner city in favour of the suburbs and rural-urban fringe.
Developments in transport enabled decentralisation, e.g. new motorways.
Economic growth was a result of the development of retail and business parks and out of town shopping from the 1970s.
Urban sprawl in the suburbs and rural-urban fringe presents challenges, e.g. congestion and countryside destruction.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Greenfield refers to land which has never been built on. Greenbelt is protected land around major cities in England and is a policy designed to prevent urban sprawl.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils can confuse greenfield and greenbelt.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how 20th and 21st century changes in Liverpool’s population and economy led to challenges and opportunities for the suburbs and rural-urban fringe.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Development of greenfield and greenbelt land sparks lots of controversey. Search for examples of conflict in your local area so pupils can relate to the challenges of developing the rural-urban fringe.

lessons.lessonTitle: Links to Liverpool: changes in a rural area
lessons.unitTitle: Liverpool: changes in a UK city

lessonKeywords.description: the movement of people away from a city and into the countryside, which may lead to a reduction in the city's population
to do with people individually or as a community
to do with money and wealth

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Aughton is a rural village easily accesible from Liverpool.
Aughton has experienced economic and social changes as a consequence of counter-urbanisation which began in the 1950s.
Counter-urbanisation led to social changes in Aughton to do with its total population and population structure.
The demand for homes in the area has led to a pressure on housing affordability.
The affluence of the area has led to high-end restaurants and increased visitors have put pressure on the area.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Population change is a balance of inflows and outflows. Migration is one of these and counter-urbanisation is a process of migration but will not be responsible for all population change in an area.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Counter-urbanisation is responsible for all population change in a rural area.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the social and economic changes to Aughton as a result of its links to Liverpool.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Compare Aughton to a village which has experienced signficiant decline in services due to its proximity to a city. A local example to your context would support understanding and could be used as an opportunity for primary or secondary research.

lessons.lessonTitle: The impacts of regeneration and rebranding on people
lessons.unitTitle: Liverpool: changes in a UK city

lessonKeywords.description: a planning strategy aimed at addressing problems associated with decline, often involving improvements to infrastructure and encouraging new industries to an area
a planning and marketing strategy aimed at creating a new image of a city to encourage growth

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Rebranding and regeneration began in Liverpool in the 1980s to reverse the decline of the city.
Significant regeneration has occurred in the centre including areas around the waterfront, RopeWalks and Lime Street.
Liverpool has been rebranded as a cultural hub due to sports, music, ethnic diversity and maritime and historical sites.
Positive impacts include greater job diversity, new leisure facilities and a higher quality urban environment.
Negative impacts include a loss of community, a persistent wealth gap and focus on tourist over local needs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: An extended explanation would be: Regeneration and rebranding in Liverpool led to economic growth as a result of more businesses and tourism. This led to more diverse jobs and has contributed to a stronger and more resilient local economy.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils can fall into the habit of writing superficial explanations or fail to extend them fully.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how Liverpool has approached rebranding and regeneration since the 1980s and describe the positive and negative impacts on people.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To reinforce the importance of extended explanations, respond to brief statements with "so what?" or get pupils to bounce this phrase between themselves to encourage further explanation.

lessons.lessonTitle: Challenges of living in rural areas
lessons.unitTitle: Liverpool: changes in a UK city

lessonKeywords.description: wellbeing of individuals or groups of people measured by criteria other than wealth such as housing, employment and environmental factors
jobs involving the extraction of raw materials including farming, fishing and mining
reduction of people living in an area

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Eden is a very rural district within the rural county of Cumbria.
Eden has the highest percentage of green space and lowest population density of any district in England.
Eden ranks 186 on the Index of Multiple Deprivation. This masks areas of high deprivation such as barriers to services.
Eden faces four challenges: housing, provision of education and healthcare and decline in primary employment.
The young and elderly are more likely to be affected by challenges due to dependency on parents or the state for income.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Index of Multiple Deprivation is calculated by combining seven indicators. The overall rank is therefore an average and can mask significant variation in different aspects of deprivation.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The rank on the Index of Multiple Deprivation tells you everything about the deprivation of an area.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use knowledge about the area of Eden to explain the challenges facing the area and their impact on the young and the elderly.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Explore the Index of Multiple Deprivation in greater detail by looking into what measures are used to calculate the rank of each of the indicators.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

lessons.unitTitle: Liverpool: changes in a UK city

lessonKeywords.description: low standard of living caused by low income, poor health and low educational attainment, sometimes described as living in poverty
wealth or opportunities are not equally shared

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Inequalities exist in Liverpool linked to high relative levels of deprivation.
The Index of Multiple Deprivation measures relative deprivation at local authority and smaller scales.
The 6 local authorities in the Liverpool City Region are all in the top 60 most deprived in England. Knowsley ranks 2nd.
Deprivation has a cause and effect link to inequalities in services, health, employment and education.
High deprivation in Liverpool correlates with poor housing, poor health, unemployment and low educational attainment.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: It is important that data is used as an average and not the characteristics of every individual. The word stereotype is useful to use in this instance.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils can make sweeping statements about people that live in places.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use data to describe deprivation across the Liverpool City Region and identify how this relates to inequalities at a variety of scales.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The Index of Multiple Deprivation contains a wealth of rich data and adding comparisons to your local area could be a useful comparison. The misconception remains critical in this and the avoidance of stereotyping is paramount.

lessons.lessonTitle: Context of the city – site, situation and connectivity
lessons.unitTitle: Liverpool: changes in a UK city

lessonKeywords.description: the point on the ground where a settlement is built
the description of a place in relation to its human and physical surroundings
a measure of how well connected (by transport and other forms of communication) a place is

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Liverpool is a coastal city sited on flat land in NW England and situated about 300 km NW of London.
Liverpool is connected to the rest of the world through rail, road, sea and air links.
Liverpool's importance nationally and globally is a consequence of its site, situation and connectivity.
Liverpool is nationally important for its diversity, city economy, role in the Industrial Revolution and population.
Liverpool is globally important for trade, sporting and cultural events and its link to the slave trade and migration.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The site of a settlement is its exact point on the surface of Earth and the situation describes it in relation to other human and physical features.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils can confuse site and situation.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe the location of Liverpool through the features of site, situation and connectivity and use these to explain Liverpool’s national, regional and global importance.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Promote local locational knowledge by adapting the example of Norwich to your location. Pupils could respond to this verbally to increase oracy skills.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Liverpool's migrations can be divided over time (historical and recent) and over space (national and international).

International inflows have been both historic and recent.
Liverpool's population, age structure, economy, ethnicity, housing, income, services and culture have been influenced.
Toxteth, Calderstones and Halewood have been influenced in different ways

lessonKeywords.description: ripples in the sea caused by wind blowing over the surface of the water
the action of water wearing away rocks
high, steep waves, typically formed by local storms, that remove sediment from beaches
low waves, typically formed by distant storms, that deposit sediment onto beaches

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Different wave types (constructive and destructive) affect the coast.
The coast is shaped by processes of erosion (hydraulic power, abrasion and attrition).
The coast is shaped by transportation (longshore drift) of sediment.
The coast is shaped by deposition.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The swash is the movement of the wave from the sea to the beach which brings sediment with it. Whereas the backwash is the movement of the wave from the beach to sea.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Swash is when a wave moves down the beach to the sea and backwash is when a wave moves up the beach from the sea.

Well done if you manage to explain that correctly.

There are two key characteristics that a wave has, swash and backwash.
A swash is the movement of water up the beach after a wave breaks, carrying sediment and debris onto the shore.
Backwash, this is the flow of water returning down the beach after swash, pulling sediment back into the sea.
This can be called erosion.
On the video on the screen, you can see the swash is the movement of water up the beach after the wave breaks, and the backwash is the flow of water back into the sea due to gravity.
This process is repeated, bringing sediment up to the beach through the swash, and removing sediment from the beach through the backwash.
There are two types of waves that we find along the coast, destructive waves and constructive waves.
Destructive waves are high-energy waves that remove sediment from the beach.
And they have specific characteristics.

Constructive waves are low-energy waves and they carry sediment onto the beach.

They also cause erosion which gradually wears away the land.
Waves erode the coastline through hydraulic power, attrition, and abrasion.
Hydraulic power is the coastal erosion process in which waves compress air in cracks and joints in rocks.

lessons.lessonTitle: Weathering and mass movement at the coast

lessonKeywords.description: the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the surface
physical disintegration of rocks, for example through freeze-thaw
chemical breakdown of rocks usually involving slightly acidic rainwater
the downhill movement of material under the influence of gravity

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The coast is shaped by weathering processes (mechanical and chemical).
The coast is shaped by processes of mass movement (sliding, slumping and rock falls).

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Mass movement includes all downhill movements of soil, rock, or debris due to gravity. It's not just rapid events like landslides but also slower processes which occur gradually and can still significantly alter the landscape over time.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Mass movement only refers to dramatic events like landslides and rockfalls.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how weathering and mass movement shape the coast.

teacherTips.teacherTip: GIS could be used in this lesson to explore the impact of landslides and identify areas most at risk. The National Trust has an ArcGIS resource on climate hazards which could be used for this called Slope Failure (Landslides) Current.

Hello and welcome.

I'm so looking forward to learning with you today.
Today's lesson is called Weathering and Mass Movement at the Coast.
Grab everything you might need for today's lesson and let's begin our learning.

Before we can begin this learning, we need to define the keywords that we'll be using throughout today's lesson.
The keywords that we'll be using throughout today's lesson are: weathering, mechanical weathering, chemical weathering, and mass movement.
Weathering: this is the breakdown or disintegration of rocks at or close to the Earth's surface.
Mechanical weathering: this is the physical disintegration of rocks, for example, through freeze-thaw.
Chemical weathering: this is the chemical breakdown of rocks usually involving slightly acidic rainwater.
And mass movement: this is the downhill movement of material under influence of gravity.
Brilliant.
Now that we've defined these keywords, we can begin our learning.
The first question that we are going to explore in today's lesson is how does weathering shape the coast? Weathering is the breakdown of rocks and minerals at or near the Earth's surface, and there are three types of weathering.
There's mechanical weathering, and this involves physically breaking rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemical structure.
There's chemical weathering, and this happens when chemical reactions occur in rocks often involving weak acids.
And finally, there's biological weathering.
Here living organisms like plants and animals contribute to breaking rocks apart.
What are the three types of weathering found at the coast? Pause the video here whilst you decide and press play when you're ready to continue.
Excellent.
The three types of weathering found at the coast are: mechanical weathering, chemical weathering, and biological weathering.
Well done if you managed to remember those correctly.
Mechanical weathering is the breakdown of rocks into smaller pieces without chemical change.
Let's look a bit more closely at freeze-thaw weathering.
This process starts when water enters cracks in rocks.
When the temperature drops below freezing, the water turns to ice and it begins to expand.
This expansion puts pressure on the surrounding rock, widening the crack.
When the ice melts, the water seeps deeper into the crack.
If this freezing and thawing cycle happens repeatedly, the rock eventually breaks into smaller pieces.
Freeze-thaw is very common in coastal areas with cold climates because of the fluctuating temperatures and the availability of water from waves and rain.
An easy way to remember this is thinking about water bottles in the summer.
In the summer, you might fill up the water bottle and put it in the freezer so it's nice and cold for you in the morning.
You'll wait for it to thaw so you can drink it, and when you're finished you'll fill it up again and freeze it.
This continued process of freezing and thawing on the same water bottle will cause this water bottle to eventually break, similar to the process we've just learned about here.
Chemical weathering occurs when rocks are broken down through chemical reactions.
Acid in rainwater can react with rocks like limestone, which contain calcium carbonate.
Aisha has cleverly noted that when carbon dioxide dissolves in rainwater, it creates carbonic acid.
Chemical weathering is more common in coastal areas because of the moist conditions and the presence of salty or slightly acidic sea spray, which can speed up the process.
Biological weathering is caused by living organisms. For example, plant roots can grow into cracks in rocks, and as the roots grow thicker, they force the cracks to widen and the rock then breaks apart.
Another example is animals that burrow into softer rock.
They loosen the material and make it more vulnerable to other types of weathering.
This type of weathering is especially noticeable in coastal areas where plants like seaweed and organisms like mollusks attach to rocks and contribute to their breakdown.

How does mass movement shape the coast? Mass movement is a key process in coastal geography.
Mass movement refers to the downward movement of rock, soil, or debris under the influence of gravity.
This process is extremely important for shaping the coastlines as it moves the material that has slowly become weakened.
The result is often really dramatic.
Think about cliff collapses, landslides, or slumping slopes.
At the coast, mass movement is influenced by factors like the type of rock, the slope's steepness, and the presence of water, such as after heavy rainfall.
Understanding these processes is really important in helping us to understand how coastal landscapes constantly evolve, and for predicting and managing hazards in vulnerable areas.
Rock falls occur when rocks or fragments of rock break away from a cliff face and fall directly to the base.
This often happens for a number of reasons, and mainly because freeze-thaw weathering has weakened the rocks, or wave action has undercut the base of the cliff, and sometimes human activities, like construction or quarry, can trigger rock falls by destabilizing the cliff.
The fallen material is called scree, and the scree piles up at the base, and can eventually be carried away by waves, further altering the cliffs and increasing erosion.
Slumping is when material moves down a slope along a curved surface, and it happens like this.
Heavy rainfall will infiltrate and saturate the cliff, making it really, really heavy.
The saturated material will then move downwards under gravity along a curved slip plain within the cliff.
The curved movement then means the material can tip back on itself to form what looks like terraces or steps at the top of the slump, like you can see in the image on the screen.
The base of the slump is called the toe, and this is often eroded by waves.
The slump often leaves a distinctive curved, concaved scar at the top of the cliff.
Sliding is different from slumping.
Here, blocks of rock or soil will move straight down a slope rather than in a curved motion, and this usually occurs along a bedding plane, which is a layer of weaker rock parallel to the slope.
Sliding happens when the upper layers of the rock become saturated and heavy, causing them to slide over the weaker layer.
This process is going to leave a jagged edge at the top and a large amount of debris at the base of the cliff.

Weathering and mass movement are key processes that shape the coast.
Weathering breaks down rocks into smaller particles through physical, chemical, and biological processes.
Mass movement is the downward movement of rock, soil, or debris due to gravity.
Sliding, slumping, and rock falls are types of mass movement that are found at the coast.

00:04:10.560 --> 00:04:13.350
between chemical weathering and biological weathering?

106
00:04:13.350 --> 00:04:16.920
Is it A: chemical weathering involves chemical reactions,

107
00:04:16.920 --> 00:04:20.070
while biological weathering is caused by living organisms?

108
00:04:20.070 --> 00:04:23.550
Is it B: chemical weathering is caused by living organisms,

109
00:04:23.550 --> 00:04:27.030
while biological weathering involves chemical reactions?

110
00:04:27.030 --> 00:04:28.230
Or is it C:

111
00:04:28.230 --> 00:04:30.780
chemical weathering only occurs in hot climates,

112
00:04:30.780 --> 00:04:34.290
while biological weathering happens in cold climates?

113
00:04:34.290 --> 00:04:36.300
Pause the video here whilst you decide

114
00:04:36.300 --> 00:04:38.550
and press play when you're ready to continue.

115
00:04:44.130 --> 00:04:44.963
Excellent.

116
00:04:44.963 --> 00:04:46.890
The statement that best describes the difference

117
00:04:46.890 --> 00:04:51.420
between chemical weathering and biological weathering is A.

118
00:04:51.420 --> 00:04:53.940
Chemical weathering involves chemical reactions,

119
00:04:53.940 --> 00:04:55.620
while biological weathering is caused

120
00:04:55.620 --> 00:04:58.290
by living organisms like plants and animals.

121
00:04:58.290 --> 00:04:59.553
Well done on this task.

122
00:05:00.620 --> 00:05:02.760
We are now going to complete two different tasks

123
00:05:02.760 --> 00:05:04.920
before we review our answers.

124
00:05:04.920 --> 00:05:07.050
For this first task, I would like you to number

125
00:05:07.050 --> 00:05:09.930
the descriptions to match the steps shown in the diagram

126
00:05:09.930 --> 00:05:11.610
of freeze-thaw weathering.

127
00:05:11.610 --> 00:05:13.860
Remember, freeze-thaw weathering is a type

128
00:05:13.860 --> 00:05:15.510
of mechanical weathering.

129
00:05:15.510 --> 00:05:17.520
Pause the video here whilst you attempt this task,

130
00:05:17.520 --> 00:05:19.720
and press play when you're ready to move on.

131
00:05:25.380 --> 00:05:27.960
Well done for attempting this task.

132
00:05:27.960 --> 00:05:30.270
Let's now attempt at the second task.

133
00:05:30.270 --> 00:05:32.070
I would like you to explain the difference

134
00:05:32.070 --> 00:05:33.540
between mechanical weathering

135
00:05:33.540 --> 00:05:35.640
and chemical weathering at the coast.

136
00:05:35.640 --> 00:05:37.260
I've provided you with some hints

137
00:05:37.260 --> 00:05:39.840
to help you formulate your answer.

138
00:05:39.840 --> 00:05:41.700
For this question, you need to make sure

139
00:05:41.700 --> 00:05:43.680
you make two distinct points.

140
00:05:43.680 --> 00:05:45.597
One needs to be for mechanical weathering,

141
00:05:45.597 --> 00:05:48.450
and the other needs to be for chemical weathering.

142
00:05:48.450 --> 00:05:50.670
You also need to make sure that you include a detailed

143
00:05:50.670 --> 00:05:52.590
description for each of your points,

144
00:05:52.590 --> 00:05:55.203
and an example of how the process occurs.

145
00:05:56.040 --> 00:05:58.050
Pause the video here whilst you give this a go,

146
00:05:58.050 --> 00:06:00.533
and press play when you're ready to check your answers.

147
00:06:06.270 --> 00:06:07.800
Excellent effort on this task.

148
00:06:07.800 --> 00:06:09.960
Let's review our answers.

149
00:06:09.960 --> 00:06:12.810
For the first task, I asked you to number the descriptions

150
00:06:12.810 --> 00:06:14.490
to match the steps shown in the diagram

151
00:06:14.490 --> 00:06:15.990
of freeze-thaw weathering.

152
00:06:15.990 --> 00:06:17.370
Let's check to see if you managed

153
00:06:17.370 --> 00:06:19.230
to sequence them correctly.

154
00:06:19.230 --> 00:06:23.190
The first one is water enters cracks in rocks.

155
00:06:23.190 --> 00:06:26.703
The second, the water freezes when temperatures drop.

156
00:06:27.600 --> 00:06:30.090
The third, freezing water expands

157
00:06:30.090 --> 00:06:32.100
and puts pressure on the rock.

158
00:06:32.100 --> 00:06:36.570
The fourth, repeated freeze-thaw cycles widen the cracks.

159
00:06:36.570 --> 00:06:40.140
And lastly, the rock breaks into smaller pieces.

160
00:06:40.140 --> 00:06:43.800
Well done if you managed to complete this task correctly.

161
00:06:43.800 --> 00:06:45.750
I then asked you to explain the difference

162
00:06:45.750 --> 00:06:46.920
between mechanical weathering

163
00:06:46.920 --> 00:06:49.230
and chemical weathering at the coast.

164
00:06:49.230 --> 00:06:52.380
Your answers could include some of the following points.

165
00:06:52.380 --> 00:06:54.360
Mechanical weathering is the process where rocks

166
00:06:54.360 --> 00:06:56.520
are broken down into smaller pieces

167
00:06:56.520 --> 00:06:58.530
without any chemical change.

168
00:06:58.530 --> 00:07:00.360
This often occurs through processes

169
00:07:00.360 --> 00:07:02.370
such as freeze-thaw weathering,

170
00:07:02.370 --> 00:07:04.380
where water enters cracks in the rock,

171
00:07:04.380 --> 00:07:07.893
freezes and expands, causing the rock to break apart.

172
00:07:08.820 --> 00:07:10.830
Chemical weathering, on the other hand,

173
00:07:10.830 --> 00:07:14.400
involves the breakdown of rocks through chemical reactions.

174
00:07:14.400 --> 00:07:17.160
One example is when weak acids in the rainwater

175
00:07:17.160 --> 00:07:18.750
gradually dissolve minerals,

176
00:07:18.750 --> 00:07:21.480
like the calcium carbonate in limestone.

177
00:07:21.480 --> 00:07:22.740
Well done if you managed to include

178
00:07:22.740 --> 00:07:24.780
some of these points in your answer.

179
00:07:24.780 --> 00:07:27.870
This answer is good because it has clearly explained

180
00:07:27.870 --> 00:07:30.750
what happens in the mechanical weathering process

181
00:07:30.750 --> 00:07:32.640
and the chemical weathering process,

182
00:07:32.640 --> 00:07:35.970
and it even provided an example in the chemical weathering

183
00:07:35.970 --> 00:07:38.670
when it said weak acids dissolved minerals

184
00:07:38.670 --> 00:07:41.040
like calcium carbonate in limestone.

185
00:07:41.040 --> 00:07:41.873
Well done.

186
00:07:42.810 --> 00:07:44.550
We're now going to explore our final question

187
00:07:44.550 --> 00:07:45.840
of this lesson.

188
00:07:45.840 --> 00:07:47.853
How does mass movement shape the coast?

189
00:07:48.930 --> 00:07:52.260
Mass movement is a key process in coastal geography.

190
00:07:52.260 --> 00:07:55.290
Mass movement refers to the downward movement of rock, soil,

191
00:07:55.290 --> 00:07:58.260
or debris under the influence of gravity.

192
00:07:58.260 --> 00:08:00.570
This process is extremely important for shaping

193
00:08:00.570 --> 00:08:02.700
the coastlines as it moves the material

194
00:08:02.700 --> 00:08:05.400
that has slowly become weakened.

195
00:08:05.400 --> 00:08:07.680
The result is often really dramatic.

196
00:08:07.680 --> 00:08:11.430
Think about cliff collapses, landslides, or slumping slopes.

197
00:08:11.430 --> 00:08:14.280
At the coast, mass movement is influenced by factors

198
00:08:14.280 --> 00:08:17.010
like the type of rock, the slope's steepness,

199
00:08:17.010 --> 00:08:20.340
and the presence of water, such as after heavy rainfall.

200
00:08:20.340 --> 00:08:23.220
Understanding these processes is really important

201
00:08:23.220 --> 00:08:24.810
in helping us to understand

202
00:08:24.810 --> 00:08:27.390
how coastal landscapes constantly evolve,

203
00:08:27.390 --> 00:08:29.130
and for predicting and managing hazards

204
00:08:29.130 --> 00:08:30.543
in vulnerable areas.

205
00:08:32.400 --> 00:08:35.910
Rock falls occur when rocks or fragments of rock

206
00:08:35.910 --> 00:08:39.390
break away from a cliff face and fall directly to the base.

207
00:08:39.390 --> 00:08:41.820
This often happens for a number of reasons,

208
00:08:41.820 --> 00:08:44.100
and mainly because freeze-thaw weathering

209
00:08:44.100 --> 00:08:45.810
has weakened the rocks,

210
00:08:45.810 --> 00:08:48.720
or wave action has undercut the base of the cliff,

211
00:08:48.720 --> 00:08:52.530
and sometimes human activities, like construction or quarry,

212
00:08:52.530 --> 00:08:55.920
can trigger rock falls by destabilizing the cliff.

213
00:08:55.920 --> 00:08:58.290
The fallen material is called scree,

214
00:08:58.290 --> 00:09:00.240
and the scree piles up at the base,

215
00:09:00.240 --> 00:09:02.640
and can eventually be carried away by waves,

216
00:09:02.640 --> 00:09:05.373
further altering the cliffs and increasing erosion.

217
00:09:06.930 --> 00:09:09.150
Slumping is when material moves down a slope

218
00:09:09.150 --> 00:09:13.260
along a curved surface, and it happens like this.

219
00:09:13.260 --> 00:09:16.350
Heavy rainfall will infiltrate and saturate the cliff,

220
00:09:16.350 --> 00:09:19.080
making it really, really heavy.

221
00:09:19.080 --> 00:09:21.690
The saturated material will then move downwards

222
00:09:21.690 --> 00:09:24.543
under gravity along a curved slip plain within the cliff.

223
00:09:25.650 --> 00:09:27.780
The curved movement then means the material

224
00:09:27.780 --> 00:09:30.960
can tip back on itself to form what looks like terraces

225
00:09:30.960 --> 00:09:32.940
or steps at the top of the slump,

226
00:09:32.940 --> 00:09:35.610
like you can see in the image on the screen.

227
00:09:35.610 --> 00:09:37.890
The base of the slump is called the toe,

228
00:09:37.890 --> 00:09:40.560
and this is often eroded by waves.

229
00:09:40.560 --> 00:09:44.550
The slump often leaves a distinctive curved, concaved scar

230
00:09:44.550 --> 00:09:45.750
at the top of the cliff.

231
00:09:46.980 --> 00:09:49.050
Sliding is different from slumping.

232
00:09:49.050 --> 00:09:52.290
Here, blocks of rock or soil will move straight down a slope

233
00:09:52.290 --> 00:09:54.150
rather than in a curved motion,

234
00:09:54.150 --> 00:09:56.520
and this usually occurs along a bedding plane,

235
00:09:56.520 --> 00:09:59.940
which is a layer of weaker rock parallel to the slope.

236
00:09:59.940 --> 00:10:02.250
Sliding happens when the upper layers of the rock

237
00:10:02.250 --> 00:10:03.930
become saturated and heavy,

238
00:10:03.930 --> 00:10:06.510
causing them to slide over the weaker layer.

239
00:10:06.510 --> 00:10:09.240
This process is going to leave a jagged edge at the top

240
00:10:09.240 --> 00:10:11.940
and a large amount of debris at the base of the cliff.

241
00:10:15.450 --> 00:10:18.120
Disaster response teams rely heavily on geographic

242
00:10:18.120 --> 00:10:21.510
information systems, GIS, to effectively manage

243
00:10:21.510 --> 00:10:24.450
and coordinate their efforts during emergencies.

244
00:10:24.450 --> 00:10:27.390
GIS technology allows responders to map out the paths

245
00:10:27.390 --> 00:10:29.400
and impacts of natural disasters

246
00:10:29.400 --> 00:10:32.490
such as mass movement events, but in real time.

247
00:10:32.490 --> 00:10:34.080
By analyzing these maps,

248
00:10:34.080 --> 00:10:36.540
teams can identify the most affected areas,

249
00:10:36.540 --> 00:10:38.430
prioritize rescue operations,

250
00:10:38.430 --> 00:10:41.340
and allocate resources more efficiently.

251
00:10:41.340 --> 00:10:43.020
One example of this occurred during

252
00:10:43.020 --> 00:10:46.680
the devastating landslide in Sierra Leone in 2017.

253
00:10:46.680 --> 00:10:49.050
In August of that year, after heavy rainfall,

254
00:10:49.050 --> 00:10:51.390
a massive landslide struck the Regent area

255
00:10:51.390 --> 00:10:53.940
which is near the capital Freetown.

256
00:10:53.940 --> 00:10:56.520
This catastrophic event tragically resulted in the deaths

257
00:10:56.520 --> 00:11:01.200
of over 500 people and left approximately 3,000 homeless.

258
00:11:01.200 --> 00:11:04.920
GIS is really important in mapping the extent of disasters.

259
00:11:04.920 --> 00:11:07.080
It helps responders to identify areas

260
00:11:07.080 --> 00:11:09.180
that are buried under mud and debris,

261
00:11:09.180 --> 00:11:11.340
coordinates search and rescue missions,

262
00:11:11.340 --> 00:11:13.950
and assess which routes are still accessible.

263
00:11:13.950 --> 00:11:16.380
This mapping process helped disaster teams plan

264
00:11:16.380 --> 00:11:18.420
how to deliver aid to survivors

265
00:11:18.420 --> 00:11:21.090
and evacuate those in immediate danger.

266
00:11:21.090 --> 00:11:23.580
GIS maps were also used to estimate the scale

267
00:11:23.580 --> 00:11:26.040
of the destruction and assist in long-term recovery

268
00:11:26.040 --> 00:11:28.140
and rebuilding efforts.

269
00:11:28.140 --> 00:11:30.240
GIS plays a really important role

270
00:11:30.240 --> 00:11:32.310
in assisting in disaster response.

271
00:11:32.310 --> 00:11:34.620
It provides accurate real-time data,

272
00:11:34.620 --> 00:11:37.590
and it also shows teams how to respond more effectively,

273
00:11:37.590 --> 00:11:39.720
and ultimately save lives.

274
00:11:39.720 --> 00:11:42.180
The 2017 Sierra Leone landslide serves

275
00:11:42.180 --> 00:11:44.310
as a really good example of how this technology

276
00:11:44.310 --> 00:11:46.653
can be used in real-world emergencies.

277
00:11:47.880 --> 00:11:50.670
What is the key difference between sliding and slumping?

278
00:11:50.670 --> 00:11:53.400
Is it A: sliding involves rotational movement

279
00:11:53.400 --> 00:11:55.710
along a curved surface, while slumping occurs

280
00:11:55.710 --> 00:11:57.210
straight down a slope?

281
00:11:57.210 --> 00:12:00.060
Is it B: slumping involves a rotational movement

282
00:12:00.060 --> 00:12:01.470
along a curved surface,

283
00:12:01.470 --> 00:12:03.990
while sliding moves material down a slope?

284
00:12:03.990 --> 00:12:07.500
Or is it C: sliding occurs when rock falls off a cliff

285
00:12:07.500 --> 00:12:09.360
while slumping involves a rotational movement

286
00:12:09.360 --> 00:12:11.370
along a curved surface?

287
00:12:11.370 --> 00:12:13.260
Pause the video here whilst you decide,

288
00:12:13.260 --> 00:12:15.960
and press play when you're ready to check your answer.

289
00:12:20.640 --> 00:12:21.473
Excellent.

290
00:12:21.473 --> 00:12:25.110
The key difference between sliding and slumping is B.

291
00:12:25.110 --> 00:12:27.000
Slumping involves a rotational movement

292
00:12:27.000 --> 00:12:29.640
along a curved surface, while sliding moves material

293
00:12:29.640 --> 00:12:31.140
straight down a slope.

294
00:12:31.140 --> 00:12:33.840
Well done if you managed to get that correct.

295
00:12:33.840 --> 00:12:37.020
True or false: Rock falls occur when loose rocks

296
00:12:37.020 --> 00:12:39.450
and debris slide slowly down a slope

297
00:12:39.450 --> 00:12:41.460
due to the force of gravity?

298
00:12:41.460 --> 00:12:43.740
Pause the video here whilst you attempt this task,

299
00:12:43.740 --> 00:12:45.990
and press play when you're ready to continue.

300
00:12:50.970 --> 00:12:51.990
Excellent.

301
00:12:51.990 --> 00:12:54.210
This statement is false.

302
00:12:54.210 --> 00:12:57.390
I would now like you to explain why this statement is false.

303
00:12:57.390 --> 00:12:58.530
Pause the video here

304
00:12:58.530 --> 00:13:00.780
and press play when you're ready to continue.

305
00:13:06.810 --> 00:13:07.643
Excellent.

306
00:13:07.643 --> 00:13:10.500
The reason why this statement is false is because:

307
00:13:10.500 --> 00:13:12.060
Rock falls involve rock or debris

308
00:13:12.060 --> 00:13:14.700
falling freely from a steep slope or cliff,

309
00:13:14.700 --> 00:13:17.850
rather than sliding slowly down a cliff.

310
00:13:17.850 --> 00:13:18.683
Well done.

311
00:13:20.040 --> 00:13:21.690
The photo on the screen shows slumping

312
00:13:21.690 --> 00:13:23.460
at the cliffs of Happisburgh.

313
00:13:23.460 --> 00:13:25.620
I would now like you to explain the process

314
00:13:25.620 --> 00:13:28.080
of slumping at the coast.

315
00:13:28.080 --> 00:13:31.650
Izzy has cleverly identified that at the top of the cliff

316
00:13:31.650 --> 00:13:33.780
she can see the scar where the material

317
00:13:33.780 --> 00:13:36.180
has recently moved down from.

318
00:13:36.180 --> 00:13:38.580
Pause the video here whilst to attempt this task,

319
00:13:38.580 --> 00:13:40.830
and press play when you're ready to continue.

320
00:13:46.470 --> 00:13:49.230
Excellent. Let's check our answers.

321
00:13:49.230 --> 00:13:52.500
Your answer could include some of the following points.

322
00:13:52.500 --> 00:13:55.410
Slumping often happens after heavy rainfall.

323
00:13:55.410 --> 00:13:57.570
When water infiltrates into a cliff,

324
00:13:57.570 --> 00:13:59.850
it makes the material in the cliff heavier

325
00:13:59.850 --> 00:14:02.970
and reduces the cohesion holding the material together.

326
00:14:02.970 --> 00:14:05.790
The saturated material moves downwards under gravity

327
00:14:05.790 --> 00:14:08.610
along a curved slip plane within the cliff.

328
00:14:08.610 --> 00:14:11.760
This curved movement leaves a curved scar behind the slump,

329
00:14:11.760 --> 00:14:14.160
and this can be seen in the photo on the screen

330
00:14:14.160 --> 00:14:16.740
and it can tip the slump material back on itself

331
00:14:16.740 --> 00:14:19.710
to form what looks like steps or terraces.

332
00:14:19.710 --> 00:14:21.720
The base of the slump is called the toe,

333
00:14:21.720 --> 00:14:24.360
and this is often eroded by waves.

334
00:14:24.360 --> 00:14:26.640
Well done if you managed to answer this question correctly,

335
00:14:26.640 --> 00:14:28.690
and include some of the following points.

336
00:14:29.640 --> 00:14:32.220
This answer is good because it has clearly explained

337
00:14:32.220 --> 00:14:35.370
the process of slumping in a step-by-step process,

338
00:14:35.370 --> 00:14:37.320
and it has also referred back to the image

339
00:14:37.320 --> 00:14:38.820
that was in the question.

340
00:14:38.820 --> 00:14:40.053
Well done on this task.

341
00:14:41.310 --> 00:14:43.380
We've now come to the end of our lesson on weathering

342
00:14:43.380 --> 00:14:46.530
and mass movement at the coast, and you've done brilliantly.

343
00:14:46.530 --> 00:14:49.440
But let's summarize our lesson before we finish.

344
00:14:49.440 --> 00:14:51.600
Weathering and mass movement are key processes

345
00:14:51.600 --> 00:14:53.280
that shape the coast.

346
00:14:53.280 --> 00:14:55.950
Weathering breaks down rocks into smaller particles

347
00:14:55.950 --> 00:14:59.520
through physical, chemical, and biological processes.

348
00:14:59.520 --> 00:15:02.460
Mass movement is the downward movement of rock, soil,

349
00:15:02.460 --> 00:15:04.890
or debris due to gravity.

350
00:15:04.890 --> 00:15:07.833
Sliding, slumping, and rock falls are types of mass movement

351
00:15:07.833 --> 00:15:09.930
that are found at the coast.

352
00:15:09.930 --> 00:15:13.290
Together, weathering and mass movement gradually reshape

353
00:15:13.290 --> 00:15:15.090
the coastal landscapes that we know.

354
00:15:15.990 --> 00:15:17.700
I've really enjoyed learning with you today,

355
00:15:17.700 --> 00:15:19.600
and I look forward to our next lesson.

00:13:47.070 --> 00:13:49.800
Hard engineering, such as large sea walls or groynes,

359
00:13:49.800 --> 00:13:51.390
may protect infrastructure,

360
00:13:51.390 --> 00:13:53.490
but they could deter tourists

361
00:13:53.490 --> 00:13:55.320
if they are perceived as unattractive

362
00:13:55.320 --> 00:13:57.153
or if they reduce the beach size.

363
00:13:58.980 --> 00:14:00.690
Local residents priorities protecting

364
00:14:00.690 --> 00:14:02.130
their homes and livelihoods.

365
00:14:02.130 --> 00:14:04.530
They often advocate for immediate action

366
00:14:04.530 --> 00:14:06.480
to prevent erosion and flooding.

367
00:14:06.480 --> 00:14:09.213
Advocate means to speak up and to take action.

368
00:14:10.050 --> 00:14:12.480
Laura has noted that if no action is taken,

369
00:14:12.480 --> 00:14:15.330

370
00:14:15.330 --> 00:14:17.610
This can be really difficult, and she's right.

371
00:14:17.610 --> 00:14:19.740
It means that they might lose their community ties,

372
00:14:19.740 --> 00:14:22.110
their jobs, their homes, places where they've lived

373
00:14:22.110 --> 00:14:24.780
for many years, and where maybe their family grew up,

374
00:14:24.780 --> 00:14:26.830
which can be really emotionally draining.

375
00:14:27.690 --> 00:14:29.490
To resolve stakeholder conflict,

376
00:14:29.490 --> 00:14:31.740
an integrated coastal zone management approach

377
00:14:31.740 --> 00:14:33.270
is often used.

378
00:14:33.270 --> 00:14:35.130
This approach ensures that the economic,

379
00:14:35.130 --> 00:14:37.860
environmental, and community needs are balanced.

380
00:14:37.860 --> 00:14:39.930
Collaboration is extremely important

381
00:14:39.930 --> 00:14:41.400
in making sustainable decisions,

382
00:14:41.400 --> 00:14:43.680
especially when it involves coastal erosion

383
00:14:43.680 --> 00:14:45.663
and people's livelihoods and homes.

384
00:14:46.770 --> 00:14:48.390
Which of these stakeholder groups

385
00:14:48.390 --> 00:14:49.740
would be most likely to support

386
00:14:49.740 --> 00:14:52.350
hard engineering methods of coastal defenses?

387
00:14:52.350 --> 00:14:55.920
Is it A, environmentalists concerned about coastal habitats,

388
00:14:55.920 --> 00:14:59.040
B, residents campaign to protect houses from erosion,

389
00:14:59.040 --> 00:15:01.800
or C, local councils facing budget cuts?

390
00:15:01.800 --> 00:15:03.330
Pause the video here whilst you decide,

00:15:03.330 --> 00:15:05.543
and press play when you're ready to continue.

392
00:15:08.880 --> 00:15:09.713
Excellent.

393
00:15:09.713 --> 00:15:12.540
The answer is B, residents campaigning to protect

394
00:15:12.540 --> 00:15:14.780
houses from erosion are more likely to be in support

395
00:15:14.780 --> 00:15:16.413
of hard engineering methods.

396
00:15:17.490 --> 00:15:18.600
True or false?

397
00:15:18.600 --> 00:15:21.000
An integrated coastal zone management approach

398
00:15:21.000 --> 00:15:22.260
is focused on saving money

00:15:22.260 --> 00:15:24.540
by choosing the least expensive method.

400

Pause the video here whilst you decide

00:15:26.070 --> 00:15:27.720
if this statement is true or false,

and press play when you're ready to continue.

00:15:34.290 --> 00:15:36.600
Fantastic. This statement is false.

I would now like you to use the stakeholder statements below

to help you explain

00:16:05.070 --> 00:16:07.830
why there can be conflicting views about coastal management.

Let's take a look at the stakeholder statements.

A local resident has said, "34 houses have already gone,

and more at risk from erosion.

If we don't invest in coastal defenses, more will be lost!"

00:16:18.270 --> 00:16:20.400
A local business owner has said, "Protecting the coast

00:16:20.400 --> 00:16:23.550
is important for tourism and helps our economy grow."

424
00:16:23.550 --> 00:16:24.727
An environmentalist said,

00:16:24.727 --> 00:16:26.730
"I'm worried about the coastal management.

426
00:16:26.730 --> 00:16:28.140
Sea walls can harm wildlife

427
00:16:28.140 --> 00:16:30.750
and might cause erosion in other areas."

00:16:30.750 --> 00:16:33.180
Local councilor, "I don't think coastal management

00:16:33.180 --> 00:16:34.170
is a good idea.

00:16:34.170 --> 00:16:35.940
The costs are high and it won't stop erosion

00:16:35.940 --> 00:16:37.140
in the long run."

00:16:37.140 --> 00:16:38.790
Pause the video here whilst you explain

00:16:38.790 --> 00:16:41.340
why there can be conflicting views about coastal management,

00:16:41.340 --> 00:16:43.973
and press play when you're ready to check your answers.

00:16:47.460 --> 00:16:49.443
Fantastic work. Let's check our answer.

00:16:50.310 --> 00:16:53.400
Your answer might include some of the following points.

00:16:53.400 --> 00:16:55.890
One argument in favor of hard engineering defenses

00:16:55.890 --> 00:16:58.170
is that they would protect homes and businesses.

00:16:58.170 --> 00:16:59.400
According to one of the statements,

00:16:59.400 --> 00:17:00.777
34 houses have already been lost

Coastal defenses could also benefit tourism,

00:17:10.320 --> 00:17:12.000
which is important for the local economy,

as a second stakeholder points out.

00:17:14.010 --> 00:17:15.180
The area could lose income

if its beaches and attractions are damaged by erosion.

00:17:19.260 --> 00:17:20.520
However, there are concerns

00:17:20.520 --> 00:17:23.250
about the effectiveness and impact of these defenses.

00:17:23.250 --> 00:17:25.080
One stakeholder mentions that sea walls,

while protecting one area,

can cause increased erosion further along the coast.

00:17:29.160 --> 00:17:30.660
This means that solving one problem

could actually create another.

00:17:32.400 --> 00:17:34.080
Another issue is the cost.

457
00:17:34.080 --> 00:17:36.330
Building sea walls and other hard engineering defenses

00:17:36.330 --> 00:17:38.940
is expensive, and as another stakeholder suggests,

00:17:38.940 --> 00:17:40.860
it might not be a long-term solution,

00:17:40.860 --> 00:17:43.233
as erosion could continue despite the efforts.

461
00:17:44.280 --> 00:17:46.170
In conclusion, while coastal management

462
00:17:46.170 --> 00:17:49.170
could help protect homes and boost the local economy,

00:17:49.170 --> 00:17:51.000
the environmental risks and high costs

464
00:17:51.000 --> 00:17:52.830
make it a difficult choice.

465
00:17:52.830 --> 00:17:55.290
Investment in coastal defenses is clearly necessary

466
00:17:55.290 --> 00:17:57.330
to protect high-value locations,

00:17:57.330 --> 00:17:59.370
but it should be balanced with environmental protection

468
00:17:59.370 --> 00:18:00.780
and long-term planning.

00:18:00.780 --> 00:18:01.950
Soft engineering methods

00:18:01.950 --> 00:18:03.540
together with coastal management strategies

471
00:18:03.540 --> 00:18:04.740
of managed retreat

00:18:04.740 --> 00:18:06.360
can meet some of the needs of stakeholders

00:18:06.360 --> 00:18:09.630
in a way that reduces costs and environmental impacts.

474
00:18:09.630 --> 00:18:10.530
This answer is great

00:18:10.530 --> 00:18:12.840
because it's provided both a for and against argument

00:18:12.840 --> 00:18:14.070
for coastal management.

00:18:14.070 --> 00:18:16.560
It's given stakeholder-specific information,

00:18:16.560 --> 00:18:17.910
and then it's provided conclusion

479
00:18:17.910 --> 00:18:19.860
that summarizes all of its points.

480
00:18:19.860 --> 00:18:21.990
It also gives direction on how coastal management

481
00:18:21.990 --> 00:18:23.130
should be implemented,

482
00:18:23.130 --> 00:18:25.590
by both using hard and soft engineering methods

483
00:18:25.590 --> 00:18:27.270
to make sure it meets social, economic,

484
00:18:27.270 --> 00:18:28.980
and environmental needs.

485
00:18:28.980 --> 00:18:29.880
Well done on this task.

486
00:18:29.880 --> 00:18:31.680
You've done brilliantly.

487
00:18:31.680 --> 00:18:33.150
We've now come to the end of our lesson

488
00:18:33.150 --> 00:18:35.910
on costs and benefits of coastal management strategies.

489
00:18:35.910 --> 00:18:38.040
You've worked fantastically in today's lesson.

490
00:18:38.040 --> 00:18:40.860
Before we end, let's summarize what we've learned.

491
00:18:40.860 --> 00:18:42.900
Hard engineering methods, like sea walls,

492
00:18:42.900 --> 00:18:44.280
offer high levels of protection,

493
00:18:44.280 --> 00:18:47.580
but are expensive and can exacerbate erosion elsewhere.

494
00:18:47.580 --> 00:18:50.040
Soft engineering methods, such as beach nourishment,

00:18:50.040 --> 00:18:53.340
are more sustainable, but require ongoing maintenance.

496
00:18:53.340 --> 00:18:56.040
Managed retreat involves allowing selected areas

00:18:56.040 --> 00:18:57.870
of the coastline to erode or flood,

00:18:57.870 --> 00:19:00.000
creating habitats that provide natural protection

499
00:19:00.000 --> 00:19:02.643
from erosion and flooding for land further inland.

500
00:19:03.630 --> 00:19:05.670
Stakeholders, including local communities,

501
00:19:05.670 --> 00:19:07.470
environmentalists, and businesses,

502
00:19:07.470 --> 00:19:08.880
have different priorities,

503
00:19:08.880 --> 00:19:10.320
leading to a need for collaboration

504
00:19:10.320 --> 00:19:13.080
to address these varied interests effectively.

505
00:19:13.080 --> 00:19:15.870
Well done on this, and we've done brilliantly today.

506
00:19:15.870 --> 00:19:18.293
I look forward to learning with you again very soon.

lessons.lessonTitle: Glacial landforms resulting from erosion and deposition

lessonKeywords.description: when a glacier pulls chunks of rock from the bedrock as it moves over it
when rocks and debris carried by a glacier scrape and wear away the surface beneath it
a valley reshaped by glacial erosion into a U-shape
accumulation of unsorted debris, such as soil and rock, deposited by a glacier

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Glacial landscapes exhibit several distinctive landforms.
Distinctive landforms formed due to erosion including corries, aretes, pyramidal peaks, truncated spurs, glacial troughs
Distinctive landforms formed due to processes of transportation and deposition include erratics, drumlins and moraine.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Glacial erosion does create new landforms, but as glaciers transport and then deposit the eroded material, this also creates new landscapes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Glacial erosion is the only process that creates new landscapes.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the characteristics and formation of glacial landforms.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It is important to understand the role of erosional processes - abrasion and plucking - in creating the glacial landforms. Previous knowledge of erosion, transportation and deposition (e.g. rivers, coasts) may help students in this lesson.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, geographers.
My name's Mrs. Hormigo.
I'm really looking forward to teaching you today.
I hope you're going to learn lots and really enjoy the lesson.
Let's get started.
Today's lesson looks at the landforms created by erosion, transportation, and deposition.
By the end of the lesson, you'll understand the characteristics and the formation of glacial landforms. There are four key words for today's lesson, plucking, abrasion, glacial trough, and moraine.
Plucking is when a glacier pulls chunks of rock from the bedrock as it moves over it.
Abrasion is when rocks and debris carried by a glacier scrape and wear away the surface beneath it.
Glacial trough is a valley reshaped by glacial erosion into a U-shape.
And moraine is accumulation of unsorted debris such as soil and rock that is deposited by a glacier.
There are two parts to today's lesson, what landforms are created by glacial erosion and what landforms are created by glacial deposition.
Let's start by looking at what landforms are created by glacial erosion.
Glacial erosion creates dramatic landform by processes such as plucking and abrasion as glaciers carve through landscapes.
In this image here, you can see a pyramidal peak, an arete, and a corrie, all landforms created by glacial erosion.
A corrie is a bowl-shaped hollow that is found on the upper slopes of glaciated valleys, and it often contains a small lake known as a tarn or a cwm after glaciation.
You can see here in this image, this is Cwm Idwal in North Wales created by glaciers.
Let's look now at how a corrie develops.
So at the start of a glacial period, this is when the corrie begins to develop.
It often happens on north-facing slopes in the northern hemisphere, and this is because snow doesn't melt in the summer, it builds up instead.
So snow accumulates in sheltered hollows on the mountain side.
You can see there in that image.
Over time, it compresses into ice, so the layers build up and it compresses into ice.
During the glacial period, there'll be some free store weathering, steepening the back wall and adding debris.
Abrasion and plucking will deepen the hollow as the glacier moves slowly downhill.
And three, rotational slip will increase the erosion at the base of the corrie, making it deeper.
At the front of the corrie, the ice becomes thinner and erosion decreases, as there's less energy, a rock lip will develop.
After the glacial period, so as the glacier retreats, a steep-sided hollow will remain.
And this is the corrie.
It will often feature a lake called a tarn.
Erosion and weathering processes will continue to act on the steep back wall.
And after the glacier melts the rock lip traps water forming a small lake.
Check for you now, can you use numbers to correctly order the process of corrie formation? Pause the video and come back when you've decided.
I hope you put the third one as number one, the first one as number two, and the middle one as your final, number three.
Well done.
An arete is a sharp knife-edged ridge that forms between two corries or glaciated valleys.
And you can see on this air diagram here, there are three aretes separating these two different valleys.
A pyramidal peak is a pointed mountain peak that's formed when three or more corries erode back into a central point.
Mount Everest is an example of a pyramidal peak with aretes leading up to it.
Can you look at this photograph and identify the pyramidal peak and the aretes? Pause the video when you've labeled them correctly.
You should have picked out that there are two aretes leading up to Mount Everest in this image in Nepal.
And a pyramidal peak right at the summit.
Well done.
Glacial troughs or U-shaped valleys are formed when glacier's transform pre-existing V-shaped river valleys.
So as the glacier moves downhill, processes of erosion carve out the V-shaped valley to create a larger U-shaped valley.
You can see there in that first image, before glaciation takes place, a river has created a V-shaped valley.
During glaciation, as a glacier moves its immense weight and erosional processes deepen and widen the valley.
So it goes from that V-shaped to a U-shape, a wider bottom with steeper sides.
Then after glaciation, you can see there that as the ice retreats, you're left with that U-shaped valley or glacial trough.
Let's have a look at the characteristics of a glacial trough.
Steep, straight sides, wide, flat valley floors, and that characteristic U-shape.
Truncated spurs are found in glacial troughs.
They're formed when the interlocking spurs, which we can see in this image that are created by river erosion, are eroded away as the glacier advances.
So these interlocking spurs are part of the V-shaped valley formation before a glacier moves through.
After the glacier has been, you have the steep, cliff-like edges on the sides of the valley, and these are known as truncated spurs.
This is Llanberis Pass in North Wales, a very famous glacial trough.
Can you add annotations to describe its key characteristics? And can you label the truncated spurs? Pause the video and come back when you've had a go.
Your labels may look like this.
The flat wide valley bottom, the U-shape, the steep, straight valley sides, and the truncated spurs.
So the vertical cliff-like edges to the valley.
Well done.
Hanging valleys are formed by smaller tributary glaciers as they join the larger main one, they erode their valleys less deeply.
So when the ice melts, these valleys are almost left hanging above the main valley floor.
They're often marked by waterfalls where the river flowing through that tributary valley flows into the main valley.
